title: Java objects and ownership quiz
summary: Review Java pass-by-value, final references, dispatch, constructor rules and object equality through ownership questions.
body:
An object-ownership self-check tests copied reference values, polymorphic dispatch and stable equality contracts.

Review the contracts

Review copied references, method dispatch, equality and hashing before answering.

Choose and explain an answer

Draw the object references first. Then decide which declaration is selected at compilation and which implementation runs at runtime.

Select an answer for every question, then check the result and read each explanation. Progress remains in this browser; this is a self-check, not a judged program submission or a credential.

Common Mistakes

Reassigning a parameter does not reassign the caller's variable. A final reference can still point to mutable state.
subject: java-quizzes

questions.prompt: A method reassigns its reference parameter. What happens to the caller’s variable?
options: It still holds its original reference
questions.explanation: The parameter receives a copy of the reference value; assigning that local copy does not assign the caller’s variable.

questions.prompt: What does final prevent for a field referring to an array?
options: Reassigning the field after its permitted initialization
questions.explanation: The reference field cannot be reassigned, but the referenced array can still be mutable.

questions.prompt: An object returns its internal mutable list. Which boundary is lost?
questions.explanation: A caller can edit that returned list without passing through the owner’s validation methods.

questions.prompt: A base constructor calls an overridable method. Which state can that method observe?
options: Subtype fields before subtype initialization completes
questions.explanation: Virtual dispatch can reach subtype code while the base constructor is still running.

questions.prompt: Which operation receives runtime instance-method dispatch?
options: A static method hidden by another static method
A field with the same name in a subtype
questions.explanation: Instance-method overrides use the actual receiver type; static methods and fields follow other selection rules.

questions.prompt: Two interface defaults conflict. What must the implementing class do?
questions.explanation: The class must supply an implementation that resolves incompatible inherited defaults.

questions.prompt: What should a rejected reservation leave unchanged?
options: Every field participating in the reservation invariant
questions.explanation: A method promising rejection without mutation must validate before applying its compound state update.

questions.prompt: Does an unmodifiable outer list prevent mutation of an element object?
options: Only if the list is short
questions.explanation: The wrapper constrains list operations, not arbitrary mutation of referenced objects.

questions.prompt: A record holds int[] counts with no copying. Is it deeply immutable?
questions.explanation: The component reference can be final while the array contents remain mutable and exposed.

questions.prompt: Which check tests title membership by value?
questions.explanation: String.equals checks its represented value; reference equality can be accidentally true for interned values.

questions.prompt: A subtype rejects a previously valid parent input. What needs review?
questions.explanation: A caller using the parent type is entitled to the parent’s accepted behavior.

questions.prompt: What does an outer-array clone do for nested arrays?
options: Copies outer membership but shares referenced rows
questions.explanation: Array clone copies outer slots; the row objects need their own ownership decision.

title: Java generics and call boundaries quiz
summary: Check Java generic invariance, wildcard reads and writes, erasure and overloaded method selection.
body:
A generics self-check tests invariant containers, wildcard bounds and the compiler's choice of a method overload.

Review the contracts

Review generic bounds, overload selection, cast boundaries before answering.

Choose and explain an answer

Track the static type and captured bound instead of substituting a value observed in one run. Determine what the compiler can permit for every legal caller.

Select an answer for every question, then check the result and read each explanation. Progress remains in this browser; this is a self-check, not a judged program submission or a credential.

Common Mistakes

A List of one numeric subtype is not a List of every numeric subtype. A cast does not validate each generic element.
subject: java-quizzes

questions.prompt: Can List<Integer> be assigned to List<Number>?
questions.explanation: Generic list declarations are invariant; permitting the assignment would allow incompatible values to be inserted.

questions.prompt: What can be read from List<? extends Number> without a cast?
questions.explanation: The bound supplies a readable Number contract without identifying the concrete captured subtype.

questions.prompt: What is generally safe to add to List<? super Integer>?
questions.explanation: The list accepts Integer or its subtypes under the lower-bound contract; reads have only the general Object type.

questions.prompt: Does a readable wildcard freeze list membership through other aliases?
questions.explanation: Variance constrains this source-level reference; it does not change the object’s ownership or mutability.

questions.prompt: Why is new T[10] unavailable for an ordinary erased type parameter?
options: The runtime array element type is not generally available
questions.explanation: Java arrays check their runtime component type, while the erased type parameter does not generally supply that type.

questions.prompt: What can raw-list insertion cause at a later typed read?
options: A guaranteed compiler error at runtime
Automatic conversion to the type argument
questions.explanation: Unchecked code can pollute a generic structure, leaving a cast failure when a typed consumer retrieves the value.

questions.prompt: Overloaded calls are selected using what initial information?
questions.explanation: Compile-time overload selection precedes runtime dispatch of an applicable overridden instance method.

questions.prompt: For List<Integer>, which call explicitly removes the first value 2?
questions.explanation: The boxed argument selects the value-removal overload rather than the index-removal overload.

questions.prompt: What is the result of narrowing the int value 260 to byte?
questions.explanation: The narrowing conversion retains the low-order bits; it does not enforce the original numeric range.

questions.prompt: Where should widening occur to avoid an int addition overflowing?
options: On an operand before the addition
questions.explanation: The operand types determine the arithmetic operation before the destination assignment occurs.

questions.prompt: Does a reference cast create a second object?
questions.explanation: A reference cast checks type compatibility; it does not copy or convert the referenced object’s fields.

questions.prompt: What is null unboxing into int?
questions.explanation: Unboxing calls the wrapper’s value conversion; a null wrapper cannot supply that value.

title: Java stream contracts quiz
summary: Review Java stream demand, reuse, encounter order, collectors and reduction laws through explained contract questions.
body:
A stream self-check tests lazy demand, one-use pipelines, encounter order and reduction contracts.

Review the contracts

Review stream execution, reduction contracts, gatherer state before answering.

Choose and explain an answer

Identify the terminal operation and any state shared across callbacks. Decide whether the result depends on ordering or a valid associative reduction.

Select an answer for every question, then check the result and read each explanation. Progress remains in this browser; this is a self-check, not a judged program submission or a credential.

Common Mistakes

A stream is not a cached collection. Parallel execution does not repair shared mutable state or an invalid reduction rule.
subject: java-quizzes

questions.prompt: Creating map/filter operations ordinarily starts traversal when?
options: When a terminal operation demands it
Only after the stream is cloned
questions.explanation: Intermediate operations describe a lazy computation; a terminal operation supplies demand.

questions.prompt: Can a stream be used for two separate terminal operations?
options: Yes; the second result is cached
Only if the first result is empty
questions.explanation: A stream is a one-use pipeline; its collection source can usually supply a new pipeline.

questions.prompt: Must a mapping callback run for every element during count?
options: Only when the mapper returns int
No, the terminal may avoid unnecessary work
questions.explanation: An implementation can exploit known sizing when the mapping does not affect the requested count.

questions.prompt: What does toMap need when two elements produce the same key?
options: A duplicate-key decision such as a merge function
questions.explanation: The collector must resolve duplicates under an explicit policy or can reject the duplicate mapping.

questions.prompt: A maximum over an empty integer stream returns which ordinary result type?
questions.explanation: There is no selected element; optional results represent that absence without inventing a value.

questions.prompt: Which identity is neutral for integer sum?
questions.explanation: A sum identity must leave a combined sum unchanged; a non-neutral value can be applied separately to partitions.

questions.prompt: Does parallel execution make a captured ArrayList safe for concurrent additions?
questions.explanation: A parallel pipeline does not change the thread-safety contract of external mutable storage.

questions.prompt: Does a preserved encounter-order result imply callbacks ran in that order?
questions.explanation: Execution order and the ordering of the final result are separate guarantees.

questions.prompt: What happens to mutable elements collected into a new list?
options: Their references can still be shared
questions.explanation: Collection membership can be new without changing the ownership of the referenced element objects.

questions.prompt: When does a file-backed stream need a close owner?
options: Across the scope consuming that resource-backed stream
questions.explanation: Resource-backed sources can hold handles after stream creation and need an owning cleanup scope.

questions.prompt: Why is associativity required for a parallel combining rule?
options: It guarantees a fixed thread count
It makes any side effect safe
Partition grouping must not change the required result
questions.explanation: Parallel reduction can group partial results differently; the combining rule must tolerate that grouping under its stated semantics.

questions.prompt: What storage grows during grouping by many distinct keys?
options: Only one counter regardless of keys
questions.explanation: Grouping materializes state per distinct key unless a different bounded aggregation policy is defined.

title: Java concurrency and completion quiz
summary: Check Java task admission, queue bounds, atomics, cancellation and worker shutdown with explained concurrency answers.
body:
A concurrency self-check tests admission, visibility, atomic transitions, cancellation and completion boundaries.

Review the contracts

Review task admission, cancellation and completion, bounded pending work before answering.

Choose and explain an answer

Ask what event the code actually observes: queued, started, stopped, or completed. Identify the owner of every shared transition.

Select an answer for every question, then check the result and read each explanation. Progress remains in this browser; this is a self-check, not a judged program submission or a credential.

Common Mistakes

A cancelled future does not prove a remote side effect was rolled back. A worker count does not bound an unbounded pending queue.
subject: java-quizzes

questions.prompt: Does volatile make count++ atomic?
questions.explanation: The read, addition and write are still a compound sequence; visibility does not make that sequence indivisible.

questions.prompt: What does timed Future.get bound?
questions.explanation: A timed wait can end while the task continues unless another stopping policy is applied.

questions.prompt: Does cancel(true) prove the worker has already released all resources?
questions.explanation: Cancellation requests interruption; an independent completion or exit observation is needed for cleanup.

questions.prompt: What must follow a failed Semaphore.tryAcquire?
options: No release for that rejected attempt
questions.explanation: Releasing an unacquired permit expands the accounted capacity.

questions.prompt: Why is a condition predicate checked in a loop?
options: A loop makes the lock optional
Wakeups and competing consumers require rechecking protected state
questions.explanation: A signalled or spuriously awakened thread must reacquire the lock and verify the predicate before consuming state.

questions.prompt: Which lock should protect a condition’s predicate update?
options: No lock if signal is called
The same associated lock used while waiting
questions.explanation: The predicate observation and state change must participate in one coordination policy.

questions.prompt: Does a fixed worker count bound an ordinary fixed pool’s pending queue?
options: Only when submit returns a Future
questions.explanation: Worker count and pending-work capacity are separate admission limits.

questions.prompt: What does successful submit prove?
options: The task was admitted under that executor’s contract
questions.explanation: Execution and task failure occur after admission and must be observed separately.

questions.prompt: What happens if an exception escapes an ordinary periodic scheduled task?
options: The executor must shut the JVM down
Later periodic executions can be suppressed
questions.explanation: The scheduled future exposes the failure; periodic continuation is not automatic after an escaping failure.

questions.prompt: Does a concurrent map make check-then-remove a single atomic operation?
questions.explanation: Use a specified conditional operation when a key and expected value form one claim.

questions.prompt: What is a CopyOnWriteArrayList iterator’s membership view?
options: A deep copy of all listeners
The snapshot array at iterator creation
questions.explanation: The cursor retains the earlier array state while element objects can still be shared.

questions.prompt: What does shutdownNow guarantee about uncooperative code?
options: It rolls back all remote effects
It does not guarantee forced task termination
questions.explanation: Interruption requests and returned pending tasks still require a cooperative cleanup policy.

title: Java input, files and network quiz
summary: Review Java validation, Unicode encoding, stream closure, partial I/O and HTTP failure policies.
body:
An input and I/O self-check tests parsing, character encoding, file ownership and network failure boundaries.

Review the contracts

Review input validation, encoding boundaries, partial file I/O before answering.

Choose and explain an answer

Distinguish bytes from characters and parsing from business validation. Check partial reads, truncated output and who closes each resource.

Select an answer for every question, then check the result and read each explanation. Progress remains in this browser; this is a self-check, not a judged program submission or a credential.

Common Mistakes

A successful read can return fewer bytes than requested. Parsed input can still violate the operation's business range.
subject: java-quizzes

questions.prompt: After nextInt, why can nextLine return an empty remainder?
options: The current line ending has not been consumed as another record
questions.explanation: Token parsing and whole-line parsing consume different boundaries.

questions.prompt: What unit does String.length count?
questions.explanation: A supplementary code point can occupy two UTF-16 units and multiple code points can form one displayed unit.

questions.prompt: What does NFC normalization address?
options: Canonical sequence equivalence under the selected normal form
questions.explanation: Normalization has a text-equivalence purpose and is not a universal sanitization or security policy.

questions.prompt: Which Matcher operation asks for a full-input match?
questions.explanation: find searches for a matching region; matches applies the pattern to the full current region.

questions.prompt: When are captured groups ordinarily readable?
questions.explanation: A group lookup requires valid match state.

questions.prompt: What does ByteBuffer.flip do after writing into a buffer?
options: Sets the readable limit and resets position
questions.explanation: flip changes buffer state for reading; it is not an I/O flush operation.

questions.prompt: Does one file-channel read guarantee a complete header?
questions.explanation: Transfers can be partial; record parsing must verify the required bytes were obtained.

questions.prompt: What does TCP preserve?
questions.explanation: An application framing rule is needed because stream reads do not preserve message boundaries.

questions.prompt: Does connect timeout also bound every later socket read?
questions.explanation: Connection establishment and subsequent reads have separate timeout boundaries.

questions.prompt: Is an HTTP 404 necessarily a transport exception?
options: No; it can be a received HTTP response
questions.explanation: Status-aware handling is separate from connection or transport failure.

questions.prompt: What does readAllLines retain for a large file?
questions.explanation: A streaming parser is needed when full materialization would exceed the accepted memory budget.

questions.prompt: Does a file move alone certify crash-durable persistence?
questions.explanation: Durability, atomic replacement capability and concurrent-writer behavior need explicit filesystem and application decisions.

title: Java algorithm invariants quiz
summary: Check Java tree ordering, trie membership, graph traversal, heap operations and algorithm invariants.
body:
An algorithm self-check tests progress, ordering, graph reachability and the invariants that justify a result.

Review the contracts

Review tree ordering, prefix membership, heap ordering before answering.

Choose and explain an answer

State the invariant before predicting the output. Separate a membership test from prefix reachability and a priority queue from sorted traversal.

Select an answer for every question, then check the result and read each explanation. Progress remains in this browser; this is a self-check, not a judged program submission or a credential.

Common Mistakes

A heap need not be globally sorted. A reachable trie prefix is not necessarily a stored complete key.
subject: java-quizzes

questions.prompt: What keeps AVL search height logarithmic?
questions.explanation: The height difference bound must be restored during updates; sorted input alone does not balance a tree.

questions.prompt: Does a trie prefix path prove the prefix is a stored word?
options: No; a terminal marker is separate
questions.explanation: Membership and prefix reachability answer different questions.

questions.prompt: Is a binary heap backing array fully sorted?
questions.explanation: The heap invariant orders parents against children; it does not totally sort array positions.

questions.prompt: What does KMP fallback reuse?
options: A proper prefix that matches an already seen suffix
questions.explanation: The prefix relation avoids restarting all earlier comparisons after a mismatch.

questions.prompt: What does Kruskal return on disconnected input under the forest contract?
options: A shortest path from vertex zero
questions.explanation: Disconnected components cannot be joined without edges; the result remains a forest.

questions.prompt: Which weights can Kruskal accept for connection cost?
questions.explanation: The cycle constraint and sorted edge selection do not require non-negative link cost.

questions.prompt: What invalidates single-source finite distances in Bellman–Ford?
options: A negative cycle reachable from the source
questions.explanation: Reachable negative cycles permit further distance improvement; an unreachable cycle cannot affect this source’s routes.

questions.prompt: Why must Dijkstra’s standard method reject negative edges?
options: Its settled-distance argument requires non-negative extension costs
questions.explanation: A negative edge can undermine the greedy distance ordering used by the standard algorithm.

questions.prompt: What dependency makes ascending quantity tabulation valid?
options: Every positive pack leads to a smaller quantity
questions.explanation: The recurrence can read already computed smaller states when every transition size is positive.

questions.prompt: What does earliest-finish interval selection optimize here?
options: Minimum waiting time for all jobs
questions.explanation: The exchange proof applies to the count objective, not automatically to weighted profit or another schedule objective.

questions.prompt: Can an interval beginning at the previous finish be accepted under half-open intervals?
options: Only if it has zero duration
questions.explanation: The previous endpoint is excluded under the stated [start,end) convention.

questions.prompt: Why is get(i) for all LinkedList positions potentially quadratic?
options: The size method must walk all nodes
Each index can trigger another traversal
questions.explanation: Summing repeated position searches can revisit links many times compared with one iterator traversal.

title: Java test boundaries: injected collaborators and behavior-focused checks
summary: An injected collaborator lets a test supply a controlled dependency while checking the caller’s validation, result and failure contract.
body:
An injected collaborator lets a test supply a controlled dependency while checking the caller’s validation, result and failure contract.

Java 8+. This is a complete program using JDK classes.

Replace the dependency, not the assertion

A quote operation needs a supplier amount and adds a fixed fee. The test supplies a deterministic gateway, so it does not depend on network access. A second gateway throws an I/O failure, letting the test verify that failure remains visible to the caller.

Another check passes an invalid destination and a gateway that must never be called. That verifies validation occurs before external work. It is a behavior requirement, not an assertion about private helper names or the number of internal methods.

This hand-written test double needs no mocking framework. A framework can create doubles for larger APIs, but the meaningful decision is still what behavior the application promises. A stubbed collaborator also does not replace a separate integration test against the real protocol.

Working program

import java.io.IOException;
public class QuoteBoundaryChecks {
    interface Gateway{int amount(String destination)throws IOException;}
    static int total(String destination,Gateway gateway)throws IOException{
        if(destination==null||destination.trim().isEmpty())throw new IllegalArgumentException("Missing destination");
        int base=gateway.amount(destination);
        if(base<0)throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative quote");
        return Math.addExact(base,10);
    }
    public static void main(String[] args)throws Exception{
        if(total("Delhi",destination->90)!=100)throw new AssertionError("Fee changed");
        try{total("",destination->{throw new AssertionError("Invalid request called gateway");});throw new AssertionError("Missing destination accepted");}
        catch(IllegalArgumentException expected){ }
        try{total("Delhi",destination->{throw new IOException("Supplier unavailable");});throw new AssertionError("Failure hidden");}
        catch(IOException expected){ }
        try{total("Delhi",destination->-1);throw new AssertionError("Negative quote accepted");}
        catch(IllegalArgumentException expected){ }
        System.out.println("4 gateway checks passed");
    }
}

Output

4 gateway checks passed

Costs and boundaries

These tests do constant-sized local work; a real gateway contributes I/O, queueing and decoding costs. Controlled doubles isolate application behavior but cannot measure external latency, wire compatibility or the supplier’s own validation. Checked arithmetic preserves the overflow boundary when adding a fee.

Common Mistakes

  • A fake success response is not a protocol integration test.
  • Test doubles should implement the dependency contract the caller actually uses.
  • Do not make tests pass merely by mirroring the private implementation.

Read next

Executable tests, Local HTTP integration.

Apply this contract in Spring

Spring tests: separate business rules, wiring and transport, Spring ApplicationContextRunner: check conditional assembly in isolation. These lessons keep framework assembly separate from the Java contract.

title: Java parameterized tests: boundary cases without arithmetic overflow
summary: A parameterized test applies one stated behavior to several input cases while keeping each failing case identifiable in the runner.
body:
A parameterized test applies one stated behavior to several input cases while keeping each failing case identifiable in the runner.

Java 21+. These tests require JUnit Jupiter 5.11.0; the downloadable Maven project declares it.

Choose boundaries that distinguish implementations

The packing function returns the number of vehicles needed for a non-negative parcel count and a positive capacity. The common expression (parcels + capacity - 1) / capacity can overflow before division. Division plus a remainder check keeps the valid maximum-int input representable.

The valid table includes zero, an exact multiple, one over capacity and Integer.MAX_VALUE. The invalid table verifies negative parcel count and non-positive capacity. Adding many repeated ordinary cases would not distinguish the overflowing formula from this implementation.

This sample uses JUnit Jupiter 5.11.0 in the downloadable Maven project. The annotation API requires the matching test dependencies and runner; copying the Java file alone into a plain javac invocation does not make it executable.

Working program

import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.CsvSource;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;
public class PackingBoundaryTest {
    static int vehicles(int parcels,int capacity){
        if(parcels<0||capacity<=0)throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid packing inputs");
        return parcels/capacity+(parcels%capacity==0?0:1);
    }
    @ParameterizedTest
    @CsvSource({"0,4,0","1,4,1","8,4,2","9,4,3","2147483647,2,1073741824"})
    void validInputs(int parcels,int capacity,int expected){assertEquals(expected,vehicles(parcels,capacity));}
    @ParameterizedTest
    @CsvSource({"-1,4","1,0","1,-4"})
    void rejectsInvalidInputs(int parcels,int capacity){assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,()->vehicles(parcels,capacity));}
}

Runner contract

The JUnit runner evaluates five valid cases and three rejected-input cases.

Costs and boundaries

Each calculation is O(1) work and storage. The test table verifies specified boundaries rather than performance. JUnit assertions execute without the JVM -ea flag. A parameterized runner reports individual invocations so the maximum-int failure can be identified directly.

Common Mistakes

  • The addition-based ceiling formula can overflow.
  • A Java annotation alone does not install a test runner.
  • Do not replace rejection checks with a print-only catch block.

Read next

Test runner setup, Arithmetic representation.

title: Java Gradle multi-project build: source ownership and a verified application task
summary: A Gradle multi-project build gives separately named projects their own source sets and connects them through explicit project dependencies.
body:
A Gradle multi-project build gives separately named projects their own source sets and connects them through explicit project dependencies.

Java 21+. This is a complete program using JDK classes.

Separate the billing rule from its caller

The downloadable build has a billing library and an app project. The library owns the checked quantity-times-price operation. The app depends on that library and supplies the command-line entry point. Keeping the rule in one source set avoids compiling slightly different copied formulas in several applications.

Both projects target the Java 21 toolchain in the supplied Gradle 8.10.2 build. The application plugin names the main class. A toolchain chooses a Java installation for compilation or execution; setting source syntax alone is not the same decision.

The root settings file includes both projects. The app’s implementation dependency names the billing project. The included command runs the application task and prints the same result as the standalone Java rule below. No external dependency is required by this two-project fixture.

Keep reproducibility outside IDE state

Use a declared build and pinned tool version so another machine can reconstruct source roots and the dependency graph. A Gradle wrapper is convenient when included; this kit declares Gradle 8.10.2 and documents the installed-tool command rather than claiming a wrapper binary is present.

A dependency lock or verification policy is useful when external libraries are added. This fixture has only a local project dependency, so it makes no claim about a production dependency audit, cached repository availability or a published artifact.

Working program

package in.aitrove.billing;
public class BillingRule {
    public static long total(int quantity,long unitCents){
        if(quantity<0||unitCents<0)throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative billing input");
        return Math.multiplyExact((long)quantity,unitCents);
    }
    public static void main(String[] args){System.out.println(total(3,50));}
}

Output

150

Costs and boundaries

The billing calculation is O(1). Build configuration, compilation and startup have separate costs dependent on source changes and the build environment. The two-project fixture verifies dependency wiring and launch; it does not measure incremental-build performance.

Common Mistakes

  • An IDE project layout is not a portable build declaration.
  • Source compatibility and toolchain selection are different settings.
  • Do not promise that an omitted wrapper is bundled.

Read next

Maven project setup, Boundary tests.

Build files and command

The settings.gradle file includes billing and app. Run the application with the declared Gradle version from the extracted gradle-multi directory.

rootProject.name = 'aitrove-billing'
include 'billing', 'app'
plugins { id 'application' }
java { toolchain { languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21) } }
dependencies { implementation project(':billing') }
application { mainClass = 'in.aitrove.app.Main' }
gradle :app:run --console=plain

title: Java JMH benchmarks: consumed results, fixtures and limited measurements
summary: JMH is a benchmarking runner that controls repeated measurements, warmup and JVM forks while keeping benchmark results observable to the runner.
body:
JMH is a benchmarking runner that controls repeated measurements, warmup and JVM forks while keeping benchmark results observable to the runner.

Java 21+. This benchmark requires JMH 1.37 and its annotation processor; the downloadable Maven project declares them.

Choose a question the fixture can answer

This benchmark compares exact integer membership in a HashSet and an ArrayList for declared sizes and lookup keys. Setup constructs both structures outside the measured method. Returning the boolean result keeps the lookup result observable instead of measuring a discarded computation.

The parameters include a present and an absent key under the selected sizes. A missing lookup scans more of the list than an early present lookup, so one carefully chosen hit cannot establish a universal container ranking. Input distribution belongs in the report.

The source is compiled with JMH 1.37 and its annotation processor in the downloadable Maven project. The processor generates runner metadata. A plain Java main with a nanoTime loop does not provide the same runner or isolation.

Separate smoke verification from a useful experiment

The local check uses one short warmup and measurement iteration to verify the packaged runner can run. Those numbers are not published as a performance conclusion. A useful experiment needs longer measurements, more forks, representative inputs, error estimates and stated JVM and hardware settings.

Dead-code elimination, constant folding, allocation and retained state can change what is measured. The thread-scoped fixture declares per-worker ownership. If the real application shares one contended structure, that is a different benchmark and needs a different state scope and operation mix.

Working program

package in.aitrove.bench;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
@State(Scope.Thread)
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
public class MembershipBenchmark {
    @Param({"64","4096"}) public int size;
    @Param({"63","8192"}) public int key;
    Set<Integer> indexed;List<Integer> scanned;
    @Setup public void prepare(){
        indexed=new HashSet<>();scanned=new ArrayList<>();
        for(int value=0;value<size;value++){indexed.add(value);scanned.add(value);}
    }
    @Benchmark public boolean indexedLookup(){return indexed.contains(key);}
    @Benchmark public boolean scannedLookup(){return scanned.contains(key);}
}

Measurement result

Measured scores depend on the selected parameters, JVM, machine and measurement configuration.

Costs and boundaries

Fixture construction and retained storage are O(n) for n inserted values. A list membership scan is O(n); hash membership has expected constant lookup work under its normal assumptions. Actual nanoseconds and allocation behavior require measurement and are not supplied as universal facts here.

  • Setup work should be included or excluded according to the question, not by accident.

title: Java access boundaries: private nests and protected receivers
summary: Java access control checks both the member declaration and the context of its use; inheriting a protected member does not make it publicly accessible through every receiver.
body:
Java access control checks both the member declaration and the context of its use; inheriting a protected member does not make it publicly accessible through every receiver.

Java 8+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

Separate inheritance from access

A delivery adapter extends a base class in another package. The adapter can access an inherited protected field through its own compatible receiver, but a general base-typed object does not automatically qualify. Code that worked inside the base package can therefore fail after it is moved into the adapter package.

Package-private access has no modifier. A child class in a different package cannot use that access as if it were protected. Public access also depends on the enclosing type being accessible; a public method on an inaccessible implementation type is not a substitute for a public interface.

Private members are accessible within the enclosing nest of classes. This program uses two nested classes that belong to one top-level declaration. It proves that case; it does not prove that any unrelated class in the same package can read the private field. The downloadable access-packages fixture checks the cross-package protected cases with both successful and rejected compilations.

Review the boundary before changing visibility

If a consumer needs a delivery status, expose a status operation with a return contract. Publishing the mutable internal queue merely to make one compiler error disappear lets callers bypass the adapter’s invariants. A package layout is useful when it separates ownership, not when every member is made public to remove friction.

Working program

public class NestAccessReceipt {
    static class Receipt { private final int accepted = 7; }
    static class Audit { static int read(Receipt receipt) { return receipt.accepted; } }
    public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(Audit.read(new Receipt())); }
}

Output

7

Costs and boundaries

The field access itself is constant work. Package and access decisions are checked when code is compiled and linked; they are not collection traversal costs. The multi-file kit includes a subclass in another package and verifies that a base-typed protected receiver is rejected.

Common Mistakes

  • Being in a subclass does not grant arbitrary cross-package protected access.
  • An unrelated same-package class does not share a private nest.
  • Visibility is not a thread-safety rule.

title: Java grapheme boundaries: truncate display text without splitting a cluster
summary: An extended grapheme cluster is a text segment used for character-boundary analysis; its UTF-16 length can be greater than one and its display width is not fixed.
body:
An extended grapheme cluster is a text segment used for character-boundary analysis; its UTF-16 length can be greater than one and its display width is not fixed.

Java 25+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

Choose the unit before truncating

A receipt label can contain a base character followed by a combining accent. Cutting after one UTF-16 unit can leave the accent behind. A supplementary symbol uses a surrogate pair, so even counting code points does not settle every displayed-character boundary.

This Java 25 fixture asks the character BreakIterator for boundaries, then keeps a declared number of clusters. The returned index is still a UTF-16 offset suitable for substring. The program uses a composed-looking sequence with a combining mark and checks its first segment. It also checks a supplementary symbol followed by a letter.

Cluster segmentation is not text shaping. A cluster can occupy several columns, and its appearance depends on font and rendering. A label limited by pixels needs measurement in the UI, not just a server-side cluster count. Java and Unicode data versions must also be part of reproducible text-processing tests.

Own the iterator state

BreakIterator holds the text being analyzed and a current position. Give an operation its own instance rather than sharing a single cursor among requests. Preserve the original label when building a shortened display string; do not overwrite the canonical stored value with a presentation limit.

Working program

import java.text.BreakIterator;
import java.util.Locale;
public class ReceiptLabelClusters {
    static String prefix(String text,int limit){
        if(limit<0)throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative cluster limit");
        java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(text);
        BreakIterator boundaries=BreakIterator.getCharacterInstance(Locale.ROOT);
        boundaries.setText(text);int end=boundaries.first();
        for(int count=0;count<limit;count++){
            int next=boundaries.next();if(next==BreakIterator.DONE)return text;end=next;
        }
        return text.substring(0,end);
    }
    public static void main(String[] args){
        String label="e\u0301clair";
        System.out.println(prefix(label,1).length());
        System.out.println(prefix("\ud83d\ude00X",1).length());
        System.out.println(prefix(label,0).isEmpty());
        System.out.println(prefix(label,20).equals(label));
    }
}

Output

2
2
true
true

Costs and boundaries

Boundary analysis examines text; budget for work proportional to the analyzed input rather than treating a character limit as a free operation. The returned substring allocates its result. This fixture targets the Java 25 character-boundary contract; it does not establish identical segmentation on every earlier runtime or font.

Common Mistakes

  • String.length counts UTF-16 units, not display clusters.
  • A cluster count is not a pixel-width limit.
  • Do not reuse a mutable iterator concurrently.

title: Java collation: display order and distinct stored labels
summary: Collation compares natural-language strings under a locale and strength policy; comparator equality can group labels that String.equals still treats as different.
body:
Collation compares natural-language strings under a locale and strength policy; comparator equality can group labels that String.equals still treats as different.

Java 8+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

Sorting is not identifier equality

A customer directory can sort labels without treating every case or accent difference as a new primary position. That is a presentation decision. An account identifier still needs its own exact or normalized equality contract; using the directory comparator as a map-key rule can merge accounts that should remain distinct.

The program uses a French collator at primary strength. It compares two labels that differ by an accent and then shows the membership effect in TreeSet. The second set adds a UTF-16 tie-break so comparator-equivalent spellings remain separate values. The set is ordered by that combined rule, not just by the collator.

The locale is explicit. A default-locale comparison can change when the application moves to a machine with another language setting. Locale data can also change across JDK releases. Store stable identifiers independently of the user’s display order, and state the runtime when a test asserts a particular ordering.

Treat configuration as owned state

Collator configuration includes strength and decomposition mode. Configure an instance before using it in a sorted collection, then keep that rule fixed for the collection’s lifetime. Changing a comparator’s behavior after insertion can invalidate search assumptions even if no label object changed.

Working program

import java.text.Collator;
import java.util.*;
public class CustomerDirectoryOrder {
    public static void main(String[] args){
        Collator french=Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRENCH);french.setStrength(Collator.PRIMARY);
        String first="cote",second="c\u00f4te";
        TreeSet<String> grouped=new TreeSet<>((a,b)->french.compare(a,b));
        grouped.add(first);grouped.add(second);
        Comparator<String> distinct=(a,b)->{int compared=french.compare(a,b);return compared!=0?compared:a.compareTo(b);};
        TreeSet<String> labels=new TreeSet<>(distinct);labels.add(first);labels.add(second);
        System.out.println(french.compare(first,second)==0);
        System.out.println(grouped.size());System.out.println(labels.size());
    }
}

Output

true
1
2

Costs and boundaries

A comparison examines the strings under the chosen locale rules. Sorting performs O(n log n) comparisons for n labels, with text-processing costs inside each comparison. A tie-break preserves distinct spellings but does not create a universal cross-version collation order.

Common Mistakes

  • Comparator equality can collapse TreeSet membership.
  • The machine’s default locale is not an explicit application policy.
  • Do not change comparator settings after insertion.

title: Java identifier input: explicit alphabets and normalized display text
summary: A machine identifier policy defines the accepted alphabet, length and equality rule before a value enters a key or path boundary.
body:
A machine identifier policy defines the accepted alphabet, length and equality rule before a value enters a key or path boundary.

Java 8+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

Keep display labels separate

A parcel reference used in a protocol can be restricted to uppercase ASCII letters, digits and hyphens. That narrow policy rejects visually similar characters from other scripts because they are outside the declared alphabet. It is appropriate for this reference field, not a rule for every person’s name.

Unicode normalization does not itself solve look-alike identifiers. Two characters can look similar while remaining different after normalization. Conversely, a compatibility normalization can merge distinctions the application intended to preserve. Decide whether the field is a human label or a protocol key before applying transformations.

The validator rejects lowercase input instead of silently changing it. A different service can choose uppercase canonicalization, but it must apply the same rule on creation and lookup and check collisions under that rule. This example also rejects an empty value, an overlong value and separators at the ends.

Validate before publishing

The function returns the accepted value without touching shared state. If validation fails, the caller has no partially registered reference to undo. That order matters when registration also writes an index, audit record or filesystem path. Accepted syntax still needs authorization and uniqueness checks in the service using it.

Working program

public class ParcelReferencePolicy {
    static String accept(String reference){
        if(reference==null||reference.length()<3||reference.length()>24)throw new IllegalArgumentException("Reference length");
        if(reference.charAt(0)=='-'||reference.charAt(reference.length()-1)=='-')throw new IllegalArgumentException("Separator position");
        for(int i=0;i<reference.length();i++){
            char c=reference.charAt(i);if(!((c>='A'&&c<='Z')||(c>='0'&&c<='9')||c=='-'))throw new IllegalArgumentException("Reference alphabet");
        }return reference;
    }
    public static void main(String[] args){
        System.out.println(accept("PK-204"));
        for(String rejected:new String[]{"pk-204","PK‑204","-PK"})
            try{accept(rejected);}catch(IllegalArgumentException invalid){System.out.println("rejected");}
    }
}

Output

PK-204
rejected
rejected
rejected

Costs and boundaries

Validation is O(n) over at most 24 UTF-16 units and uses constant auxiliary storage. The strict alphabet is a field-specific decision. It does not prove that an accepted reference belongs to the current user, is unique, or is safe to concatenate into an arbitrary external command.

Common Mistakes

  • Normalization is not a complete confusable-character policy.
  • Do not apply a protocol alphabet to international display names.
  • Syntax validation does not replace authorization.

title: Java 25 scoped values: request context with a bounded lifetime
summary: A ScopedValue binds a value to the current execution scope and restores the previous binding when that scope returns or throws.
body:
A ScopedValue binds a value to the current execution scope and restores the previous binding when that scope returns or throws.

Java 25+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

Pass one-way context

A reporting operation needs a request identifier deep inside callbacks. Keeping an explicitly passed context object is still a valid choice. A scoped value fits when intermediate methods do not need the value but selected downstream code does. Keep its key private so unrelated code cannot read or rebind it merely because it knows a field name.

The binding is not a writable thread-local slot that remains until remove is called. A nested binding temporarily shadows the outer value; leaving the nested operation restores the outer binding even when the nested code throws. The program checks that path instead of assuming every callback returns normally.

Binding lifetime does not freeze an object. This example binds an immutable String. A mutable request object can still be changed through another reference. Ordinary newly created threads do not automatically receive this binding; structured sharing has its own API rules. No preview structured-concurrency API is used in this lesson.

Make missing context explicit

Calling get outside a binding is a misuse unless the API contract permits an optional context and checks it deliberately. The operation should not silently invent a request identifier just because a caller forgot to establish its scope. The final isBound check proves cleanup after the operation.

Working program

public class ReportRequestScope {
    private static final ScopedValue<String> REQUEST=ScopedValue.newInstance();
    public static void main(String[] args)throws Exception{
        ScopedValue.where(REQUEST,"REQ-51").call(()->{
            System.out.println(REQUEST.get());
            try{ScopedValue.where(REQUEST,"AUDIT-51").run(()->{throw new IllegalStateException("audit failed");});}
            catch(IllegalStateException failed){System.out.println(REQUEST.get());}
            Thread child=Thread.ofVirtual().start(()->System.out.println(REQUEST.isBound()));
            child.join();return null;
        });
        System.out.println(REQUEST.isBound());
    }
}

Output

REQ-51
REQ-51
false
false

Costs and boundaries

Binding and lookup do not traverse application collections. Lookup cost depends on the scope implementation and its cache; this program makes no nanosecond claim. Referenced context remains reachable while the binding needs it. Java 25 finalizes this API; earlier preview versions are not the baseline used here.

Common Mistakes

  • A bounded binding does not make a mutable payload immutable.
  • A raw child thread does not imply scoped inheritance.
  • Do not expose the key as a public application-wide permission.

title: Java stream gatherers: batching and ordered running totals
summary: A stream gatherer transforms a sequence while retaining operation state, which lets a pipeline express batching and ordered accumulation beyond a one-element map.
body:
A stream gatherer transforms a sequence while retaining operation state, which lets a pipeline express batching and ordered accumulation beyond a one-element map.

Java 25+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

State the output shape

A dispatch pipeline batches receipt quantities into fixed windows and then computes running totals for an audit trace. Those are different transformations: one emits lists, while the other emits an accumulated value for each input. A final reduce would return only the aggregate, losing the intermediate totals.

windowFixed emits a smaller final window when the input does not fill the requested size. An empty input produces no windows. Validate the batch size at the configuration boundary rather than discovering an invalid size after work has been admitted. The program checks the trailing batch and the empty stream.

Window lists are unmodifiable membership structures. Their element objects can still be shared mutable values. This fixture uses Integer values, so that particular ownership issue is absent. A batch of mutable receipt objects would need an explicit snapshot or transfer-of-ownership rule.

Know what retained output costs

The pipeline below materializes all windows with toList. An online consumer could process windows as they arrive, but returning every window retains the batch references. For running totals, the order of the input is part of the result. Do not substitute an order-dependent recurrence into an operation that assumes an interchangeable grouping rule.

Working program

import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Gatherers;
public class DispatchBatchGatherers {
    public static void main(String[] args){
        List<Integer> counts=List.of(4,7,2,9,3);
        System.out.println(counts.stream().gather(Gatherers.windowFixed(2)).toList());
        System.out.println(counts.stream().gather(Gatherers.scan(()->0,Math::addExact)).toList());
        System.out.println(List.<Integer>of().stream().gather(Gatherers.windowFixed(2)).count());
    }
}

Output

[[4, 7], [2, 9], [3]]
[4, 11, 13, 22, 25]
0

Costs and boundaries

Both transformations inspect n elements. Materializing the windows or every running total retains O(n) output. A configured large window can allocate substantial temporary storage even for a shorter stream. Gatherers are final from Java 24; this checked source targets Java 25 rather than earlier preview releases.

Common Mistakes

  • A final partial window is valid output.
  • Unmodifiable windows do not deep-copy arbitrary elements.
  • toList still retains the complete returned result.

title: Java 25 constructor validation before superclass initialization
summary: A flexible constructor body can perform permitted statements before its explicit superclass or delegated-constructor invocation while respecting early-construction restrictions.
body:
A flexible constructor body can perform permitted statements before its explicit superclass or delegated-constructor invocation while respecting early-construction restrictions.

Java 25+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

Reject before passing the value onward

A shipment quantity is required by the superclass constructor. Validate and convert the incoming quantity before invoking super, so the base object receives a checked value. The validation is about the input argument; it does not read partially initialized instance state.

Java 25 permits this prologue under specific construction rules. It is not permission to call arbitrary instance methods before the superclass exists. Local computations and input checks should remain separate from callbacks that expect the full object invariant. Publishing this from construction still needs its own review.

The example uses a long input and Math.toIntExact before the base constructor. That keeps both negative quantities and values too large for the base representation out of the initialized object. The failed construction creates no application registry entry because publication is not part of this constructor.

Keep delegating paths consistent

If the class has several constructors, make each path converge on the same validated invariant. Duplicated checks tend to drift when a new parameter is introduced. A constructor that accepts already validated data can be private, while the public boundary owns conversion and rejection.

Working program

public class CheckedShipmentConstruction {
    static class Quantity { final int units;Quantity(int units){this.units=units;} }
    static class Shipment extends Quantity {
        Shipment(long requested){
            if(requested<0)throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative shipment");
            int validated=Math.toIntExact(requested);
            super(validated);
        }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args){
        System.out.println(new Shipment(9).units);
        try{new Shipment(-1);}catch(IllegalArgumentException rejected){System.out.println("negative rejected");}
        try{new Shipment(3_000_000_000L);}catch(ArithmeticException rejected){System.out.println("range rejected");}
    }
}

Output

9
negative rejected
range rejected

Costs and boundaries

Scalar validation and conversion take constant work. This language feature changes permitted constructor structure, not the arithmetic range or object-publication rules. The source requires Java 25 without preview flags; it is not a Java 8-compatible constructor.

Common Mistakes

  • The prologue is not a fully initialized instance.
  • A constructor failure does not undo unrelated external side effects.
  • Do not claim a newer language feature compiles under an earlier release.

title: Java 25 module imports: source names without a deployment shortcut
summary: A module import declaration makes public types in exported packages available for source-level name resolution; it does not replace module readability or deployment configuration.
body:
A module import declaration makes public types in exported packages available for source-level name resolution; it does not replace module readability or deployment configuration.

Java 25+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

Import names and resolve dependencies separately

The program imports the java.base module and uses several exported types without individual package imports. It remains an ordinary class-path application. Nothing in this source creates a module descriptor for the application or packages a missing external library.

An import can expose many simple names, so collisions need deliberate qualification. Date from java.util and Date from java.sql are different types. Importing more packages does not make those names interchangeable or choose the desired business meaning.

Module import declarations are a Java 25 language feature. An IDE accepting the syntax with a newer SDK does not prove that a Java 21 build target can compile it. Keep the compiler release and the application’s required runtime in the build definition.

Keep the dependency visible to reviewers

For a small file, individual imports can make dependencies easier to read. A module import is useful where the module is the intended source namespace. That choice is about source organization; it is not a claim that every exported class is loaded into memory at startup.

Working program

import module java.base;
public class ModuleImportedReceipts {
    public static void main(String[] args){
        List<String> references=List.of("R-23","R-11","R-23");
        Set<String> unique=new TreeSet<>(references);
        System.out.println(unique);
        System.out.println(LocalDate.of(2026,9,29));
    }
}

Output

[R-11, R-23]
2026-09-29

Costs and boundaries

The list and tree operations determine this program’s runtime cost. Import syntax affects source name resolution and does not promise shorter startup, a smaller artifact, or automatic library discovery. A named application module still needs its descriptor and launch configuration.

Common Mistakes

  • An import is not a requires declaration.
  • Ambiguous simple names still need qualification.
  • The selected module must be observable under the compilation setup.

Java 25+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

Read the instance lifecycle

This file defines receipt references as instance state and prints their count from main. The launcher creates the enclosing instance before invoking that method. Removing the static modifier does not turn fields into global state or remove ordinary initialization rules.

The implicit source environment provides the java.base type imports used here, and IO supplies the console operation. A regular explicit class can also use an eligible instance main under the Java 25 launch rules. Neither syntax removes the need to validate external arguments or own resources.

Save this exact source as ShipmentSummary.java. The file name determines the implicit class name used in the compiled launch command. The source kit includes this file, its minimum release and its entrypoint mode rather than wrapping the method in another main during verification.

Choose the form for the application

A compact file suits a small entrypoint. Package structure, explicit APIs and multi-file builds still matter when the program grows. Keep business operations separate from console output so tests can check return values and rejected inputs without intercepting every printed line.

Working program

List<String> references = List.of("R-19", "R-20", "R-21");
void main() {
    IO.println(references.size());
    IO.println(references.getFirst());
}

R-19

Costs and boundaries

The stored references occupy O(n) list membership storage for n references. This fixture has three elements and does no external input. Compact syntax changes source structure; it does not change list access contracts or provide a performance optimization. Compile and launch with Java 25.

Common Mistakes

  • The source file name is part of the launch contract.
  • Instance fields are initialized before this instance main runs.

title: Java 25 virtual threads and monitors: version boundaries still matter
summary: A virtual thread executes on carrier threads, and the monitor-related carrier-pinning behavior changed in JDK 24 without removing the monitor’s mutual-exclusion contract.
body:
A virtual thread executes on carrier threads, and the monitor-related carrier-pinning behavior changed in JDK 24 without removing the monitor’s mutual-exclusion contract.

Java 25+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

Separate contention from carrier retention

A synchronized operation still allows only one holder of a particular monitor at a time. Removing the older monitor-related pinning behavior does not make all requests inside that critical section execute concurrently. A slow operation under one shared monitor can remain an application bottleneck.

The Java 21 lesson is labelled for that release. Its synchronized-block pinning warning should not be generalized to every newer JDK. This Java 25 fixture checks completed increments under a monitor and uses virtual threads, but it does not infer carrier behavior from elapsed time.

Native or foreign calls can introduce other blocking or pinning boundaries. Runtime diagnostics and the actual call path matter. A virtual thread also does not create more database connections, CPU cores or queue capacity; downstream admission remains a separate application rule.

Wait for completion before reading shared state

The program joins every worker before printing the count. The protected increment prevents lost updates, while joining supplies a completion boundary for the final read. A collection of started Thread objects alone does not prove that their operations finished successfully in a larger application.

Working program

import java.util.*;
public class MonitoredVirtualReceipts {
    final Object monitor=new Object();int accepted;
    void accept(){synchronized(monitor){accepted++;}}
    public static void main(String[] args)throws Exception{
        MonitoredVirtualReceipts service=new MonitoredVirtualReceipts();List<Thread> workers=new ArrayList<>();
        for(int i=0;i<40;i++)workers.add(Thread.ofVirtual().start(service::accept));
        for(Thread worker:workers)worker.join();
        System.out.println(service.accepted);
    }
}

Output

40

Costs and boundaries

There are n operations and n retained worker handles. The monitor serializes their increments, so virtual threads do not establish parallel speedup for that section. This program verifies the state result on Java 25; timing, native-call behavior and carrier scheduling need separate diagnostic evidence.

Common Mistakes

  • Less monitor pinning does not remove lock contention.
  • A release-specific warning is not a timeless rule.
  • Uncaught worker failure requires explicit reporting in application code.

title: Java AVL deletion: rebalance every surviving ancestor
summary: AVL deletion removes a search-tree key and repairs subtree heights on the path back to the root, including rotations caused by the reduced subtree.
body:
AVL deletion removes a search-tree key and repairs subtree heights on the path back to the root, including rotations caused by the reduced subtree.

Java 8+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

Insertion cases are not enough

A shipment index can stay balanced during insertion and become skewed after deletion. Removing a leaf changes the height seen by its parent. That parent may rotate, and the height change can continue upward. Stopping after the first repaired node can leave another ancestor outside the balance rule.

For a node with two children, this implementation copies its successor key and removes that successor from the right subtree. Key copying is acceptable for this integer-set model. An index storing node identities or mutable payloads needs a separate decision about identity and ownership.

The child balance chooses the rotation. After deletion, a heavy child can have balance zero; that case still permits a single rotation. Reusing insertion’s newly inserted-key tests would make the deletion decision depend on a key that no longer describes the surviving subtree.

Treat absent keys as a normal result

Deleting an absent shipment leaves membership unchanged. The recursive path still returns the existing subtree roots, and cached heights are recomputed before they are used. The property suite compares repeated deletions with TreeSet and checks ordering, cached height and balance at every node.

Working program

public class DeletableShipmentAvl {
    static class Node {int key,height=1;Node left,right;Node(int key){this.key=key;}}
    Node root;
    static int height(Node n){return n==null?0:n.height;}
    static int balance(Node n){return n==null?0:height(n.left)-height(n.right);}
    static void update(Node n){n.height=1+Math.max(height(n.left),height(n.right));}
    static Node right(Node n){Node next=n.left;n.left=next.right;next.right=n;update(n);update(next);return next;}
    static Node left(Node n){Node next=n.right;n.right=next.left;next.left=n;update(n);update(next);return next;}
    static Node repair(Node n){
        if(n==null)return null;update(n);
        if(balance(n)>1){if(balance(n.left)<0)n.left=left(n.left);return right(n);}
        if(balance(n)<-1){if(balance(n.right)>0)n.right=right(n.right);return left(n);}
        return n;
    }
    static Node add(Node n,int key){
        if(n==null)return new Node(key);
        if(key<n.key)n.left=add(n.left,key);else if(key>n.key)n.right=add(n.right,key);else return n;
        return repair(n);
    }
    static Node remove(Node n,int key){
        if(n==null)return null;
        if(key<n.key)n.left=remove(n.left,key);else if(key>n.key)n.right=remove(n.right,key);
        else {
            if(n.left==null)return n.right;if(n.right==null)return n.left;
            Node successor=n.right;while(successor.left!=null)successor=successor.left;
            n.key=successor.key;n.right=remove(n.right,successor.key);
        }return repair(n);
    }
    static void ordered(Node n,java.util.List<Integer> values){if(n!=null){ordered(n.left,values);values.add(n.key);ordered(n.right,values);}}
    public static void main(String[] args){
        DeletableShipmentAvl index=new DeletableShipmentAvl();
        for(int key:new int[]{40,20,60,10,30,50,70,5})index.root=add(index.root,key);
        index.root=remove(index.root,40);index.root=remove(index.root,5);index.root=remove(index.root,999);
        java.util.List<Integer> values=new java.util.ArrayList<>();ordered(index.root,values);System.out.println(values);
    }
}

Output

[10, 20, 30, 50, 60, 70]

Costs and boundaries

A maintained AVL height makes lookup, insertion and deletion O(log n). Recursive stack storage is O(log n). Exporting the ordered list is O(n) and allocates n result positions. This set model does not preserve the identity of a two-child node’s former key.

Common Mistakes

  • Repair every surviving ancestor on the return path.
  • Deletion must handle a heavy child with zero balance.
  • Key copying can be wrong for an identity-sensitive payload model.

title: Java trie deletion: preserve shared prefixes and prune dead branches
summary: Trie deletion clears a word’s terminal marker and removes only branches that contain no remaining word or descendant.
body:
Trie deletion clears a word’s terminal marker and removes only branches that contain no remaining word or descendant.

Java 8+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

A prefix is shared storage

A command index stores pack and parcel. Deleting pack must not remove the shared pa path needed by parcel. A stored word can also be a prefix of another word, so clearing its terminal marker is separate from deleting the node itself.

The program records the path as it walks toward the word, then prunes backward after clearing the terminal marker. That avoids recursion proportional to an arbitrarily long input. The alphabet is deliberately restricted to lowercase ASCII, with a 4096-unit input budget.

Validation happens before mutation. An invalid final character must not cause the earlier valid prefix to disappear or create partial branches. A missing path or an unmarked prefix returns false without changing another word’s membership.

Do not invent ranking semantics

This structure answers exact membership and deletion. It does not rank suggestions, define language collation or compress long single-child paths. Those features need their own stored counts or ordering rules. Node pruning is a storage operation, not a popularity score update.

Working program

public class DeletableCommandTrie {
    static class Node {Node[] children=new Node[26];boolean terminal;}
    final Node root=new Node();
    static void validate(String word){
        if(word==null||word.isEmpty()||word.length()>4096)throw new IllegalArgumentException("Word budget");
        for(int i=0;i<word.length();i++)if(word.charAt(i)<'a'||word.charAt(i)>'z')throw new IllegalArgumentException("Alphabet");
    }
    void add(String word){validate(word);Node n=root;for(int i=0;i<word.length();i++){int slot=word.charAt(i)-'a';if(n.children[slot]==null)n.children[slot]=new Node();n=n.children[slot];}n.terminal=true;}
    boolean contains(String word){validate(word);Node n=root;for(int i=0;i<word.length();i++){n=n.children[word.charAt(i)-'a'];if(n==null)return false;}return n.terminal;}
    static boolean empty(Node n){if(n.terminal)return false;for(Node child:n.children)if(child!=null)return false;return true;}
    boolean remove(String word){
        validate(word);Node[] path=new Node[word.length()+1];path[0]=root;
        for(int i=0;i<word.length();i++){path[i+1]=path[i].children[word.charAt(i)-'a'];if(path[i+1]==null)return false;}
        if(!path[word.length()].terminal)return false;path[word.length()].terminal=false;
        for(int i=word.length();i>0&&empty(path[i]);i--)path[i-1].children[word.charAt(i-1)-'a']=null;
        return true;
    }
    public static void main(String[] args){
        DeletableCommandTrie commands=new DeletableCommandTrie();commands.add("pack");commands.add("packing");commands.add("parcel");
        System.out.println(commands.remove("pack"));System.out.println(commands.contains("packing"));
        System.out.println(commands.remove("pack"));System.out.println(commands.remove("parcel"));
    }
}

Output

true
true
false
true

Costs and boundaries

For a word of length m, validation, traversal and pruning are O(m) with a fixed 26-slot alphabet. The recorded path uses O(m) temporary references. Live nodes retain 26 child positions each, so this representation can be wasteful for sparse or much larger alphabets.

Common Mistakes

  • Clearing a terminal marker is not permission to remove live descendants.
  • Validate the complete word before mutation.
  • A fixed ASCII trie is not a Unicode search index.

title: Java Floyd–Warshall: all-pairs distances and negative-cycle rejection
summary: Floyd–Warshall computes shortest-path distances between every pair of vertices by successively allowing each vertex as an intermediate point.
body:
Floyd–Warshall computes shortest-path distances between every pair of vertices by successively allowing each vertex as an intermediate point.

Java 8+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

Keep the intermediate vertex outside

The recurrence asks whether a path through the current intermediate vertex improves an existing distance. That intermediate loop is the outer loop. Reordering the loops changes which already computed paths are available and can break the recurrence.

An absent edge uses a sentinel and is never added to a finite value. A graph with negative edges can still have finite shortest paths, but a negative cycle makes some paths unbounded below. This implementation rejects the whole result when any diagonal becomes negative rather than returning a matrix with undefined entries mixed into ordinary distances.

The input matrix is copied. Parallel edges must already be reduced to their minimum direct cost, and each diagonal must represent the zero-length path. The program sets each diagonal to the smaller of zero and the supplied value so a negative self-loop is preserved for cycle detection.

Bound the model before allocating

The fixture accepts at most 200 vertices and finite edge magnitudes at most one million. That is a learning budget, not a claim that a 200-vertex matrix suits every graph. Sparse graphs with far more vertices usually need a different representation and shortest-path strategy.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
public class DepotAllPairs {
    static final long ABSENT=Long.MAX_VALUE;
    static long[][] distances(long[][] input){
        int n=input.length;if(n>200)throw new IllegalArgumentException("Matrix budget");
        long[][] result=new long[n][n];
        for(int i=0;i<n;i++){
            if(input[i]==null||input[i].length!=n)throw new IllegalArgumentException("Square matrix required");
            for(int j=0;j<n;j++){
                long value=input[i][j];if(value!=ABSENT&&(value<-1_000_000||value>1_000_000))throw new IllegalArgumentException("Edge budget");result[i][j]=value;
            }result[i][i]=Math.min(0,result[i][i]);
        }
        for(int via=0;via<n;via++)for(int from=0;from<n;from++)for(int to=0;to<n;to++)
            if(result[from][via]!=ABSENT&&result[via][to]!=ABSENT)result[from][to]=Math.min(result[from][to],Math.addExact(result[from][via],result[via][to]));
        for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if(result[i][i]<0)throw new IllegalStateException("Negative cycle");
        return result;
    }
    public static void main(String[] args){
        long[][] edges={{0,5,ABSENT},{ABSENT,0,-2},{ABSENT,ABSENT,0}};
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(distances(edges)[0]));System.out.println(edges[0][2]==ABSENT);
    }
}

Output

[0, 5, 3]
true

Costs and boundaries

Time is O(V³) and matrix storage is O(V²). A negative-cycle input can amplify intermediate distances; checked addition can reject arithmetic overflow before the final cycle check. This implementation rejects such an input rather than claiming a usable finite result.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not add the absent sentinel to an edge weight.
  • The intermediate loop belongs outside the endpoint loops.
  • A negative cycle is different from a negative edge.

title: Java strongly connected components: mutual reachability with two traversals
summary: A strongly connected component groups directed-graph vertices that can each reach every other vertex in the group.
body:
A strongly connected component groups directed-graph vertices that can each reach every other vertex in the group.

Java 8+. The program uses JDK classes and requires no preview flags.

Direction changes the membership rule

A dependency graph can have one-way reachability without a cycle. Union-find on undirected endpoints would group that relation differently. Strong components need both directions of reachability, so this algorithm first records a finishing order and then walks the reversed graph.

The first pass below uses explicit DFS frames represented by each vertex’s next edge index. Marking a vertex when it is pushed prevents repeated pending entries from being mistaken for separate visits. A vertex enters the finishing list only after its outgoing edges have been considered.

The reversed pass visits vertices in reverse finishing order and assigns one component number per reached group. The numbers are traversal labels, not stable business identifiers. Reordering adjacency lists can change their numeric values while preserving the same component partition.

Validate every endpoint

Validate the whole graph before computing the partition. An invalid edge should not leave a half-built result that a caller mistakes for a complete grouping. The property tests compare component equality with an independent transitive-reachability matrix; they do not require one particular label numbering.

Working program

import java.util.*;
public class DependencyComponents {
    static int[] groups(int[][] edges){
        int n=edges.length;List<List<Integer>> reverse=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<n;i++)reverse.add(new ArrayList<>());
        for(int v=0;v<n;v++){if(edges[v]==null)throw new IllegalArgumentException("Missing adjacency");for(int next:edges[v]){if(next<0||next>=n)throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid endpoint");reverse.get(next).add(v);}}
        boolean[] seen=new boolean[n];int[] cursor=new int[n];List<Integer> finished=new ArrayList<>();ArrayDeque<Integer> stack=new ArrayDeque<>();
        for(int start=0;start<n;start++)if(!seen[start]){
            seen[start]=true;stack.push(start);
            while(!stack.isEmpty()){
                int v=stack.peek();if(cursor[v]<edges[v].length){int next=edges[v][cursor[v]++];if(!seen[next]){seen[next]=true;stack.push(next);}}
                else {stack.pop();finished.add(v);}
            }
        }
        int[] group=new int[n];Arrays.fill(group,-1);int label=0;
        for(int i=finished.size()-1;i>=0;i--){int start=finished.get(i);if(group[start]>=0)continue;group[start]=label;stack.push(start);
            while(!stack.isEmpty()){int v=stack.pop();for(int next:reverse.get(v))if(group[next]<0){group[next]=label;stack.push(next);}}
            label++;
        }return group;
    }
    public static void main(String[] args){
        int[] group=groups(new int[][]{{1},{0,2},{3},{2},{}});
        System.out.println(group[0]==group[1]);System.out.println(group[2]==group[3]);System.out.println(group[1]==group[2]);
    }
}

Output

true
true
false

Costs and boundaries

Both passes take O(V+E). The reversed adjacency storage uses O(V+E); traversal state uses O(V). Explicit stacks avoid recursion depth proportional to the graph path, but they do not remove the memory needed for a large graph.

Common Mistakes

  • Undirected connectivity is not strong connectivity.
  • Numeric component labels are not stable external IDs.
  • Finishing order differs from discovery order.
