title: Java native Linker: declare a C call and reject undefined input
summary: A native Linker creates a method handle for a foreign function using a descriptor that matches the platform calling convention.
body:
A native Linker creates a method handle for a foreign function using a descriptor that matches the platform calling convention.

This complete program targets Java 25. Its displayed output is checked by the tutorial validation script.

Match the foreign signature

The fixture calls the platform C abs function for a bounded signed adjustment. It obtains the canonical C int layout from the linker instead of assuming that every foreign integer type has the Java long layout. A signature mismatch at this boundary can corrupt execution rather than produce an ordinary type error.

The program rejects Integer.MIN_VALUE before entering C, because its positive magnitude does not fit the same signed int representation. That condition is an input rule, not an exception the native function is expected to throw back into Java. The checked fixture uses a Java int carrier on this platform.

Grant access deliberately

Run the downloaded class with --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED because this kit uses the classpath. A named-module application should grant the intended module rather than copying that flag indiscriminately. Native access is a trust decision; it does not validate a function descriptor or make foreign code memory-safe.

The checked call has no pointers or allocated foreign buffers. Larger APIs need an ownership rule for each pointer and callback, including how long the callee retains it. Memory segments and Shared arena lifetime cover separate parts of that contract.

Working program

import java.lang.foreign.*;
import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle;
public class NativeAdjustmentMagnitude {
    static int magnitude(MethodHandle operation,int adjustment) throws Throwable {
        if (adjustment == Integer.MIN_VALUE) throw new IllegalArgumentException("magnitude exceeds signed int");
        return (int) operation.invokeExact(adjustment);
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Throwable {
        Linker linker=Linker.nativeLinker();
        MemoryLayout integer=linker.canonicalLayouts().get("int");
        if (!(integer instanceof ValueLayout.OfInt)) throw new UnsupportedOperationException("C int carrier");
        MethodHandle operation=linker.downcallHandle(linker.defaultLookup().find("abs").orElseThrow(),
            FunctionDescriptor.of(integer,integer));
        System.out.println(magnitude(operation,-125));
        System.out.println(magnitude(operation,0));
        try {magnitude(operation,Integer.MIN_VALUE);}
        catch(IllegalArgumentException rejected){System.out.println("range rejected");}
    }
}

Output

125
0
range rejected

Costs and boundaries

The scalar operation has bounded work, but downcall setup and foreign-transition costs are not measured here. The example is checked on the local platform, not every ABI. It does not make a claim that native abs is a better choice than Java arithmetic.

Common Mistakes

  • Match the actual C signature and carrier.
  • Reject values outside the foreign function contract before calling it.
  • Native access does not sandbox a foreign library.

title: Java Flow: request items and observe publisher completion
summary: Flow separates publishers, subscribers and subscriptions so a subscriber can request a number of items rather than accepting an unspecified push rate.
body:
Flow separates publishers, subscribers and subscriptions so a subscriber can request a number of items rather than accepting an unspecified push rate.

This complete program targets Java 11. Its displayed output is checked by the tutorial validation script.

Completion belongs to the subscription

The receipt subscriber requests one amount at subscription time and requests another after each received amount. The publisher sends ten and twenty, then closes. The completion future is joined before the total is read, making successful completion distinct from merely calling submit twice.

SubmissionPublisher owns buffering and delivery behavior. This fixture chooses a direct executor for deterministic local observation; it does not represent a worker pool or network transport. A one-at-a-time request policy here does not prove that a remote importer retains only one record.

Keep errors visible

onError completes the same future exceptionally so join cannot return a successful total after a delivery failure. Production callbacks should define cancellation and downstream failure handling without throwing errors into unrelated application work. Do not treat normal close as a way to repair a failed record.

The atomic total avoids relying on an undocumented thread choice in the subscriber. A real payment amount needs a unit and overflow policy too. Compare this API-level contract with Reactor demand before assuming they provide an identical set of operators or runtime services.

Working program

import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
public class ReceiptFlowTotal {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        AtomicInteger total=new AtomicInteger();
        CompletableFuture<Void> finished=new CompletableFuture<>();
        try(SubmissionPublisher<Integer> publisher=new SubmissionPublisher<>(Runnable::run,8)) {
            publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<Integer>() {
                Flow.Subscription subscription;
                public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription value){subscription=value;subscription.request(1);}
                public void onNext(Integer amount){total.addAndGet(amount);subscription.request(1);}
                public void onError(Throwable failure){finished.completeExceptionally(failure);}
                public void onComplete(){finished.complete(null);}
            });
            publisher.submit(10);publisher.submit(20);
        }
        finished.join();System.out.println(total.get());
    }
}

Output

30

Costs and boundaries

The fixture processes two integers with a configured buffer capacity and direct delivery. Application storage depends on retained subscriptions, buffered items and callbacks. A blocking submit or slow subscriber can affect caller latency; no throughput measurement is provided.

Common Mistakes

  • Request demand through the subscription.
  • Read results after observing completion or failure.
  • Do not infer a network buffer limit from this local sequence.

title: Java LinkedHashMap LRU cache: access order changes eviction
summary: An access-ordered LinkedHashMap tracks recently accessed entries so a bounded cache can remove the least recently used entry after insertion.
body:
An access-ordered LinkedHashMap tracks recently accessed entries so a bounded cache can remove the least recently used entry after insertion.

This complete program targets Java 8. Its displayed output is checked by the tutorial validation script.

A read changes the eviction order

A document cache has space for two keys. It inserts invoice and receipt, reads invoice, then inserts statement. Receipt is evicted because the read promoted invoice to the most recent position. The printed key order makes that policy visible.

The capacity check belongs to removeEldestEntry and runs after insertion. The constructor rejects non-positive capacity rather than letting a zero-sized cache conceal a configuration error. This is a count bound, not a byte-size bound: one enormous document can still consume too much memory.

Define what the cache does not own

This fixture stores immutable strings in one thread. It has no expiry clock, fetch coalescing or persistence. A synchronized wrapper can serialize individual calls, but a lookup-then-load-then-put workflow needs its own coordination if duplicate remote work matters.

An access-ordered get changes iteration order. Do not assume that a read is harmless while another thread walks the keys. For a framework cache, Key identity and invalidation rules still determine whether a returned document belongs to the intended tenant.

Working program

import java.util.*;
public class DocumentLruCache extends LinkedHashMap<String,String> {
    private final int capacity;
    DocumentLruCache(int capacity) {
        super(16,0.75f,true);
        if(capacity<1)throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity");
        this.capacity=capacity;
    }
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<String,String> eldest){return size()>capacity;}
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        DocumentLruCache cache=new DocumentLruCache(2);
        cache.put("invoice","I");cache.put("receipt","R");cache.get("invoice");cache.put("statement","S");
        System.out.println(cache.keySet());System.out.println(cache.containsKey("receipt"));
        try{new DocumentLruCache(0);}catch(IllegalArgumentException rejected){System.out.println("capacity rejected");}
    }
}

Output

[invoice, statement]
false
capacity rejected

Costs and boundaries

Expected hash lookup and access-order maintenance are constant work under ordinary key behavior. The cache retains at most capacity entries after insertion returns, plus a temporary new entry during the operation. Key/value sizes and hash quality remain part of the memory and latency budget.

Common Mistakes

  • Access ordering requires the access-order constructor setting.
  • A count limit is not a byte limit.
  • Do not assume cache get leaves iteration order unchanged.

title: Java NavigableMap ranges: distinguish a live window from a snapshot
summary: A NavigableMap exposes ordered boundary lookups and range views whose contents can remain connected to the backing map.
body:
A NavigableMap exposes ordered boundary lookups and range views whose contents can remain connected to the backing map.

This complete program targets Java 8. Its displayed output is checked by the tutorial validation script.

A view is still the same data owner

A dispatch ledger stores timestamps ten, twenty and thirty. The half-open window from ten to thirty excludes the record at thirty. Replacing twenty through that window replaces it in the original ledger as well. A TreeMap copy captures the selected entries at that moment and does not observe a later insert.

The fixture also asks floorEntry for twenty-four and receives the entry at twenty. That is a predecessor lookup, not exact equality. Pick floor, ceiling, lower or higher from the boundary rule instead of adding ad hoc off-by-one arithmetic to an exact-key lookup.

The window rejects outside writes

Inserting forty into the selected window raises IllegalArgumentException. That is a range restriction on the view, not proof of a domain-level permission check. A different reference to the backing map can still write forty.

Copying the map copies entry references rather than making mutable values independent. Here strings make the snapshot distinction straightforward; a mutable dispatch record needs a separate copy policy. View ownership and Response snapshots explain why returning a view can expose more ownership than intended.

Working program

import java.util.*;
public class DispatchRangeWindow {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        NavigableMap<Integer,String> ledger=new TreeMap<>();
        ledger.put(10,"queued");ledger.put(20,"review");ledger.put(30,"sent");
        NavigableMap<Integer,String> window=ledger.subMap(10,true,30,false);
        NavigableMap<Integer,String> snapshot=new TreeMap<>(window);
        window.put(20,"approved");ledger.put(25,"packed");
        System.out.println(window);System.out.println(snapshot);System.out.println(ledger.floorEntry(24).getKey());
        try{window.put(40,"outside");}catch(IllegalArgumentException rejected){System.out.println("range rejected");}
    }
}

Output

{10=queued, 20=approved, 25=packed}
{10=queued, 20=review}
20
range rejected

Costs and boundaries

TreeMap predecessor lookup and insertion take O(log n) time. A live range view does not copy all matching entries, while building a snapshot retains O(k) entry data for k selected entries. Iterating the range still visits the entries requested.

Common Mistakes

  • State whether each endpoint is inclusive.
  • Do not describe a live view as an independent snapshot.
  • A range restriction is not an authorization policy.

title: Java ByteBuffer byte order: decode the protocol before reading integers
summary: A ByteBuffer byte order determines how multi-byte primitive values are assembled from their stored bytes.
body:
A ByteBuffer byte order determines how multi-byte primitive values are assembled from their stored bytes.

This complete program targets Java 8. Its displayed output is checked by the tutorial validation script.

The bytes have a format, not a machine preference

The receipt header uses four bytes with the value one in little-endian order. Reading the same bytes with the default big-endian order produces 16777216. Both reads are mechanically valid; only one matches the protocol. Set the agreed order explicitly before reading an integer.

The duplicate shares the same bytes but has its own position and order setting. The fixture changes the original to little-endian and observes that the duplicate still reads its own configured order. A buffer view is not a decoded value, and sharing storage is different from sharing cursor state.

Bound the header first

The parser rejects a header that is not exactly four bytes before reading. A larger message needs bounds for each field, declared payload length and total retained bytes. Treating a transmitted length as a trusted allocation request can turn an ordinary header parser into an oversized allocation path.

An unsigned field also needs a deliberate Java representation. Byte order does not solve signedness. See Byte input before assuming that an integer read validates a complete packet or verifies who sent it.

Working program

import java.nio.*;
public class ReceiptHeaderOrder {
    static int read(byte[] header) {
        if(header.length!=4)throw new IllegalArgumentException("four-byte header required");
        return ByteBuffer.wrap(header).order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN).getInt();
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        byte[] bytes={1,0,0,0};ByteBuffer original=ByteBuffer.wrap(bytes);
        ByteBuffer view=original.duplicate();original.order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN);
        System.out.println(original.getInt());System.out.println(view.getInt());System.out.println(read(bytes));
        try{read(new byte[3]);}catch(IllegalArgumentException rejected){System.out.println("length rejected");}
    }
}

Output

1
16777216
1
length rejected

Costs and boundaries

The fixed four-byte read has bounded time and storage. Wrapping shares the supplied byte array; it is not a defensive copy. Larger protocols must budget retained byte buffers and reject lengths before allocating or reading their declared payloads.

Common Mistakes

  • Use protocol byte order, not host assumptions.
  • Configure each view according to its read contract.
  • Validate field length before primitive access.

title: Java CRC32: detect a byte change without claiming authenticity
summary: CRC32 computes a checksum of a byte sequence for detecting accidental changes; it is not proof of who produced that sequence.
body:
CRC32 computes a checksum of a byte sequence for detecting accidental changes; it is not proof of who produced that sequence.

This complete program targets Java 8. Its displayed output is checked by the tutorial validation script.

Compare the same encoded bytes

The manifest fixture calculates the checksum of a UTF-8 record, checks it again without changing the bytes, then changes one byte and observes a different value. The comparison is on encoded bytes, not characters, because encoding and line-ending changes alter the stored representation.

A checksum match is useful evidence that an accidental transmission change was not observed by that check. It is not a guarantee that two different messages cannot share a checksum. A sender can also replace a payload and its unchecked checksum together.

Choose the trust boundary separately

The checksum object keeps mutable running state. Reset or create a fresh instance for an independent record, otherwise the result includes earlier bytes. The fixture uses a new instance per call so the record boundary is explicit.

When adversarial modification matters, define a signature or keyed authentication design and key ownership instead of upgrading a checksum label. Random token material and authenticated transport solve other problems; neither makes an untrusted supplied CRC an authentication mechanism.

Working program

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.zip.CRC32;
public class ManifestChecksum {
    static long checksum(byte[] bytes){CRC32 crc=new CRC32();crc.update(bytes);return crc.getValue();}
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        byte[] manifest="receipt=125".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        long expected=checksum(manifest);System.out.println(expected==checksum(manifest));
        byte[] changed=manifest.clone();changed[changed.length-1]=(byte)'6';
        System.out.println(expected==checksum(changed));
    }
}

Output

true
false

Costs and boundaries

Checksum calculation takes O(b) time for b bytes and bounded checksum state. The fixture already holds the byte array; a streaming calculation can avoid retaining the entire file. No collision-resistance or authenticity guarantee is made.

Common Mistakes

  • Calculate over the exact bytes whose integrity you want to check.
  • Do not reuse running state across unrelated records accidentally.
  • Do not use an untrusted CRC as an authentication decision.

title: Java MessageFormat apostrophes: keep placeholders visible to the parser
summary: MessageFormat interprets apostrophes as quoting syntax, so literal apostrophes in a message pattern require the correct escaping.
body:
MessageFormat interprets apostrophes as quoting syntax, so literal apostrophes in a message pattern require the correct escaping.

This complete program targets Java 8. Its displayed output is checked by the tutorial validation script.

Message text is a pattern

The receipt pattern doubles its apostrophe so the final text reads Customer’s receipt with the customer’s identifier inserted at the placeholder. A second pattern deliberately quotes the placeholder braces and returns them literally. Translators editing that text are editing a small grammar, not an arbitrary string.

The sample uses an ASCII apostrophe in the actual pattern. A typographic apostrophe is another character and should not be substituted as a hidden parser fix. Test the exact pattern that will be shipped in the resource bundle.

Formatting does not escape the output context

The fixture inserts plain record labels and prints them as text. If a formatted message is later inserted into HTML or an SQL statement, MessageFormat does not supply the escaping or binding required for that different sink. Render text safely and keep database parameters separate.

Pin the locale when output stability matters, and avoid sharing a mutable formatter without a thread-ownership policy. Resource bundles organize localized patterns; they do not validate every placeholder or automatically execute your translation tests.

Working program

import java.text.MessageFormat;
import java.util.Locale;
public class ReceiptMessagePattern {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MessageFormat receipt=new MessageFormat("Customer''s receipt: {0}",Locale.ROOT);
        MessageFormat literal=new MessageFormat("Pending '{0}'",Locale.ROOT);
        System.out.println(receipt.format(new Object[]{"R125"}));
        System.out.println(literal.format(new Object[]{"R125"}));
    }
}

Output

Customer's receipt: R125
Pending {0}

Costs and boundaries

Pattern parsing and formatting depend on pattern size, argument count and chosen subformats. A single local formatter avoids shared mutable state but still allocates formatting objects. This fixture checks quoting, not an entire locale catalogue.

Common Mistakes

  • Double literal apostrophes in the pattern where required.
  • Test the actual translated patterns.
  • Formatting is not HTML escaping or SQL parameter binding.

title: Java CountDownLatch: completion counting does not count successful work
summary: A CountDownLatch releases waiting threads when its count reaches zero and cannot be reset for another batch.
body:
A CountDownLatch releases waiting threads when its count reaches zero and cannot be reset for another batch.

This complete program targets Java 8. Its displayed output is checked by the tutorial validation script.

Release the obligation on every exit

The import batch has two worker obligations. One succeeds and increments accepted; the other fails and records failure. Both decrement the latch in finally. The coordinator can then report one accepted record and one failed record without waiting forever for the failed worker.

The latch count records completion obligations, not business success. A loop that decrements only after a successful operation can hang when an exception exits the worker. Keep a separate result or failure channel so reaching zero cannot be mistaken for a successful import.

Bound the wait in the actual service

This program starts two small local threads and joins them after the latch completes. A real import needs a deadline and an interruption policy for stuck I/O. A timed-out coordinator cannot assume the workers stopped or their committed effects disappeared.

Reuse requires a new latch for a new batch. If participants change across several phases, Phaser may describe the coordination better. Either primitive still needs an explicit cancellation contract around tasks and external effects.

Working program

import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
public class ImportCompletionCount {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        CountDownLatch completed=new CountDownLatch(2);
        AtomicInteger accepted=new AtomicInteger(),failed=new AtomicInteger();
        Thread first=new Thread(()->{try{accepted.incrementAndGet();}finally{completed.countDown();}});
        Thread second=new Thread(()->{try{throw new IllegalStateException("bad record");}
            catch(IllegalStateException failure){failed.incrementAndGet();}finally{completed.countDown();}});
        first.start();second.start();completed.await();first.join();second.join();
        System.out.println("accepted="+accepted.get());System.out.println("failed="+failed.get());
        System.out.println("remaining="+completed.getCount());
    }
}

Output

accepted=1
failed=1
remaining=0

Costs and boundaries

The latch holds bounded coordination state while the fixture creates two threads and two counters. Waiting duration depends on worker completion; the latch supplies no deadline on its own. Retaining all individual failures would add storage proportional to the batch size.

Common Mistakes

  • Count down in finally for every registered completion obligation.
  • Keep success and failure evidence separately.
  • Do not reuse a completed latch for a second batch.

title: Java records with arrays: copy on input and output
summary: A record makes its component references final, but an array component remains mutable unless the record defines a defensive-copy policy.
body:
A record makes its component references final, but an array component remains mutable unless the record defines a defensive-copy policy.

This complete program targets Java 17. Its displayed output is checked by the tutorial validation script.

Protect both directions

The batch record clones its incoming amounts array in the compact constructor. A caller then changes the original array without changing the record’s stored amount. The accessor also returns a clone, preventing a later caller from changing the record through the returned array.

Copying only in the constructor protects against the original reference but leaves the accessor as a mutation path. Copying only in the accessor leaves the caller’s original input reference connected to the stored array. Both directions are part of this ownership contract.

Equality needs its own decision

The fixture checks retained values and prints false when comparing two batches containing equal array values. The generated equality method treats an array component as an array object rather than promising element-by-element value equality for the batch. Decide whether that is appropriate before putting such records into sets or caches.

A clone of a primitive array copies its values. An object-array clone copies references, so nested mutable values need another policy. Equality contracts and Shallow ownership become relevant when replacing the amounts with richer business objects.

Working program

public class DefensiveReceiptBatch {
    record Batch(int[] amounts) {
        Batch {amounts=amounts.clone();}
        public int[] amounts(){return amounts.clone();}
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] input={125,75};Batch batch=new Batch(input);input[0]=0;
        int[] output=batch.amounts();output[1]=0;
        System.out.println(batch.amounts()[0]);System.out.println(batch.amounts()[1]);
        System.out.println(batch.equals(new Batch(new int[]{125,75})));
    }
}

Output

125
75
false

Costs and boundaries

Construction and each accessor call take O(n) time and allocate an O(n) array. Repeated accessor calls inside a loop can turn one traversal into repeated copying. A scalar query or explicitly immutable representation may fit a large batch better.

Common Mistakes

  • Final references do not make array contents immutable.
  • Copy both entry and exit paths when that is the ownership contract.
  • Do not assume generated array equality is element-wise.

title: Java Z algorithm: find overlapping pattern matches in linear time
summary: The Z algorithm records how many values at each position match the prefix of a sequence, allowing pattern matches to reuse earlier comparison work.
body:
The Z algorithm records how many values at each position match the prefix of a sequence, allowing pattern matches to reuse earlier comparison work.

This complete program targets Java 8. Its displayed output is checked by the tutorial validation script.

Keep the pattern boundary unambiguous

The search builds one integer sequence from the pattern, a negative separator and the text. UTF-16 code units are nonnegative, so the separator cannot be mistaken for part of either input. A literal character chosen as a separator could already occur in a user’s text and break the boundary.

The stored matching interval supplies a lower bound for comparisons inside it. The algorithm extends beyond that interval only when necessary. A match is reported when the prefix length reaches the entire pattern, so overlapping occurrences such as aba in ababa are retained.

State what an offset measures

Returned offsets count Java UTF-16 code units. They are not grapheme positions for a user-visible caret. The program rejects an empty pattern and caps both input lengths before allocating the combined sequence. Another API can choose an empty-pattern convention, but it must state it rather than inherit it accidentally.

The implementation materializes the input sequence and the Z array, then stores every match. A caller processing enormous text needs a different retention strategy. KMP search is useful when evaluating a streaming pattern workflow, while Grapheme boundaries address display offsets.

Working program

import java.util.*;
public class ReceiptPatternOffsets {
    static List<Integer> find(String pattern,String text) {
        if(pattern.isEmpty() || pattern.length()>100000 || text.length()>100000)throw new IllegalArgumentException("input bounds");
        int boundary=pattern.length();int[] values=new int[boundary+1+text.length()];
        for(int i=0;i<boundary;i++)values[i]=pattern.charAt(i);values[boundary]=-1;
        for(int i=0;i<text.length();i++)values[boundary+1+i]=text.charAt(i);
        int[] matched=new int[values.length];int left=0,right=0;
        List<Integer> offsets=new ArrayList<>();
        for(int index=1;index<values.length;index++) {
            if(index<right)matched[index]=Math.min(right-index,matched[index-left]);
            while(index+matched[index]<values.length && values[matched[index]]==values[index+matched[index]])matched[index]++;
            if(index+matched[index]>right){left=index;right=index+matched[index];}
            if(index>boundary && matched[index]>=boundary)offsets.add(index-boundary-1);
        }
        return offsets;
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(find("aba","ababa"));System.out.println(find("#","a##"));
        try{find("","receipt");}catch(IllegalArgumentException rejected){System.out.println("empty pattern rejected");}
    }
}

Output

[0, 2]
[1, 2]
empty pattern rejected

Costs and boundaries

For pattern length m and text length n, construction and matching take O(m+n) time and O(m+n) working storage. Storing k returned offsets takes O(k) more space. This is an in-memory search over code units, not a streaming or grapheme-aware implementation.

Common Mistakes

  • Use a separator outside the input alphabet.
  • Retain overlapping matches if the contract requires them.
  • Do not label UTF-16 offsets as user-visible character positions.

title: Java graph bridges: track edge identity when parallel edges exist
summary: A bridge is an undirected edge whose removal increases the number of connected components in the graph.
body:
A bridge is an undirected edge whose removal increases the number of connected components in the graph.

This complete program targets Java 8. Its displayed output is checked by the tutorial validation script.

Skip the parent edge, not the parent vertex

The transport graph assigns one identity to each undirected edge and uses that identity on both adjacency entries. DFS skips only the exact edge used to reach the current vertex. If two parallel links connect the same vertices, the other link remains a valid return path and neither is a bridge.

Discovery order and the lowest reachable discovery order supply the bridge test. After visiting an unvisited neighbor, its low value is compared with the current discovery value. The fixture starts a new DFS for every unvisited vertex so a disconnected component is not silently omitted.

The recursion limit is part of this implementation

The API caps vertices at five hundred and edges at five thousand, validates both endpoints and returns sorted original edge IDs. It supports self-loops and parallel links. Larger graphs need an explicit stack or a measured recursion policy; changing the input bound without that review changes the failure risk.

A bridge describes graph connectivity, not a guarantee that a real network fails when that connection stops. Routing, capacity and external paths are different evidence. DFS traversal and Directed components answer related but distinct graph questions.

Working program

import java.util.*;
public class TransportBridgeEdges {
    static class Edge {final int target,id;Edge(int target,int id){this.target=target;this.id=id;}}
    static void visit(int vertex,int parentEdge,List<List<Edge>> graph,int[] discovered,int[] low,int[] clock,List<Integer> bridges) {
        discovered[vertex]=low[vertex]=++clock[0];
        for(Edge edge:graph.get(vertex)) {
            if(edge.id==parentEdge)continue;
            if(discovered[edge.target]==0) {
                visit(edge.target,edge.id,graph,discovered,low,clock,bridges);
                low[vertex]=Math.min(low[vertex],low[edge.target]);
                if(low[edge.target]>discovered[vertex])bridges.add(edge.id);
            } else low[vertex]=Math.min(low[vertex],discovered[edge.target]);
        }
    }
    static List<Integer> bridges(int vertices,int[][] links) {
        if(vertices<1 || vertices>500 || links.length>5000)throw new IllegalArgumentException("graph bounds");
        List<List<Edge>> graph=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<vertices;i++)graph.add(new ArrayList<>());
        for(int id=0;id<links.length;id++) {
            int[] edge=links[id];if(edge.length!=2 || edge[0]<0 || edge[0]>=vertices || edge[1]<0 || edge[1]>=vertices)throw new IllegalArgumentException("endpoint");
            graph.get(edge[0]).add(new Edge(edge[1],id));graph.get(edge[1]).add(new Edge(edge[0],id));
        }
        List<Integer> critical=new ArrayList<>();int[] discovered=new int[vertices],low=new int[vertices],clock={0};
        for(int vertex=0;vertex<vertices;vertex++)if(discovered[vertex]==0)visit(vertex,-1,graph,discovered,low,clock,critical);
        Collections.sort(critical);return critical;
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(bridges(4,new int[][]{{0,1},{1,2},{2,0},{1,3}}));
        System.out.println(bridges(2,new int[][]{{0,1},{0,1}}));
    }
}

Output

[3]
[]

Costs and boundaries

DFS and adjacency construction take O(v+e) time and storage. Sorting b returned bridge IDs adds O(b log b) time. Recursive stack depth can reach v, which is why this fixture bounds vertices; a simple path is an adversarial depth case.

Common Mistakes

  • Skip the exact parent edge when parallel links are allowed.
  • Visit every disconnected component.
  • Do not omit stack depth from the input contract.

title: Java matrix-chain DP: minimize multiplication work without reordering matrices
summary: Matrix-chain interval DP chooses the multiplication parentheses that minimize scalar work while preserving matrix order.
body:
Matrix-chain interval DP chooses the multiplication parentheses that minimize scalar work while preserving matrix order.

This complete program targets Java 8. Its displayed output is checked by the tutorial validation script.

Order is fixed, grouping is not

The dimension sequence ten, twenty, thirty, forty describes three compatible matrices. Multiplying the first two before the third costs 18000 scalar multiplications; the other grouping costs 32000. The recurrence considers every split of an interval instead of applying a local cheapest-pair rule.

An interval containing one matrix costs zero because no multiplication is required. Larger intervals combine the two smaller interval costs with the product of their outer and split dimensions. The program returns the cost, not the parenthesized expression or the numeric matrix result.

Bound arithmetic before allocating state

The fixture accepts at most ten matrices and dimensions between one and one thousand. Multiplication is promoted to long before the product is formed. Those declared bounds keep every candidate cost within long; unrestricted dimensions would need checked arithmetic or a wider representation.

The algorithm assumes ordinary dense matrix multiplication as its cost model. Cache behavior, sparsity and different multiplication algorithms can change real runtime. Benchmark boundaries prevent an operation-count model from being mistaken for a measured performance ranking.

Working program

public class MatrixPlanCost {
    static long minimum(int[] dimensions) {
        if(dimensions.length<2 || dimensions.length>11)throw new IllegalArgumentException("chain size");
        for(int dimension:dimensions)if(dimension<1 || dimension>1000)throw new IllegalArgumentException("dimension");
        int count=dimensions.length-1;long[][] cost=new long[count][count];
        for(int length=2;length<=count;length++)for(int left=0;left+length<=count;left++) {
            int right=left+length-1;cost[left][right]=Long.MAX_VALUE;
            for(int split=left;split<right;split++) {
                long candidate=cost[left][split]+cost[split+1][right]
                    +(long)dimensions[left]*dimensions[split+1]*dimensions[right+1];
                cost[left][right]=Math.min(cost[left][right],candidate);
            }
        }
        return cost[0][count-1];
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(minimum(new int[]{10,20,30,40}));System.out.println(minimum(new int[]{10,20}));
        try{minimum(new int[]{10,0,20});}catch(IllegalArgumentException rejected){System.out.println("dimension rejected");}
    }
}

Output

18000
0
dimension rejected

Costs and boundaries

For n matrices the recurrence takes O(n cubed) time and O(n squared) storage. Returning the actual grouping needs split storage and reconstruction. This fixture caps n at ten and does not allocate or multiply the matrices themselves.

Common Mistakes

  • Preserve matrix order while changing parentheses.
  • Promote before multiplying dimensions.
  • Do not interpret a scalar-count estimate as a runtime benchmark.

title: Java LinkedList null elements: an empty-head ambiguity
summary: LinkedList permits null elements, so a null result from peekFirst does not prove that the list is empty.
body:
LinkedList permits null elements, so a null result from peekFirst does not prove that the list is empty.

This complete Java 8 program has a checked output. Compile it as the named public class, then run it without additional libraries.

Separate absence from payload

A work queue that accepts null cannot distinguish an empty queue from a queue whose first work item is null by calling peekFirst alone. Check isEmpty before reading, or reject null at the application's admission boundary.

getFirst throws on an empty list but returns null when the first stored value is null. That exception is a different contract, not a substitute for explicit input validation. An ArrayDeque rejects null, which removes this particular ambiguity if the application only needs deque operations. See the ArrayDeque lesson before choosing a representation.

Keep the invariant near insertion

The fixture prints the empty and populated states without conflating them. It removes the null element only after checking membership. A real queue should decide whether null is legal before adding a worker, rather than forcing each consumer to guess what null means.

Working program

import java.util.LinkedList;
public class ReceiptQueueNullBoundary {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> receipts = new LinkedList<>();
        System.out.println("empty=" + receipts.isEmpty() + ", head=" + receipts.peekFirst());
        receipts.addFirst(null);
        System.out.println("empty=" + receipts.isEmpty() + ", head=" + receipts.peekFirst());
        System.out.println("removedNull=" + (receipts.removeFirst() == null));
    }
}

Output

empty=true, head=null
empty=false, head=null
removedNull=true

Costs and boundaries

Endpoint access is constant time; storing n nodes takes linear memory plus per-node references. Null handling changes the API meaning, not those asymptotic costs.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use peekFirst() == null as the sole empty check when null is allowed.
  • Do not switch to ArrayDeque while still inserting null.
  • Do not hide a null admission policy in each consumer.

title: Java Deque empty operations: choose return values or exceptions
summary: Deque offers endpoint operations that either report an empty container with null or throw NoSuchElementException.
body:
Deque offers endpoint operations that either report an empty container with null or throw NoSuchElementException.

This complete Java 8 program has a checked output. Compile it as the named public class, then run it without additional libraries.

Choose one failure shape

pollFirst returns null when an empty deque has no head; removeFirst throws. peekFirst and getFirst make the same distinction without removal. Which pair fits the caller depends on whether empty is ordinary control flow or a broken precondition.

This program uses ArrayDeque, which refuses null members. That makes a null poll result unambiguous. LinkedList can hold null, so a caller using its nullable methods must check emptiness separately. The null-head case shows the collision.

Do not confuse capacity with emptiness

offerFirst reports insertion acceptance as a boolean; addFirst may throw when a capacity-constrained deque refuses an insertion. ArrayDeque grows as required, so this example does not exercise a capacity limit. The failure behavior belongs to the implementation and workload, not just the method name.

Working program

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;
public class DispatchDequeContracts {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ArrayDeque<String> pending = new ArrayDeque<>();
        System.out.println("poll=" + pending.pollFirst());
        try { pending.removeFirst(); }
        catch (NoSuchElementException empty) { System.out.println("remove rejected"); }
        pending.offerLast("receipt-37");
        System.out.println("peek=" + pending.peekFirst());
        System.out.println("take=" + pending.removeFirst());
    }
}

Output

poll=null
remove rejected
peek=receipt-37
take=receipt-37

Costs and boundaries

These endpoint calls have amortized constant-time behavior for ArrayDeque. Memory grows with retained elements and backing-array capacity; this example is not a bounded work queue.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat a null poll result as universally unambiguous across implementations.
  • Do not handle an empty deque by catching every RuntimeException.
  • Do not assume offer means a producer has durable acceptance.

title: Java LinkedList clone: copied nodes, shared element objects
summary: LinkedList.clone creates a new list structure while retaining references to the original element objects.
body:
LinkedList.clone creates a new list structure while retaining references to the original element objects.

This complete Java 8 program has a checked output. Compile it as the named public class, then run it without additional libraries.

Membership and element ownership differ

Removing a record from the copy does not remove a node from the original. Changing a mutable record already present in both lists is visible from both. This is a shallow copy, and an ordinary copy constructor has the same element-sharing issue.

The fixture uses a named InvoiceFlag object so the shared reference is observable. The two collections are distinct, but their first element has the same identity. An immutable element model or deliberate element-copy operation is needed when consumers must not share state.

Do not call this a snapshot of a mutable graph

Copying n node references costs linear time and additional node storage. It does not copy every object reachable through those references. A process boundary needs serialization rules and schema handling; clone supplies neither. Views and snapshots examines the related membership question.

Working program

import java.util.LinkedList;
public class InvoiceFlagCopy {
    static final class InvoiceFlag {
        String state;
        InvoiceFlag(String state) { this.state = state; }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<InvoiceFlag> original = new LinkedList<>();
        original.add(new InvoiceFlag("queued"));
        LinkedList<InvoiceFlag> copy = (LinkedList<InvoiceFlag>) original.clone();
        copy.getFirst().state = "reviewed";
        System.out.println("shared=" + (original.getFirst() == copy.getFirst()));
        System.out.println("original=" + original.getFirst().state);
        copy.clear();
        System.out.println("sizes=" + original.size() + "," + copy.size());
    }
}

Output

shared=true
original=reviewed
sizes=1,0

Costs and boundaries

Cloning a list with n elements costs O(n) time and O(n) new node space. The memory of each referenced element is still shared until the application copies it separately.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not infer deep copy from distinct list identities.
  • Do not expose mutable elements as though an unmodifiable wrapper froze them.
  • Do not use clone as a serialization or tenant-isolation boundary.

title: Java LinkedList indexed loops: a hidden quadratic traversal
summary: LinkedList.get(index) walks from the nearer endpoint, so a full indexed loop repeats walks and can take quadratic time.
body:
LinkedList.get(index) walks from the nearer endpoint, so a full indexed loop repeats walks and can take quadratic time.

This complete Java 8 program has a checked output. Compile it as the named public class, then run it without additional libraries.

Iteration keeps a moving cursor

Both loops in the fixture produce the same receipt sequence. The first calls get for each position; each call can start a new traversal from the head or tail. The second advances one iterator, so the total traversal is linear.

A tiny list will not reveal this difference in a wall-clock test. The cost follows from the operation contract and traversal pattern; do not publish a fabricated speedup percentage. If random indexing is the requirement, ArrayList better matches the access pattern.

Keep mutation under the iterator

The program only reads. When removing items during traversal, use the iterator's remove method and respect its state rules. Repeated external removals also change positions and can invalidate an iterator. The cursor lesson covers local edits.

Working program

import java.util.LinkedList;
public class ReceiptScanCost {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> receipts = new LinkedList<>();
        receipts.add("R-71"); receipts.add("R-72"); receipts.add("R-73");
        StringBuilder indexed = new StringBuilder();
        for (int position = 0; position < receipts.size(); position++) indexed.append(receipts.get(position)).append(' ');
        StringBuilder iterated = new StringBuilder();
        for (String receipt : receipts) iterated.append(receipt).append(' ');
        System.out.println(indexed.toString().trim());
        System.out.println(iterated.toString().trim());
    }
}

Output

R-71 R-72 R-73
R-71 R-72 R-73

Costs and boundaries

An indexed full scan is O(n²) in the worst and aggregate sense; a single iterator traversal is O(n). Both hold only a constant amount of traversal state apart from output storage.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume List.get has the same cost for every implementation.
  • Do not claim timing from a three-item fixture.
  • Do not repeatedly obtain listIterator(index) inside a traversal loop.

title: Java LinkedList duplicate removal: first and last occurrence
summary: LinkedList can remove the first or last equal element, and those choices produce different order-preserving results when duplicates exist.
body:
LinkedList can remove the first or last equal element, and those choices produce different order-preserving results when duplicates exist.

This complete Java 8 program has a checked output. Compile it as the named public class, then run it without additional libraries.

Define which duplicate is retired

A receipt feed may contain two events with the same code separated by another event. removeFirstOccurrence removes the earlier one; removeLastOccurrence removes the later one. Neither method is an idempotent record-key policy by itself, because equality may cover fewer fields than the domain's identity.

Both operations scan to find a match. LinkedList removes a known node cheaply after locating it, but lookup is still linear. A map or set with a stable key is a better fit when repeated membership checks dominate.

Check the return value

The boolean reports whether an equal value was found and removed. A false result should not be reported as successful cleanup if the caller expected a pending item. The fixture compares the remaining order after each operation.

Working program

import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.Arrays;
public class ReceiptDuplicateRetirement {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> events = new LinkedList<>(Arrays.asList("R-9", "R-10", "R-9"));
        System.out.println("first=" + events.removeFirstOccurrence("R-9") + " " + events);
        events.addFirst("R-9");
        System.out.println("last=" + events.removeLastOccurrence("R-9") + " " + events);
        System.out.println("missing=" + events.removeLastOccurrence("R-11"));
    }
}

Output

first=true [R-10, R-9]
last=true [R-9, R-10]
missing=false

Costs and boundaries

Each occurrence search takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space; the existing list retains O(n) nodes. The call is not a transactional deduplication operation.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not ignore a false removal result when absence is an error.
  • Do not confuse object equality with a business event identifier.
  • Do not sell fast relinking as fast value lookup.

title: Java List.remove with Integer: index or value
summary: List.remove(int) removes by position, while List.remove(Object) removes the first equal value.
body:
List.remove(int) removes by position, while List.remove(Object) removes the first equal value.

This complete Java 8 program has a checked output. Compile it as the named public class, then run it without additional libraries.

The compile-time argument type selects the overload

For List<Integer>, passing the literal 2 calls remove(int), not remove(Object). A queue of numeric receipt codes can silently delete the wrong element if that index exists. Cast to Integer or call Integer.valueOf when the intended operation is value removal.

The fixture prints both outcomes from separate lists. The first list loses the element at index two. The second loses the element whose value is two. Both operations are legal, which makes this easy to miss during review.

Check the representation cost

ArrayList shifts later references after removal; LinkedList searches for a matching value and then relinks nodes. Neither representation turns value lookup into constant time. When code needs key-based deletion at scale, a map keyed by the receipt identifier may be the better model.

Working program

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Arrays;
public class NumericReceiptRemoval {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> byIndex = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(2, 7, 9));
        byIndex.remove(2);
        List<Integer> byValue = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(2, 7, 9));
        byValue.remove(Integer.valueOf(2));
        System.out.println("index=" + byIndex);
        System.out.println("value=" + byValue);
    }
}

Output

index=[2, 7]
value=[7, 9]

Costs and boundaries

Value removal requires O(n) search in a list. ArrayList index removal may shift O(n) references; a LinkedList positional lookup also traverses O(n) nodes. The overload decision happens at compile time.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume a numeric literal means a numeric value in remove.
  • Do not use a cast to change the stored element type accidentally.
  • Do not omit the absent-value behavior from an API contract.

title: Java synchronizedList iteration: hold the wrapper lock
summary: Collections.synchronizedList serializes individual calls, but a compound iteration still needs a caller-held lock on the wrapper.
body:
Collections.synchronizedList serializes individual calls, but a compound iteration still needs a caller-held lock on the wrapper.

This complete Java 8 program has a checked output. Compile it as the named public class, then run it without additional libraries.

The lock covers the whole traversal

A worker may mutate a shared list between the iterator's next calls even when every individual list operation is synchronized. The caller must synchronize on the returned wrapper while iterating. Synchronizing on the original backing list is a different monitor and does not coordinate with the wrapper.

The fixture does not start a competing thread. It demonstrates the required monitor placement and a stable sum in a single process; it is not evidence that a production workload avoids contention or starvation.

Prefer a clearer ownership model when possible

A copied snapshot avoids holding a shared lock during slow processing, but it is stale as soon as the copy finishes and shares mutable element objects. A concurrent queue or a single owning worker may make the application contract easier to reason about. View and snapshot ownership covers that distinction.

Working program

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
public class SharedReceiptBatchRead {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> amounts = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
        amounts.add(12); amounts.add(18);
        int total = 0;
        synchronized (amounts) {
            for (int amount : amounts) total += amount;
        }
        System.out.println("total=" + total);
    }
}

Output

total=30

Costs and boundaries

A full protected traversal is O(n) and keeps the monitor for its duration. Concurrent writers wait for that lock; the code provides mutual exclusion, not parallel read scalability or a durable snapshot.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not rely on synchronized individual calls to make a multi-call loop atomic.
  • Do not lock the unsynchronized backing list instead of the wrapper.
  • Do not run blocking network work while holding the list lock.

title: Java nested classes: instance capture versus static ownership
summary: A non-static inner class carries an enclosing instance reference; a static nested class has no implicit reference to an outer object.
body:
A non-static inner class carries an enclosing instance reference; a static nested class has no implicit reference to an outer object.

This complete Java 8 program has a checked output. Compile it as the named public class, then run it without additional libraries.

Make retained ownership explicit

A dispatch queue holding an inner ReceiptTask also retains its owning DispatchSession. That can keep session state reachable after the request that created it. A static nested task stores only the fields passed to its constructor, so its ownership is visible in the class definition.

The fixture prints a task from each form. It does not measure heap retention; the reachability consequence follows from the implicit enclosing reference. If the task really needs live session state, passing that dependency deliberately may still be the right design.

Package boundaries remain separate

Static nested does not mean globally shared or thread-safe. Access modifiers still determine visibility across packages, and a mutable field remains mutable. For an API payload, a top-level or record type may be clearer than either nested form.

Working program

public class DispatchSessionOwnership {
    private final String tenant;
    DispatchSessionOwnership(String tenant) { this.tenant = tenant; }
    final class InnerTask {
        String label() { return tenant + ":inner"; }
    }
    static final class StaticTask {
        private final String tenant;
        StaticTask(String tenant) { this.tenant = tenant; }
        String label() { return tenant + ":static"; }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        DispatchSessionOwnership session = new DispatchSessionOwnership("east");
        System.out.println(session.new InnerTask().label());
        System.out.println(new StaticTask("west").label());
    }
}

Output

east:inner
west:static

Costs and boundaries

Both task forms have constant-time construction in this fixture. The inner task includes an implicit owner reference, which can extend the owner's lifetime while the task remains reachable.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat static nested as an automatic concurrency guarantee.
  • Do not queue an inner object without considering its retained owner.
  • Do not confuse package access with nested-class membership.

title: Java Properties precedence: merge sources deliberately
summary: Properties stores string keys and values; application precedence is determined by the order and policy used to combine sources.
body:
Properties stores string keys and values; application precedence is determined by the order and policy used to combine sources.

This complete Java 8 program has a checked output. Compile it as the named public class, then run it without additional libraries.

Choose which source wins

This fixture starts with packaged defaults and then overlays a local override. The second putAll wins on duplicate keys. java.util.Properties does not impose a standard deployment precedence between files, environment variables and command-line flags for an application.

A caller should define and test the priority of each accepted source. In a Spring application the framework has its own property-source ordering, covered by Spring profile and property precedence. Do not copy this fixture's order into Spring and assume it overrides Boot's behavior.

Validate before starting work

The program parses the merged timeout as a number and rejects a nonpositive value. Real services also need bounds, units and a policy for unknown keys. Never print a secret just to prove precedence; this example uses a harmless timeout setting.

Working program

import java.util.Properties;
public class ImportTimeoutConfiguration {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Properties defaults = new Properties();
        defaults.setProperty("import.timeout.seconds", "8");
        Properties local = new Properties();
        local.setProperty("import.timeout.seconds", "12");
        Properties effective = new Properties();
        effective.putAll(defaults);
        effective.putAll(local);
        int seconds = Integer.parseInt(effective.getProperty("import.timeout.seconds"));
        if (seconds <= 0 || seconds > 60) throw new IllegalArgumentException("timeout range");
        System.out.println("timeout=" + seconds);
    }
}

Output

timeout=12

Costs and boundaries

Merging n entries takes O(n) expected map work and retains a new map of O(n) references and strings. Parsing and validation should happen once at startup, not on every request.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume Properties chooses file or environment precedence for you.
  • Do not treat a parsed integer as a validated duration.
  • Do not log effective secret values during diagnostics.

title: Java LinkedList subList: a live window, not a snapshot
summary: LinkedList.subList returns a backed view whose permitted edits change the original list.
body:
LinkedList.subList returns a backed view whose permitted edits change the original list.

The Java 8 program below compiles without external libraries; its output is checked against a real run.

Treat the window as shared state

A billing batch keeps four receipt identifiers and exposes only its middle two to a correction step. Setting one value through the window updates the original list. Clearing the window removes those two nodes from the backing list; the end elements remain.

The method returns a view, not a detached copy. If a caller needs a stable membership snapshot, construct a new list from the window and decide separately whether its element objects must be copied. View ownership covers that second question.

Keep structural changes inside the view

The List contract says the view's semantics become undefined if the backing list is structurally changed outside the view. A particular JVM may throw a ConcurrentModificationException after that mistake, but code should not depend on the exception. Instead, keep one owner for structural edits or rebuild the window after the parent changes.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.List;
public class ReceiptCorrectionWindow {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> receipts = new LinkedList<>(Arrays.asList("R-11", "R-12", "R-13", "R-14"));
        List<String> window = receipts.subList(1, 3);
        window.set(0, "R-12-rechecked");
        System.out.println(receipts);
        window.clear();
        System.out.println(receipts);
    }
}

Output

[R-11, R-12-rechecked, R-13, R-14]
[R-11, R-14]

Costs and boundaries

Obtaining a subList is a view operation; locating and changing a linked-list position may traverse nodes. Clearing k elements still changes the backing structure. The view retains a reference to that structure rather than allocating k independent elements.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call a backed view an immutable snapshot.
  • Do not structurally mutate the parent while continuing to use an old view.
  • Do not assume copying list membership deep-copies mutable elements.

title: Java LinkedList descendingIterator: inspect and remove from the tail
summary: LinkedList.descendingIterator visits nodes from tail to head without first copying them into another collection.
body:
LinkedList.descendingIterator visits nodes from tail to head without first copying them into another collection.

The Java 8 program below compiles without external libraries; its output is checked against a real run.

Use the iterator for the edit

A retry queue holds three receipt states. The cursor reads the newest state first and removes the retry state through its own remove method. That is a cursor-local structural edit. Calling queue.remove while the cursor is active would create a different mutation path.

The fixture records the order it saw and then prints the remaining queue in its original head-to-tail order. Reverse traversal does not reverse the underlying list. For a permanent reordered list, use an explicit mutation or copy policy.

Do not use fail-fast as a lock

This iterator is still part of a mutable LinkedList. If another thread changes the queue, synchronize access or give a single worker ownership; an exception is a best-effort bug signal, not an isolation guarantee. See whole-traversal locking for the wrapper contract.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class RetryQueueReverseRead {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> states = new LinkedList<>(Arrays.asList("queued", "retry", "settled"));
        StringBuilder seen = new StringBuilder();
        for (Iterator<String> cursor = states.descendingIterator(); cursor.hasNext();) {
            String state = cursor.next();
            if (seen.length() > 0) seen.append(',');
            seen.append(state);
            if (state.equals("retry")) cursor.remove();
        }
        System.out.println(seen);
        System.out.println(states);
    }
}

Output

settled,retry,queued
[queued, settled]

Costs and boundaries

A full descending scan is O(n) time with O(1) cursor state, excluding the output string. Removing the current known node avoids a separate value search; it does not make arbitrary lookup constant time.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call list.remove while expecting an existing cursor to stay valid.
  • Do not mistake reverse iteration for a reversed copy.
  • Do not use fail-fast behavior for thread coordination.

title: Java LinkedList toArray(T[]): the null terminator boundary
summary: LinkedList.toArray(T[]) writes list members into a typed array and sets the first spare slot to null when the supplied array is larger.
body:
LinkedList.toArray(T[]) writes list members into a typed array and sets the first spare slot to null when the supplied array is larger.

The Java 8 program below compiles without external libraries; its output is checked against a real run.

Only one spare slot is reset

The supplied array starts with old values. Two receipt identifiers replace its first two positions, index two becomes null, and index three retains its old value. The API does not promise to clear the entire unused tail. A downstream reader that scans every slot can accidentally process stale data.

If the supplied array is too small, the method allocates another array with the supplied runtime component type. Always use the returned reference; assuming the original was filled is wrong in that case.

Null may also be a member

LinkedList permits null elements. The first null in a typed array is not a reliable length marker unless the application prohibits null members. Use the known list size or the returned array length according to the receiving API's contract. Null head ambiguity is the same policy problem at a different boundary.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class ReceiptArrayExport {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> receipts = new LinkedList<>(Arrays.asList("R-21", "R-22"));
        String[] reusable = {"old-0", "old-1", "old-2", "old-3"};
        String[] exported = receipts.toArray(reusable);
        System.out.println("same array=" + (exported == reusable));
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(exported));
    }
}

Output

same array=true
[R-21, R-22, null, old-3]

Costs and boundaries

Copying n references into an array is O(n) time. A sufficiently large supplied array avoids allocating a new array, but retained element objects are still shared; the operation does not deep-copy them.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not read the entire oversized array as fresh list data.
  • Do not use null as a length marker while null list elements are legal.
  • Do not discard the returned array when the input array may be too small.

title: Java LinkedList sort: stable order needs temporary array work
summary: List.sort orders a modifiable LinkedList by a comparator while preserving the relative order of equal-ranked elements.
body:
List.sort orders a modifiable LinkedList by a comparator while preserving the relative order of equal-ranked elements.

The Java 8 program below compiles without external libraries; its output is checked against a real run.

State the tie rule

Three receipts arrive in order R-11, R-12, R-13. Sorting by priority moves R-12 first while R-11 remains before R-13 because both have priority two. That stable tie behavior is useful only if encounter order itself is meaningful and retained through earlier processing.

A comparator must provide a consistent ordering. Subtracting large integer priorities to compare them can overflow; Comparator.comparingInt avoids that arithmetic. Comparator contracts covers transitivity and equality issues.

Do not assume pointer relinking removes memory cost

The Java 8 List default sort obtains an array, sorts it, then writes values back through a list iterator. LinkedList nodes remain, but the algorithm still needs array storage. For repeated indexed queries after sorting, an array-backed representation may serve the workload better.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class ReceiptPrioritySort {
    static final class Receipt {
        final String id; final int priority;
        Receipt(String id, int priority) { this.id = id; this.priority = priority; }
        public String toString() { return id; }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<Receipt> receipts = new LinkedList<>(Arrays.asList(
            new Receipt("R-11", 2), new Receipt("R-12", 1), new Receipt("R-13", 2)));
        receipts.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(receipt -> receipt.priority));
        System.out.println(receipts);
    }
}

Output

[R-12, R-11, R-13]

Costs and boundaries

General comparison sorting is O(n log n) in the worst case. The Java 8 default List.sort uses an array of n references plus sorting workspace; no claim of in-place constant memory is made.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use subtraction as a general integer comparator.
  • Do not assume stable order can repair an earlier unordered source.
  • Do not assume a linked structure removes the sort's array allocation.

title: Java LinkedList binarySearch: comparisons are not the whole cost
summary: Collections.binarySearch can search a sorted LinkedList, but locating positions in a non-random-access list still traverses links.
body:
Collections.binarySearch can search a sorted LinkedList, but locating positions in a non-random-access list still traverses links.

The Java 8 program below compiles without external libraries; its output is checked against a real run.

Sort under the same ordering

The search contract requires ascending order under the same comparison used by the search. The fixture finds twenty at position one. Thirty is absent, so the negative result encodes insertion point two. Decode a negative result as -result-1, not as an array position to index directly.

If equal values occur several times, the returned matching index is not specified to be the first duplicate. A range lookup needs a separate lower-bound policy.

Choose a structure for repeated reads

For a large non-RandomAccess list, the JDK uses iterator-based search with O(n) link traversals and O(log n) comparisons. A small fixture cannot measure that cost. If the workload needs repeated random-access binary searches, an ArrayList or primitive array may better fit; if it needs key lookup, consider a map.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class SortedReceiptCodeLookup {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<Integer> codes = new LinkedList<>(Arrays.asList(10, 20, 40));
        int found = Collections.binarySearch(codes, 20);
        int missing = Collections.binarySearch(codes, 30);
        System.out.println("found=" + found);
        System.out.println("missing=" + missing + ", insert=" + (-missing - 1));
    }
}

Output

found=1
missing=-3, insert=2

Costs and boundaries

For a large LinkedList, the API documents O(n) link traversals and O(log n) comparisons. The index returned is a position, not a constant-time path to that node for later get(index) calls.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not search an unsorted list and interpret the result.
  • Do not promise O(log n) total work solely from the algorithm's name.
  • Do not assume the first equal element is returned.

title: Java LinkedList fail-fast iterators: a bug signal, not safety
summary: A LinkedList iterator may detect structural changes made outside that iterator and report ConcurrentModificationException.
body:
A LinkedList iterator may detect structural changes made outside that iterator and report ConcurrentModificationException.

The Java 8 program below compiles without external libraries; its output is checked against a real run.

The single-thread fixture exposes the mistake

The cursor reads one receipt, then the program appends another through the list. On this checked runtime the next cursor step throws. That is a diagnostic for a violated traversal contract. The original list still contains the new receipt.

A correct single-thread edit can use the iterator's own remove method, as in reverse traversal, or finish the traversal before mutating the list. Do not catch the exception and pretend the loop completed all items.

No concurrency guarantee follows

Oracle describes fail-fast behavior as best effort under unsynchronized concurrent change. It cannot be used to assert that all races are detected or that partial work rolled back. A shared queue needs a synchronization or ownership policy, not an exception handler.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.ConcurrentModificationException;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class ReceiptCursorInvalidation {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> receipts = new LinkedList<>(Arrays.asList("R-31", "R-32"));
        Iterator<String> cursor = receipts.iterator();
        System.out.println("first=" + cursor.next());
        receipts.addLast("R-33");
        try { cursor.next(); }
        catch (ConcurrentModificationException invalidated) { System.out.println("cursor invalidated"); }
        System.out.println(receipts);
    }
}

Output

first=R-31
cursor invalidated
[R-31, R-32, R-33]

Costs and boundaries

The example has no concurrent thread; it checks one deterministic misuse on the local runtime. Iterator traversal is O(n) for n elements. Exception detection is not an atomic snapshot or a synchronization mechanism.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not depend on fail-fast exceptions to prove absence of races.
  • Do not continue a partially processed batch as though traversal succeeded.
  • Do not make structural changes through the list while an iterator owns the edit path.

title: Java LinkedList ListIterator: the add, set and remove state machine
summary: A LinkedList list iterator can edit around its cursor, but set and remove require a preceding next or previous call.
body:
A LinkedList list iterator can edit around its cursor, but set and remove require a preceding next or previous call.

The cursor sits between nodes

Start between the first and second receipt. add inserts a new receipt before the next node. It leaves the cursor after the inserted node; it does not make that insertion the most recently returned element. Calling set immediately after add therefore fails with IllegalStateException.

After next returns the original second node, set can replace it. remove can then delete that returned node. The result keeps the inserted receipt. This is safer than editing the list directly while the cursor is active. Fail-fast behavior is only a bug signal for competing edits.

Choose cursor work for sequential edits

A listIterator(index) starts at a position, and locating a middle position may traverse links. Once positioned, walking and editing adjacent nodes avoids repeated indexed scans. See indexed traversal cost before writing a loop that calls get(i) on every pass.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.ListIterator;
public class ReceiptCursorEdit {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> receipts = new LinkedList<>(Arrays.asList("R-10", "R-30"));
        ListIterator<String> cursor = receipts.listIterator(1);
        cursor.add("R-20");
        try { cursor.set("invalid"); }
        catch (IllegalStateException rejected) { System.out.println("set requires a returned node"); }
        System.out.println("next=" + cursor.next());
        cursor.set("R-30-reviewed");
        cursor.remove();
        System.out.println(receipts);
    }
}

Output

set requires a returned node
next=R-30
[R-10, R-20]

Costs and boundaries

Initial positioning may take O(n); a full cursor walk takes O(n) time and O(1) cursor state. The fixture checks Java 8 behavior and one invalid transition. It does not make concurrent edits safe.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call set or remove immediately after add.
  • Do not edit the backing list through another path while the cursor is active.
  • Do not turn sequential edits into repeated get(index) calls.

title: Java checkedList on LinkedList: runtime checks at a raw boundary
summary: Collections.checkedList returns a backed view that rejects inserts of the wrong runtime element type through that view.
body:
Collections.checkedList returns a backed view that rejects inserts of the wrong runtime element type through that view.

Guard the boundary that receives raw values

A legacy plugin exposes a raw List. Its attempt to insert an Integer through the checked view throws ClassCastException immediately, where the bad value enters. The original LinkedList still accepts valid strings and the view reflects them because it is backed by the same list.

The guard is not a copy and cannot protect the underlying list if some caller still holds a direct reference. It checks runtime classes on attempted writes through the wrapper; generic type parameters alone are erased. Generics explains compile-time checking, while backed views explains ownership.

Do not treat this as data validation

A String can still contain an invalid receipt identifier. Validate domain rules separately. A checked list also does not deeply inspect mutable elements or make access thread-safe.

Working program

import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.List;
public class CheckedReceiptBoundary {
    @SuppressWarnings({"rawtypes", "unchecked"})
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> receipts = new LinkedList<>();
        List<String> checked = Collections.checkedList(receipts, String.class);
        List legacyPlugin = checked;
        try { legacyPlugin.add(41); }
        catch (ClassCastException rejected) { System.out.println("wrong runtime type"); }
        checked.add("R-41");
        System.out.println(receipts);
    }
}

Output

wrong runtime type
[R-41]

Costs and boundaries

The wrapper delegates to the backing list and adds a runtime type check on its write paths. It does not deep-copy n elements, isolate callers holding the backing list, or validate receipt syntax.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expose the unwrapped list to code expected to respect the guard.
  • Do not confuse a String type check with receipt-format validation.
  • Do not assume a checked view is immutable or synchronized.

title: Java LinkedList retainAll: duplicates survive membership filtering
summary: LinkedList.retainAll removes each element absent from the supplied collection; it does not turn the list into a set.
body:
LinkedList.retainAll removes each element absent from the supplied collection; it does not turn the list into a set.

Keep list multiplicity separate from membership

The allowed collection contains one receipt code and null. The source list holds that code twice. Both copies survive, the rejected code disappears, and null remains because the membership policy included it. If null is invalid in the domain, reject it before filtering rather than assuming retainAll cleans it.

Matching uses equality as implemented by the elements and the argument collection. Mutable keys, inconsistent equality or unexpectedly expensive membership checks can change both behavior and cost. For a stable policy, build a dedicated immutable set of allowed identifiers and decide whether order and duplicates matter.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.Set;
public class ReceiptRetentionPolicy {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> receipts = new LinkedList<>(Arrays.asList("R-11", "R-12", "R-11", null));
        Set<String> allowed = new HashSet<>(Arrays.asList("R-11", null));
        System.out.println("changed=" + receipts.retainAll(allowed));
        System.out.println(receipts);
    }
}

Output

changed=true
[R-11, R-11, null]

Costs and boundaries

A pass must inspect the n source elements; membership cost depends on the supplied collection's contains behavior. A hash-based allowed set normally reduces repeated lookup work, subject to correct hashCode and equals. The operation mutates the list; it is not an audit trail.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume retainAll deduplicates.
  • Do not let an allowed null silently bypass a domain rule.
  • Do not pass a slow membership collection into a large repeated filter without measuring.
