title: Arrays.asList in Java: fixed-size list backed by the original array
summary: Arrays.asList creates a fixed-size List view over an array, so element replacement is shared in both directions.
body:
Arrays.asList creates a fixed-size List view over an array, so element replacement is shared in both directions.

Separate size from value mutation

The list permits set, and that write changes the array slot. Updating the array slot also changes what the list reads. Structural operations such as add or remove are unsupported because the underlying array length cannot change. The view retains the array; neither side is a snapshot.

The generic varargs signature has a trap with primitive arrays: Arrays.asList(int[]) produces a one-element List<int[]> rather than boxing each integer. For boxed integers, use Integer[] or an explicit stream/loop conversion.

Make the copy boundary explicit

When a caller needs an independent mutable list, construct an ArrayList from this view. That copies element references, not mutable element objects. List.copyOf instead gives an unmodifiable container snapshot, while unmodifiableList stays backed by its source.

Passing the view across ownership boundaries lets later array edits change the recipient's observations. Treat that shared backing as part of the API contract.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;

public class ArrayBackedDispatchList {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] dispatchIds = {"load-15", "seal-47"};
        List<String> view = Arrays.asList(dispatchIds);
        view.set(0, "load-82");
        System.out.println(dispatchIds[0]);
        dispatchIds[1] = "seal-35";
        System.out.println(view);
        try { view.add("ship-20"); }
        catch (UnsupportedOperationException rejected) { System.out.println("size change rejected"); }
        int[] primitiveKeys = {47, 82};
        System.out.println(Arrays.asList(primitiveKeys).size());
    }
}

Output

load-82
[load-82, seal-35]
size change rejected
1

Cost and ownership

Creating the view does not copy the array and uses a small wrapper allocation. Indexed reads and replacements are O(1). Copying into a separate list costs O(n) references and still does not clone referenced objects.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call Arrays.asList a resizable ArrayList.
  • Do not expect primitive array elements to become separate boxed list members.
  • Do not hand off the view if later array edits must be invisible.

title: Collections.unmodifiableList is a live view, not a snapshot
summary: Collections.unmodifiableList rejects mutation through the wrapper but reflects changes made through its backing list.
body:
Collections.unmodifiableList rejects mutation through the wrapper but reflects changes made through its backing list.

Block one path, not every alias

The wrapper's add and remove methods throw UnsupportedOperationException. A code path that still owns the mutable source can append, and the wrapper then exposes the appended element. This is read-only access through one reference, not immutability of the underlying state.

If an API must freeze the container membership at handoff time, List.copyOf takes an unmodifiable container snapshot. It still retains references to mutable elements. Stronger isolation requires a policy for those elements too.

Protect traversal when sharing across threads

An unmodifiable view does not synchronize its source. A writer on the backing LinkedList can invalidate a reader's traversal. Synchronized wrappers require a specific locking discipline, and a private snapshot can avoid shared mutation when its copying cost is acceptable.

The wrapper also retains the backing list. Holding the wrapper for a long time keeps that backing collection and its elements reachable.

Working program

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;

public class LiveDispatchReadOnlyView {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> mutable = new ArrayList<>();
        mutable.add("load-15");
        List<String> readOnly = Collections.unmodifiableList(mutable);
        mutable.add("seal-47");
        System.out.println(readOnly);
        try { readOnly.add("ship-82"); }
        catch (UnsupportedOperationException rejected) { System.out.println("wrapper edit rejected"); }
        System.out.println(mutable.size());
    }
}

Output

[load-15, seal-47]
wrapper edit rejected
2

Cost and ownership

Wrapping does not copy n elements. Reads delegate to the backing list, so their cost follows its implementation. The wrapper and source share one mutable container and all referenced element objects.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not describe an unmodifiable view as a frozen snapshot.
  • Do not keep a mutable backing alias if the consumer requires stable membership.
  • Do not infer thread safety from the word unmodifiable.

title: List.copyOf freezes container membership but not mutable elements
summary: List.copyOf returns an unmodifiable list with the source collection's elements at copy time, while retaining references to those elements.
body:
List.copyOf returns an unmodifiable list with the source collection's elements at copy time, while retaining references to those elements.

Separate container snapshot from object snapshot

Appending a new shipment record to the source list does not append it to the copied list. Mutating a ShipmentRecord already present changes the status observed through both lists because both hold the same object. This distinction matters for cached responses, audit trails, and cross-thread handoffs.

Null elements are rejected. A copy operation can also avoid a fresh allocation when its input is already an unmodifiable list, so code must not rely on a distinct list identity. Its content contract matters more than whether the returned reference is new.

Choose the needed isolation level

For an independent mutable container, use a new ArrayList. For immutable record values, a shallow container copy may be enough. For mutable nested objects, create purpose-built value snapshots before List.copyOf. Record defensive copies address a related boundary for array fields.

Collections.unmodifiableList leaves membership live through the backing collection. These two APIs solve different ownership problems despite both rejecting edits through the returned reference.

Working program

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class DispatchContainerSnapshot {
    static final class ShipmentRecord {
        final String dispatchId;
        String status;
        ShipmentRecord(String dispatchId, String status) {
            this.dispatchId = dispatchId; this.status = status;
        }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ShipmentRecord first = new ShipmentRecord("load-15", "queued");
        List<ShipmentRecord> source = new ArrayList<>();
        source.add(first);
        List<ShipmentRecord> snapshot = List.copyOf(source);
        source.add(new ShipmentRecord("seal-47", "queued"));
        first.status = "sent";
        System.out.println(snapshot.size());
        System.out.println(snapshot.get(0).status);
        try { List.copyOf(java.util.Arrays.asList("ship-82", null)); }
        catch (NullPointerException rejected) { System.out.println("null rejected"); }
    }
}

Output

1
sent
null rejected

Cost and ownership

Copying n element references costs O(n) traversal and generally O(n) container storage, though an implementation may reuse a suitable immutable input. Mutable element objects are shared; copying the container alone does not isolate their state.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call a shallow container snapshot a deep copy.
  • Do not assume List.copyOf accepts null elements.
  • Do not rely on a fresh returned object identity.

title: Java 21 access-order LinkedHashMap: reads change a reversed view
summary: An access-order LinkedHashMap moves a successfully accessed mapping toward its backing tail, so a reversed view reports that mapping first.
body:
An access-order LinkedHashMap moves a successfully accessed mapping toward its backing tail, so a reversed view reports that mapping first.

Make the ordering policy visible

The third LinkedHashMap constructor argument selects access order. A successful get changes encounter order even though no mapping is inserted or removed. If a reverse-ordered view is already held, its first key can change after that read. A renderer that assumes reads are observational can produce different output after a cache lookup.

The fixture prints both orientations before and after accessing the oldest key. The mapping count stays fixed. The order change comes from the chosen map policy, not from copying or rebuilding the reverse view.

Separate explicit placement from access

putFirst and putLast reposition an entry because the caller requested an endpoint. Access order repositions an entry as a side effect of operations such as get. Use one policy deliberately; a cache and a stable report have different needs.

Iteration over either view while another thread accesses the map needs a concurrency rule. Access-order movement can count as structural change for iterator behavior, so fail-fast exceptions remain diagnostics rather than coordination.

Working program

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.SequencedMap;

public class AccessOrderedDispatchCache {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedHashMap<String, Integer> cache = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true);
        cache.put("load-15", 1);
        cache.put("seal-47", 2);
        cache.put("ship-82", 3);
        SequencedMap<String, Integer> reverse = cache.reversed();
        System.out.println(reverse.sequencedKeySet());
        System.out.println(cache.get("load-15"));
        System.out.println(cache.keySet());
        System.out.println(reverse.sequencedKeySet());
    }
}

Output

[ship-82, seal-47, load-15]
1
[seal-47, ship-82, load-15]
[load-15, ship-82, seal-47]

Cost and ownership

The view does not copy map entries. A successful lookup is expected constant-time under ordinary hash distribution but also changes ordering in this map mode. Traversing either orientation is O(n), and both references share the same mutable mappings.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume get leaves an access-order map's iteration order unchanged.
  • Do not treat a reversed view as a frozen cache report.
  • Do not rely on fail-fast iteration to make concurrent access safe.

title: Java InputStream short reads: assemble a complete record header
summary: InputStream.read(byte[]) may return fewer bytes than requested even when the stream has not ended.
body:
InputStream.read(byte[]) may return fewer bytes than requested even when the stream has not ended.

Treat the return count as the contract

A read call reports how many bytes it placed into the destination, or -1 at end of stream. A network stream, decompressor, or wrapper can deliver only part of a header. Parse only after the declared header width is present. A short positive read is progress, not proof of truncation.

The loop below reads a four-byte message length from a stream that deliberately releases one byte per call. It rejects EOF before four bytes arrive. Follow the length with a separate payload boundary; a valid header never proves that the body is complete.

Keep parser state local

Do not publish a partially filled header to downstream code. The caller receives a length only after all four bytes are assembled. A real framing protocol should also reject negative lengths and cap allocations before reading its payload; byte-stream copying covers the general read loop.

Working program

import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.io.EOFException;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.InputStream;

public class InventoryFrameHeader {
    static int readLength(InputStream source) throws IOException {
        byte[] header = new byte[4];
        int received = 0;
        while (received < header.length) {
            int count = source.read(header, received, header.length - received);
            if (count == -1) throw new EOFException("short header");
            if (count == 0) continue;
            received += count;
        }
        return ((header[0] & 255) << 24) | ((header[1] & 255) << 16)
                | ((header[2] & 255) << 8) | (header[3] & 255);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        byte[] wire = {0, 0, 0, 47};
        InputStream throttled = new ByteArrayInputStream(wire) {
            @Override public synchronized int read(byte[] target, int offset, int length) {
                return super.read(target, offset, Math.min(length, 1));
            }
        };
        System.out.println(readLength(throttled));
        try { readLength(new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[] {0, 0, 0})); }
        catch (EOFException truncated) { System.out.println(truncated.getMessage()); }
    }
}

Output

47
short header

Cost and ownership

The header uses four bytes of fixed storage and O(4) read work, although a slow source can require four separate calls. A production loop also needs a deadline or cancellation policy for sources that can stall; the byte count alone does not impose one.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume one read fills the requested array.
  • Do not parse a header after a positive but short read.
  • Do not allocate a body directly from an unchecked length field.

title: Java readNBytes: reject a truncated payload after the header
summary: InputStream.readNBytes(n) returns at most n bytes; an early end of stream can make the returned array shorter.
body:
InputStream.readNBytes(n) returns at most n bytes; an early end of stream can make the returned array shorter.

Validate the declared length

A wire header is untrusted input. Check its sign and a protocol maximum before asking readNBytes to allocate. Then compare the returned array length with the declared size. End of stream after the header is a truncated frame, not an empty field or a successful partial message.

This example uses a one-byte length prefix to isolate the rule. Larger frames should use a bounded header reader and a fixed-size chunk loop when allocation pressure matters.

Decide who owns the bytes

The returned array belongs to the caller. Do not expose it as mutable shared application state without a copy or a clear ownership transfer. A readFully call provides a different API contract but still requires a maximum before buffer allocation.

Working program

import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.io.EOFException;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.InputStream;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

public class ShipmentFrameReader {
    static String readShipment(InputStream wire) throws IOException {
        int declared = wire.read();
        if (declared < 0) throw new EOFException("missing length");
        if (declared > 64) throw new IOException("frame too large");
        byte[] payload = wire.readNBytes(declared);
        if (payload.length != declared) throw new EOFException("truncated payload");
        return new String(payload, StandardCharsets.US_ASCII);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        System.out.println(readShipment(new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[] {4, 'A', 'B', '4', '7'})));
        try { readShipment(new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[] {5, 'A', 'B'})); }
        catch (EOFException truncated) { System.out.println(truncated.getMessage()); }
    }
}

Output

AB47
truncated payload

Cost and ownership

readNBytes allocates up to the requested payload size, so the cap is a memory policy, not an optional validation. Time is O(n) for n bytes received. This example targets Java 11 or later; a streaming decoder can avoid retaining the whole frame.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not infer that readNBytes always returns the requested count.
  • Do not let a header dictate an unbounded allocation.
  • Do not treat an incomplete payload as a valid message.

title: Java DataInputStream.readFully: EOF can leave partial bytes in the buffer
summary: DataInputStream.readFully fills the requested region or throws EOFException, and an EOF failure may occur after some destination bytes were changed.
body:
DataInputStream.readFully fills the requested region or throws EOFException, and an EOF failure may occur after some destination bytes were changed.

Keep tentative data private

A caller should not reuse a partially filled buffer as though it were a complete record. Allocate the record buffer inside the operation, invoke readFully, then return it only on success. The exception is part of the framing contract; it is not permission to process the bytes already copied.

The first read succeeds. The second throws after two bytes, and the program prints the private buffer so the partial mutation is visible. readNBytes expresses a similar boundary through a short returned array instead.

Bound the destination before reading

readFully does not decide whether a declared record size is safe. Validate the protocol length before allocating. For a long-running stream, also consider cancellation and deadlines; a blocking read can wait for remaining bytes.

Working program

import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.io.DataInputStream;
import java.io.EOFException;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.Arrays;

public class InvoiceRecordBoundary {
    static byte[] record(byte[] wire) throws IOException {
        byte[] destination = new byte[4];
        try (DataInputStream input = new DataInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(wire))) {
            input.readFully(destination);
        }
        return destination;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(record(new byte[] {7, 8, 9, 10})));
        byte[] tentative = new byte[4];
        try (DataInputStream input = new DataInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[] {7, 8}))) {
            try { input.readFully(tentative); }
            catch (EOFException truncated) { System.out.println(Arrays.toString(tentative)); }
        }
    }
}

Output

[7, 8, 9, 10]
[7, 8, 0, 0]

Cost and ownership

The fixed four-byte buffer costs O(1) space here; a general record of length n costs O(n) storage and read work. A failed read retains only tentative local data, so callers cannot accidentally publish an incomplete record.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume an exception leaves the destination unchanged.
  • Do not expose a record buffer before readFully returns.
  • Do not allocate an unbounded buffer from an external length.

title: Java CharsetDecoder: reject malformed UTF-8 instead of replacing bytes
summary: CharsetDecoder can report malformed and unmappable input as errors rather than silently substituting replacement characters.
body:
CharsetDecoder can report malformed and unmappable input as errors rather than silently substituting replacement characters.

Make the data-loss policy explicit

A replacement character can hide a damaged identifier or signature. Set both error actions to REPORT when the text is a protocol field that must round-trip exactly. If replacement is acceptable for display-only content, make that a separate path and label it accordingly.

The fixture decodes one valid identifier and rejects a malformed two-byte sequence. A strict UTF-8 reader covers file input; this lesson shows the decoder policy directly for in-memory bytes.

Keep character and byte lengths separate

A byte cap does not imply the same character cap. UTF-8 characters can occupy multiple bytes, and a Java String uses UTF-16 code units. Enforce each limit at the layer where it matters, before allocating or persisting.

Working program

import java.nio.ByteBuffer;
import java.nio.charset.CharacterCodingException;
import java.nio.charset.CodingErrorAction;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

public class SupplierIdentifierDecoder {
    static String decode(byte[] bytes) throws CharacterCodingException {
        return StandardCharsets.UTF_8.newDecoder()
                .onMalformedInput(CodingErrorAction.REPORT)
                .onUnmappableCharacter(CodingErrorAction.REPORT)
                .decode(ByteBuffer.wrap(bytes)).toString();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws CharacterCodingException {
        System.out.println(decode(new byte[] {'S', 'U', 'P', '-', '4', '7'}));
        try { decode(new byte[] {(byte) 0xC3, (byte) 0x28}); }
        catch (CharacterCodingException invalid) { System.out.println("invalid UTF-8 rejected"); }
    }
}

Output

SUP-47
invalid UTF-8 rejected

Cost and ownership

Decoding is O(n) in input bytes and materializes characters in memory. A per-call decoder keeps mutable decoding state local; for a streaming pipeline, reuse one decoder within a single stream and handle underflow and overflow explicitly.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not accept replacement characters silently in identifiers.
  • Do not count UTF-8 bytes as Java characters.
  • Do not share one mutable decoder across unrelated concurrent operations.

title: Java ByteBuffer flip and compact: preserve an incomplete frame
summary: ByteBuffer.flip changes a buffer from writing to reading, while compact moves unread bytes to the front for the next write cycle.
body:
ByteBuffer.flip changes a buffer from writing to reading, while compact moves unread bytes to the front for the next write cycle.

Carry unfinished input across reads

A stream chunk may end halfway through a record. After flip, consume only complete records; compact retains the unread suffix and sets the position after it. The next chunk appends there. Clearing the buffer would discard the partial record, while flipping twice without a write would distort the limit.

This three-byte record arrives in two chunks. The parser waits until all three bytes are present. Short reads explain why chunk boundaries cannot be treated as message boundaries.

Cap the record format

A fixed buffer works only if the largest accepted record fits. For variable-length frames, reject oversize declarations or move to a bounded spill strategy before compact can leave the buffer permanently full. Byte order matters when a frame contains multibyte numeric fields.

Working program

import java.nio.ByteBuffer;

public class DispatchFrameAccumulator {
    static void accept(ByteBuffer pending, byte[] chunk) {
        pending.put(chunk);
        pending.flip();
        while (pending.remaining() >= 3) {
            int site = pending.get() & 255;
            int quantity = pending.get() & 255;
            int checksum = pending.get() & 255;
            System.out.println(site + ":" + quantity + ":" + checksum);
        }
        pending.compact();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ByteBuffer pending = ByteBuffer.allocate(6);
        accept(pending, new byte[] {47, 2});
        System.out.println("pending=" + pending.position());
        accept(pending, new byte[] {49, 82, 3, 85});
        System.out.println("pending=" + pending.position());
    }
}

Output

pending=2
47:2:49
82:3:85
pending=0

Cost and ownership

Each complete three-byte frame is parsed once. compact copies the unread suffix, so repeated compaction of a large partial record can add copy cost; a size cap and chunk plan keep that cost predictable. The buffer owns six bytes here.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call clear when unread bytes must survive.
  • Do not parse a record merely because a transport read ended.
  • Do not call put when the buffer lacks space for the next chunk.

title: Java WritableByteChannel short writes: drain the ByteBuffer
summary: WritableByteChannel.write may consume only part of a ByteBuffer, so a complete write requires checking remaining bytes.
body:
WritableByteChannel.write may consume only part of a ByteBuffer, so a complete write requires checking remaining bytes.

Loop on the buffer state

The buffer position advances by the count actually written. Continue until hasRemaining is false. The fixture uses a channel that accepts at most two bytes per call, making the short-write path deterministic instead of relying on a particular filesystem or socket.

FileChannel writing follows the same position rule. For a nonblocking channel, write can return zero because it is not ready; register for writability or apply a deadline instead of spinning forever.

Define completion before publication

Only publish or acknowledge a record once its entire buffer has been accepted by the channel. Acceptance by a channel is not always durable storage: a file may also require a force policy, while a socket needs an application-level acknowledgment if remote processing matters. Atomic file publication handles a separate visibility boundary.

Working program

import java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.ByteBuffer;
import java.nio.channels.WritableByteChannel;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

public class ManifestChannelWriter {
    static class TwoByteChannel implements WritableByteChannel {
        private final ByteArrayOutputStream sink = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        private boolean open = true;
        public int write(ByteBuffer source) {
            int count = Math.min(2, source.remaining());
            for (int index = 0; index < count; index++) sink.write(source.get());
            return count;
        }
        public boolean isOpen() { return open; }
        public void close() { open = false; }
        String contents() { return new String(sink.toByteArray(), StandardCharsets.US_ASCII); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        TwoByteChannel channel = new TwoByteChannel();
        ByteBuffer record = ByteBuffer.wrap("LOT-47".getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII));
        int calls = 0;
        while (record.hasRemaining()) { channel.write(record); calls++; }
        System.out.println(channel.contents());
        System.out.println("calls=" + calls);
        channel.close();
    }
}

Output

LOT-47
calls=3

Cost and ownership

The loop processes n bytes in O(n) total transfer work and keeps only the input buffer plus the sink. A production nonblocking channel must wait for readiness on zero-byte writes; this blocking-style demonstration always advances and therefore cannot spin.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume one write drains the buffer.
  • Do not reset position between partial writes.
  • Do not busy-loop on a nonblocking channel that returns zero.

title: Java ZIP entry extraction: cap expanded bytes while reading
summary: A ZIP entry can expand far beyond its compressed size, so enforce a decompressed-byte limit during extraction.
body:
A ZIP entry can expand far beyond its compressed size, so enforce a decompressed-byte limit during extraction.

Count actual output

Metadata such as an entry's compressed size is not a safe allocation or acceptance limit. Count bytes returned by ZipInputStream.read and stop as soon as a configured expanded limit is exceeded. The fixture creates its own in-memory ZIP; its extraction path rejects a 47-byte entry under a 32-byte cap.

Path traversal is a different boundary. If extracting to disk, validate destination paths as described in ZIP path validation and decide how to clean up a partial file after rejection.

Budget the whole archive

A per-entry cap alone permits many entries to consume unlimited total output. Add entry count, aggregate expanded bytes, compression ratio or CPU budget where appropriate. Read incrementally; a bounded copy loop avoids materializing the entire expanded entry in memory.

Working program

import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.zip.ZipEntry;
import java.util.zip.ZipInputStream;
import java.util.zip.ZipOutputStream;

public class ArchiveExpansionGate {
    static byte[] archive(int payloadLength) throws IOException {
        ByteArrayOutputStream bytes = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        try (ZipOutputStream zip = new ZipOutputStream(bytes)) {
            zip.putNextEntry(new ZipEntry("inventory.txt"));
            for (int index = 0; index < payloadLength; index++) zip.write('X');
            zip.closeEntry();
        }
        return bytes.toByteArray();
    }

    static int expandedSize(byte[] archive, int maximum) throws IOException {
        try (ZipInputStream zip = new ZipInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(archive))) {
            if (zip.getNextEntry() == null) throw new IOException("missing entry");
            byte[] chunk = new byte[16];
            int total = 0;
            int count;
            while ((count = zip.read(chunk)) != -1) {
                if (count > maximum - total) throw new IOException("expanded limit exceeded");
                total += count;
            }
            return total;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        System.out.println(expandedSize(archive(12), 32));
        try { expandedSize(archive(47), 32); }
        catch (IOException rejected) { System.out.println(rejected.getMessage()); }
    }
}

Output

12
expanded limit exceeded

Cost and ownership

The extractor uses a 16-byte chunk and constant working memory per entry. Counting is O(n) in expanded bytes read until rejection. The in-memory test archive itself uses O(n) storage only to keep this standalone program runnable.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not trust ZIP size metadata as the only limit.
  • Do not omit an aggregate archive budget.
  • Do not treat a byte cap as protection against unsafe destination paths.

title: Java bounded line reader: reject oversized records without buffering the file
summary: A line-oriented parser should cap each record before accumulating an unbounded String or list of lines.
body:
A line-oriented parser should cap each record before accumulating an unbounded String or list of lines.

Apply the limit while reading

The reader accepts a fixed maximum of content characters per line. A newline ends the record; a preceding carriage return is removed for CRLF input. Count characters as they arrive and reject the first one beyond the limit. Reading every line first and checking lengths afterward loses the memory bound.

The implementation returns null only when EOF arrives before any record character. A final line without a newline is still valid. See file I/O ownership for closing an actual file reader and strict decoding if malformed bytes must be rejected before characters reach this parser.

Define what a character limit means

This limit counts UTF-16 code units because Reader.read returns char values. A protocol limit expressed in UTF-8 bytes or Unicode code points needs a different counter. Keep the unit explicit in the API contract, especially when supplementary characters are permitted.

Working program

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.Reader;
import java.io.StringReader;

public class BoundedManifestLine {
    static String readLine(Reader source, int maximumChars) throws IOException {
        if (maximumChars < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative limit");
        StringBuilder line = new StringBuilder();
        int next;
        while ((next = source.read()) != -1) {
            if (next == '\n') break;
            if (line.length() >= maximumChars + 1L) throw new IOException("line too long");
            line.append((char) next);
        }
        if (next == -1 && line.length() == 0) return null;
        if (line.length() > 0 && line.charAt(line.length() - 1) == '\r') line.setLength(line.length() - 1);
        if (line.length() > maximumChars) throw new IOException("line too long");
        return line.toString();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        System.out.println(readLine(new StringReader("lot-47\r\n"), 6));
        try { readLine(new StringReader("shipment-82"), 6); }
        catch (IOException rejected) { System.out.println(rejected.getMessage()); }
    }
}

Output

lot-47
line too long

Cost and ownership

The parser is O(n) in characters read and O(limit) in retained line storage. It allows one extra code unit temporarily so a terminal CR can be distinguished from content, then enforces the final content cap. A Reader still needs a byte-level input cap if decoding expansion or source volume matters.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call readAllLines on an untrusted large file before validation.
  • Do not confuse UTF-16 code units with UTF-8 bytes.
  • Do not discard a valid last line merely because it lacks a newline.

title: Java InputStream.available is not the remaining stream length
summary: InputStream.available estimates bytes readable without blocking; it is not an end-of-stream test or total-size query.
body:
InputStream.available estimates bytes readable without blocking; it is not an end-of-stream test or total-size query.

Read until the stream contract ends

A stream may have data even when available returns zero. The fixture overrides available to report zero while three bytes remain, then reads those bytes normally. Code that allocates available bytes and calls the job complete would silently drop the record.

Use a read loop or a bounded framed read instead. If the input format has a length prefix, validate that prefix independently of available.

Avoid false size assumptions

Some in-memory streams return a convenient remaining count, but code that works only on those streams can fail on sockets and wrappers. available is a scheduling hint for a narrow purpose. It does not replace protocol framing, EOF handling, or an input budget.

Working program

import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.InputStream;

public class InventoryInputAvailability {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        InputStream source = new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[] {47, 82, 15}) {
            @Override public synchronized int available() { return 0; }
        };
        System.out.println("available=" + source.available());
        int total = 0;
        int next;
        while ((next = source.read()) != -1) total += next;
        System.out.println("sum=" + total);
    }
}

Output

available=0
sum=144

Cost and ownership

This single-byte loop is O(n) calls and constant storage; a buffered block read reduces call overhead for larger inputs. The important boundary is semantic: only read returning -1 identifies EOF for this stream.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat available equal to zero as EOF.
  • Do not allocate the entire input from available.
  • Do not generalize an in-memory stream's available behavior to network streams.

title: Java ByteBuffer.slice: shared storage and independent cursors
summary: ByteBuffer.slice creates a new view over the selected remaining bytes, with independent position and limit but shared content.
body:
ByteBuffer.slice creates a new view over the selected remaining bytes, with independent position and limit but shared content.

Separate cursor independence from data independence

Moving the slice position does not move the parent's position. Writing through the slice does change the parent's bytes. A slice is useful for parsing a framed region without copying it, but it is unsafe as a long-lived snapshot when the parent buffer is reused for more input.

The fixture selects bytes at parent indexes one through three, writes into the slice, and observes the parent changed while its cursor stays at one. flip and compact manage buffer reuse; those operations can make a retained slice point at different logical data.

Copy at ownership boundaries

If an asynchronous task needs stable bytes after the read loop continues, copy the selected range or transfer exclusive ownership of the backing buffer. Array copying addresses the same distinction for arrays; a read-only view prevents writes through that view but still reflects writes through other aliases.

Working program

import java.nio.ByteBuffer;
import java.util.Arrays;

public class ManifestFieldSlice {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ByteBuffer parent = ByteBuffer.wrap(new byte[] {10, 20, 30, 40, 50});
        parent.position(1);
        parent.limit(4);
        ByteBuffer field = parent.slice();
        field.put(0, (byte) 82);
        field.position(2);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(parent.array()));
        System.out.println("parent=" + parent.position() + ", field=" + field.position());
    }
}

Output

[10, 82, 30, 40, 50]
parent=1, field=2

Cost and ownership

Creating a slice is O(1) and does not copy bytes. The memory retained by the view can include the parent's entire backing storage; a small long-lived slice can therefore keep a large parent allocation reachable.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call a slice a snapshot.
  • Do not assume parent and slice share cursor positions.
  • Do not retain a slice after the backing buffer is repurposed without an ownership rule.

title: Java Duration versus Period across a daylight-saving change
summary: Duration measures elapsed seconds, while Period advances calendar fields on a date or zoned date-time.
body:
Duration measures elapsed seconds, while Period advances calendar fields on a date or zoned date-time.

Choose a timeline

A shipping deadline 24 hours from now needs Duration. A daily collection at noon needs calendar-day arithmetic. In Europe/Paris, the spring clock change makes those two rules produce different wall times even though both are described casually as one day later.

The fixture starts before the 2024 spring transition. Calendar addition keeps noon and spans 23 elapsed hours; a 24-hour duration lands at 13:00. Gap and overlap rules explain why a local date-time cannot always be converted to one instant without policy.

Persist the right value

An absolute expiry belongs on the instant timeline. A recurring local appointment needs its local rule and region zone, not merely the next computed instant. Injected clocks make expiry tests deterministic.

Working program

import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Period;
import java.time.ZoneId;
import java.time.ZonedDateTime;

public class ParisCollectionSchedule {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ZonedDateTime pickup = ZonedDateTime.of(2024, 3, 30, 12, 0, 0, 0, ZoneId.of("Europe/Paris"));
        ZonedDateTime calendarNext = pickup.plus(Period.ofDays(1));
        ZonedDateTime elapsedNext = pickup.plus(Duration.ofDays(1));
        System.out.println(calendarNext.toLocalTime());
        System.out.println(elapsedNext.toLocalTime());
        System.out.println(Duration.between(pickup, calendarNext).toHours());
    }
}

Output

12:00
13:00
23

Cost and ownership

Both operations use fixed-size time objects and constant application storage. Their computational cost is small relative to persistence or scheduling, but their business meanings differ by an hour here; converting a recurring rule into a duration loses that rule.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not substitute 24 hours for a calendar day in a regional schedule.
  • Do not store only the next instant for a recurring local-time rule.
  • Do not compare LocalDateTime values as if they were elapsed timestamps.

title: Java ZonedDateTime zone conversion: preserve the instant or the wall clock
summary: withZoneSameInstant preserves a point on the timeline; withZoneSameLocal preserves displayed local fields and may change the instant.
body:
withZoneSameInstant preserves a point on the timeline; withZoneSameLocal preserves displayed local fields and may change the instant.

State what a transfer means

A meeting transferred to another region usually keeps its instant. A store schedule copied to a new branch may keep its local opening time instead. Calling a zone conversion without naming that choice silently changes the business rule.

The fixture moves a Delhi dispatch to Paris on a fixed date. The same-instant conversion changes the wall clock; the same-local conversion keeps 09:30 and moves the underlying instant. OffsetDateTime comparisons show why equal instants need not have equal representations.

Handle invalid local times

A same-local conversion can land in a gap or overlap in the target region. It applies zone-resolution rules; if a booking must never shift, validate the target local fields first with valid offsets and reject ambiguity according to the product contract.

Working program

import java.time.ZoneId;
import java.time.ZonedDateTime;

public class DispatchZoneTransfer {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ZonedDateTime delhi = ZonedDateTime.of(2024, 1, 15, 9, 30, 0, 0, ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata"));
        ZoneId paris = ZoneId.of("Europe/Paris");
        ZonedDateTime sameInstant = delhi.withZoneSameInstant(paris);
        ZonedDateTime sameLocal = delhi.withZoneSameLocal(paris);
        System.out.println(sameInstant.toLocalTime());
        System.out.println(sameLocal.toLocalTime());
        System.out.println(delhi.toInstant().equals(sameInstant.toInstant()));
        System.out.println(delhi.toInstant().equals(sameLocal.toInstant()));
    }
}

Output

05:00
09:30
true
false

Cost and ownership

Each conversion creates an immutable value with constant application storage. Rule lookup depends on the zone database. A region's future rules may change, so persist the region and scheduling intent when future local time is the requirement.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use withZoneSameLocal for a completed event timestamp.
  • Do not assume the same wall clock means the same instant.
  • Do not silently accept a target-region gap for an exact appointment.

title: Java OffsetDateTime equality versus isEqual for event timestamps
summary: OffsetDateTime.equals compares local fields and offset, while isEqual tests whether two values identify the same instant.
body:
OffsetDateTime.equals compares local fields and offset, while isEqual tests whether two values identify the same instant.

Pick an identity rule

Two services can serialize the same event using different offsets. A Set keyed by OffsetDateTime uses equals and can retain both representations. If deduplication is about the event's position on the timeline, normalize to Instant or compare with isEqual. Do not redefine that rule accidentally through formatting.

The two values below are one event seen at UTC and at +05:30. Their printed local clocks differ. Zone conversion has the same representation-versus-instant distinction for region-based values.

Preserve context when required

An Instant is enough for ordering a completed event, but it does not tell you the customer's original offset or region. Store those separately when audit or display policy requires them. Time-type selection starts from the question the application needs to answer.

Working program

import java.time.OffsetDateTime;

public class ReceiptTimestampIdentity {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        OffsetDateTime utc = OffsetDateTime.parse("2024-08-12T04:00:00Z");
        OffsetDateTime delhiOffset = OffsetDateTime.parse("2024-08-12T09:30:00+05:30");
        System.out.println(utc.equals(delhiOffset));
        System.out.println(utc.isEqual(delhiOffset));
        System.out.println(utc.toInstant().equals(delhiOffset.toInstant()));
    }
}

Output

false
true
true

Cost and ownership

The comparison uses fixed-size immutable values. The important cost is logical: a collection keyed by representation can double-count one event. Normalize once at the identity boundary rather than repeatedly converting every time the set is read.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use equals as an instant-equivalence test for OffsetDateTime.
  • Do not discard original offset context if an audit requires it.
  • Do not confuse a numeric offset with a region's future zone rules.

title: Java YearMonth.atEndOfMonth: calculate a month boundary without guessed days
summary: YearMonth.atEndOfMonth returns the actual final LocalDate of a month, including leap-year February.
body:
YearMonth.atEndOfMonth returns the actual final LocalDate of a month, including leap-year February.

Compute the boundary from the calendar

A billing period ending in February does not have a constant day count. YearMonth carries the year and month without inventing a day; atEndOfMonth resolves the final date. The fixture prints February in a leap year and a non-leap year.

For a half-open timestamp range, use the first day of the next month as the exclusive end, then resolve that local boundary in the customer's zone. Exclusive date ranges avoid a fabricated last instant with guessed precision.

Keep policy separate from representation

A calendar month is not thirty elapsed days. If a contract renews on the last day, recompute from YearMonth each cycle. Repeated plusMonths can drift after a short month.

Working program

import java.time.YearMonth;

public class InvoiceMonthBoundary {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(YearMonth.of(2024, 2).atEndOfMonth());
        System.out.println(YearMonth.of(2025, 2).atEndOfMonth());
        System.out.println(YearMonth.of(2024, 2).plusMonths(1).atDay(1));
    }
}

Output

2024-02-29
2025-02-28
2024-03-01

Cost and ownership

YearMonth and LocalDate are immutable fixed-size values. The operation is constant application work and storage; the larger risk is using a guessed day count and billing a different range from the one stated to users.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not hard-code February 28 as its last day.
  • Do not model a calendar month as a fixed Duration.
  • Do not append 23:59:59 as a substitute for an exclusive upper bound.

title: Java DateTimeFormatter week-year Y versus calendar year u
summary: DateTimeFormatter pattern Y prints the week-based year, which can differ from the calendar year printed by u.
body:
DateTimeFormatter pattern Y prints the week-based year, which can differ from the calendar year printed by u.

Keep identifiers out of the wrong calendar

A date near New Year can belong to the first ISO week of the following week-based year. If an invoice ID uses YYYY-MM-dd by mistake, its year can disagree with its month and day. Use uuuu-MM-dd for a calendar date, or explicitly format a week date when that is the intended business identifier.

The fixture fixes Locale.UK so week conventions do not depend on the machine default. December 30, 2019 has calendar year 2019 but belongs to week 1 of week-based year 2020. Strict input parsing covers validation after choosing the correct fields.

Make locale part of the contract

Week numbering varies by locale. A persisted week identifier needs a declared convention; changing the JVM default locale must not change existing keys. Prefer explicit WeekFields or a fixed formatter locale, and test year boundaries.

Working program

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter;
import java.util.Locale;

public class ShipmentWeekIdentifier {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LocalDate shipped = LocalDate.of(2019, 12, 30);
        DateTimeFormatter calendar = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("uuuu-MM-dd", Locale.UK);
        DateTimeFormatter week = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("YYYY-'W'ww-e", Locale.UK);
        System.out.println(shipped.format(calendar));
        System.out.println(shipped.format(week));
    }
}

Output

2019-12-30
2020-W01-1

Cost and ownership

Formatting a fixed date uses bounded application storage and work. Persisted identifiers carry a larger migration cost if the wrong year field was used; changing the formatter later does not repair keys already issued.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use YYYY for a calendar-year date field.
  • Do not rely on the process default locale for persisted week keys.
  • Do not change an existing week convention without a migration plan.

title: Java Instant toEpochMilli: detect lost submillisecond precision
summary: Instant.toEpochMilli converts a timestamp to whole milliseconds, dropping its finer nanosecond fraction.
body:
Instant.toEpochMilli converts a timestamp to whole milliseconds, dropping its finer nanosecond fraction.

Declare storage precision

An Instant can represent nanosecond fields, but a database column or wire field holding epoch milliseconds cannot. Converting and rebuilding the value loses the last six digits of the nanosecond field. That is a schema choice, not a harmless serialization detail.

The fixture shows an event with 123456789 nanoseconds becoming 123000000 after a millisecond round trip. Offset representations are a separate concern: equal instants can be written with different offsets even without precision loss.

Bound comparisons to stored precision

If the store truncates to milliseconds, compare against an Instant truncated to that unit or use an agreed tolerance. Never silently assume that a round trip preserves equality. For ordering events with the same stored millisecond, add a separate sequence or stable tie-break key.

Working program

import java.time.Instant;

public class LedgerTimestampPrecision {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Instant captured = Instant.parse("2024-08-12T04:00:00.123456789Z");
        Instant stored = Instant.ofEpochMilli(captured.toEpochMilli());
        System.out.println(captured.getNano());
        System.out.println(stored.getNano());
        System.out.println(captured.equals(stored));
    }
}

Output

123456789
123000000
false

Cost and ownership

The conversion is constant application work and storage. Precision loss is irreversible after persistence; if a service needs finer ordering, choose a matching schema and serialization format before writing data.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expect toEpochMilli to preserve nanoseconds.
  • Do not use timestamp equality across storage systems with different precision without a policy.
  • Do not infer event order solely from a coarse timestamp when collisions are possible.

title: Java LocalDate half-open ranges: define an exclusive end
summary: A half-open date range includes its start and excludes its end, so adjacent ranges meet without overlap.
body:
A half-open date range includes its start and excludes its end, so adjacent ranges meet without overlap.

Use one boundary convention

A monthly report can represent February as [February 1, March 1). The next report starts exactly where the first ends. No last-second adjustment is needed, and leap years are handled by calendar arithmetic rather than manual day counts.

The fixture checks the final day of February and the next day's exclusion. YearMonth can supply the start of the next month; a timestamp query must convert each local boundary using an explicit zone and its transition policy.

Keep date ranges and instant ranges distinct

A LocalDate range answers which civil dates belong to a report. An Instant range answers which events fall on a timeline. The conversion between them requires the user's zone and may span 23 or 25 hours around daylight-saving changes; calendar versus elapsed time explains that difference.

Working program

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.YearMonth;

public class InvoiceDateWindow {
    static boolean includes(LocalDate candidate, LocalDate start, LocalDate endExclusive) {
        if (!start.isBefore(endExclusive)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("empty window");
        return !candidate.isBefore(start) && candidate.isBefore(endExclusive);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        YearMonth period = YearMonth.of(2024, 2);
        LocalDate start = period.atDay(1);
        LocalDate endExclusive = period.plusMonths(1).atDay(1);
        System.out.println(includes(LocalDate.of(2024, 2, 29), start, endExclusive));
        System.out.println(includes(LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 1), start, endExclusive));
    }
}

Output

true
false

Cost and ownership

Each membership test is constant work and storage. A database query should use the same inclusive lower and exclusive upper bound. If its columns are timestamps, resolve the local dates to instants before querying rather than comparing formatted strings.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use an inclusive 23:59:59 upper timestamp; it misses finer precision.
  • Do not combine local dates with UTC timestamps without a zone rule.
  • Do not accept reversed or empty bounds silently.

title: Java ZoneRules: validate a saved offset against a local booking
summary: A local date-time and region zone can have zero, one, or two valid offsets, so a saved offset must be checked against that zone's rules.
body:
A local date-time and region zone can have zero, one, or two valid offsets, so a saved offset must be checked against that zone's rules.

Reject mismatched booking data

An offset sent with a booking is useful during an autumn overlap, when the same local time occurs twice. It is not arbitrary. Check that the offset is among the region's valid offsets before creating the scheduled instant. A stale or forged offset can point to a different instant from the one implied by the region.

The fixture uses a Paris overlap with two accepted offsets and rejects +03:00. Gap and overlap detection introduces the transition rules; this lesson applies them to persisted input validation.

Separate validation from future rule changes

A future booking may be affected by time-zone database updates. Store the local intention, region, and chosen overlap policy. A saved instant is useful for current execution, but a long-lived recurring schedule may need recomputation when rules change.

Working program

import java.time.LocalDateTime;
import java.time.ZoneId;
import java.time.ZoneOffset;
import java.time.zone.ZoneRules;

public class BookingOffsetGate {
    static boolean accepted(LocalDateTime local, ZoneId region, ZoneOffset supplied) {
        ZoneRules rules = region.getRules();
        return rules.getValidOffsets(local).contains(supplied);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LocalDateTime booking = LocalDateTime.of(2024, 10, 27, 2, 30);
        ZoneId paris = ZoneId.of("Europe/Paris");
        System.out.println(accepted(booking, paris, ZoneOffset.ofHours(2)));
        System.out.println(accepted(booking, paris, ZoneOffset.ofHours(1)));
        System.out.println(accepted(booking, paris, ZoneOffset.ofHours(3)));
    }
}

Output

true
true
false

Cost and ownership

Validation uses a small list of valid offsets and constant application storage. Zone-rule lookup is cheap for a single booking, but the rule database is versioned; policy and stored values must be reviewed when scheduling far into the future.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not accept any syntactically valid offset for a region booking.
  • Do not assume an overlap has only one valid instant.
  • Do not store a bare LocalDateTime as the full identity of an overlapped booking.

title: Java negative Duration fields: seconds and nanos are normalized
summary: A negative Duration stores a signed seconds field and a nonnegative nanosecond adjustment, so its components can surprise callers.
body:
A negative Duration stores a signed seconds field and a nonnegative nanosecond adjustment, so its components can surprise callers.

Compare the whole duration

A duration of negative 1.5 seconds is represented as seconds -2 plus 500 million nanos. Printing getSeconds and getNano separately can look contradictory if the reader assumes both components share a sign. Use toMillis, compareTo, or the whole value when making a deadline decision.

The fixture prints the components and the total milliseconds. Expiry checks should compare Instants directly when the business rule is before or after a deadline.

Keep unit conversion explicit

Conversions to whole units can discard a fractional remainder. A negative duration close to zero needs careful treatment if a UI displays rounded seconds or an API accepts integer milliseconds. Do not make a retry decision from a rounded display value.

Working program

import java.time.Duration;

public class RetryDelayDebt {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Duration overdue = Duration.ofMillis(-1500);
        System.out.println(overdue.getSeconds());
        System.out.println(overdue.getNano());
        System.out.println(overdue.toMillis());
        System.out.println(overdue.isNegative());
    }
}

Output

-2
500000000
-1500
true

Cost and ownership

Duration is a fixed-size immutable value, and these conversions use constant application work. The failure risk is interpreting one component as the signed total or truncating a fractional duration before a boundary comparison.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not infer the total sign from getNano.
  • Do not rebuild a negative duration by giving both fields the same sign.
  • Do not round a deadline interval before deciding whether work is overdue.

title: Java plusMonths at month end: prevent renewal-date drift
summary: Adding one month to a date near month end can clamp the day, so repeated additions may differ from an addition anchored to the original date.
body:
Adding one month to a date near month end can clamp the day, so repeated additions may differ from an addition anchored to the original date.

Keep the original recurrence rule

A contract signed on January 31 may intend the last day of every month. Repeatedly adding one month to the previous invoice date loses that intent after February clamps the day. Calculate each occurrence from the anchor month and a declared day policy instead.

The fixture shows January 31, 2024 plus one month becomes February 29; another plus one month becomes March 29. Directly adding two months to January 31 yields March 31. YearMonth.atEndOfMonth expresses an explicit last-day policy.

Make the policy testable

Some products want the 31st where it exists and the last day otherwise; others want the 29th after the first clamp. Either can be valid. The error is allowing the library's chained arithmetic to choose the policy without review.

Working program

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.YearMonth;

public class ContractRenewalAnchor {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LocalDate signed = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 31);
        LocalDate chained = signed.plusMonths(1).plusMonths(1);
        LocalDate anchored = signed.plusMonths(2);
        LocalDate lastDayPolicy = YearMonth.from(signed).plusMonths(2).atEndOfMonth();
        System.out.println(signed.plusMonths(1));
        System.out.println(chained);
        System.out.println(anchored);
        System.out.println(lastDayPolicy);
    }
}

Output

2024-02-29
2024-03-29
2024-03-31
2024-03-31

Cost and ownership

Each calculation uses fixed-size immutable dates. A billing scheduler should retain its anchor and recurrence rule rather than derive future dates solely from the last emitted date; otherwise a one-time clamp can permanently alter the sequence.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume repeated plusMonths preserves the original day of month.
  • Do not encode a last-day rule as an accidental side effect of clamping.
  • Do not model a renewal month as a fixed number of elapsed hours.

title: Java StampedLock optimistic reads: validate before publishing state
summary: A StampedLock optimistic read observes fields without holding a read lock, so the observation must be validated before it becomes a result.
body:
A StampedLock optimistic read observes fields without holding a read lock, so the observation must be validated before it becomes a result.

Treat the stamp as a version check

Copy only the primitive fields or safe references needed for the decision, then call validate. A writer can change several related fields between reads. If validation fails, retry under a read lock. The fixture forces a write between observation and validation so the failed path is visible without relying on scheduler timing.

This is not a substitute for a transaction across unrelated objects. Basic lock ownership is easier to reason about when reads are not extremely frequent; read-write lock downgrading covers a different transition.

Keep locked sections small

StampedLock is not reentrant. Calling an unknown method while holding one of its locks can deadlock if that method tries to acquire the same lock. For mutable object graphs, a validated primitive stamp does not prove every dereference was safe; copy a stable snapshot under a read lock instead.

Working program

import java.util.concurrent.locks.StampedLock;

public class WarehouseStockSnapshot {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StampedLock guard = new StampedLock();
        int[] stock = {47};
        long optimistic = guard.tryOptimisticRead();
        int tentative = stock[0];
        long writer = guard.writeLock();
        try { stock[0] = 82; }
        finally { guard.unlockWrite(writer); }
        System.out.println("tentative=" + tentative);
        System.out.println("valid=" + guard.validate(optimistic));
        long reader = guard.readLock();
        try { System.out.println("current=" + stock[0]); }
        finally { guard.unlockRead(reader); }
    }
}

Output

tentative=47
valid=false
current=82

Cost and ownership

The optimistic attempt avoids read-lock acquisition when no writer intervenes; this fixture deliberately pays for a fallback read lock. Both paths use constant storage. Under frequent writes, failed retries may cost more than ordinary locking, so measure the actual workload.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not return tentative fields before validate succeeds.
  • Do not treat an optimistic stamp as a held lock.
  • Do not call reentrant code while holding a StampedLock mode.

title: Java ReentrantReadWriteLock downgrade: publish then keep a read lock
summary: A thread holding a ReentrantReadWriteLock write lock can acquire its read lock before releasing the write lock, preserving read protection across the transition.
body:
A thread holding a ReentrantReadWriteLock write lock can acquire its read lock before releasing the write lock, preserving read protection across the transition.

Avoid an unlocked gap

A writer may need to update a report and then inspect the committed value while excluding other writers. Acquire the read lock before releasing the write lock. If the write lock is released first, another writer may intervene before the read begins. The fixture prints the new revision while a read hold remains active.

A read-to-write upgrade is different and is not generally available by simply acquiring the write lock while holding a read lock. Release and retry with a version check, or use a design with a single owner. Optimistic reads offer another policy with explicit validation.

Release every hold

Each acquisition needs its own finally path. Leaking a read hold blocks future writers even after the update is complete. Keep I/O and callbacks outside the critical section when their duration is not bounded.

Working program

import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock;

public class PricingRevisionGate {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ReentrantReadWriteLock guard = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
        int[] revision = {47};
        guard.writeLock().lock();
        try {
            revision[0] = 82;
            guard.readLock().lock();
        } finally {
            guard.writeLock().unlock();
        }
        try {
            System.out.println("revision=" + revision[0]);
            System.out.println("read holds=" + guard.getReadHoldCount());
        } finally {
            guard.readLock().unlock();
        }
        System.out.println("read holds=" + guard.getReadHoldCount());
    }
}

Output

revision=82
read holds=1
read holds=0

Cost and ownership

The transition adds one lock acquisition without copying the report. Throughput depends on contention and how long readers hold the lock; a long read can delay every writer. The program owns one lock and one revision cell.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not release the write lock before taking the read lock when a gap is forbidden.
  • Do not assume a read lock can be upgraded to a write lock.
  • Do not forget to release the downgraded read hold.

title: Java AtomicStampedReference: reject a stale A-to-B-to-A update
summary: AtomicStampedReference compares both a reference and a version stamp, so a stale compare-and-set can detect an intervening change that returned to the original reference.
body:
AtomicStampedReference compares both a reference and a version stamp, so a stale compare-and-set can detect an intervening change that returned to the original reference.

Make history part of the condition

A worker reads READY. Another worker changes the state to PACKED and then back to READY. A reference-only comparison would see READY again and miss that history. Increment the stamp on each state transition; the original worker's stale stamp then fails. The fixture performs those transitions sequentially to make the result deterministic.

This is an in-process coordination tool. It does not provide database durability or a distributed version check. Atomic primitives cover single-reference updates; concurrent maps cover keyed state with different contracts.

Keep versions meaningful

A stamp can wrap after enough updates. Choose a version width and lifetime policy that fits the system, and do not treat the stamp as a cryptographic token. Compare-and-set still does not make a multi-object transaction atomic.

Working program

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference;

public class ParcelStateVersion {
    enum State { READY, PACKED, SHIPPED }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        AtomicStampedReference<State> parcel = new AtomicStampedReference<>(State.READY, 1);
        int staleStamp = parcel.getStamp();
        parcel.set(State.PACKED, 2);
        parcel.set(State.READY, 3);
        boolean accepted = parcel.compareAndSet(State.READY, State.SHIPPED, staleStamp, 4);
        System.out.println("accepted=" + accepted);
        System.out.println(parcel.getReference() + ":" + parcel.getStamp());
    }
}

Output

accepted=false
READY:3

Cost and ownership

Each operation uses constant application storage and an atomic reference update. Retries under contention can increase work; the example isolates the version condition and does not claim a latency bound.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not compare only the current reference when intervening transitions matter.
  • Do not use set as a conditional update in a contended workflow.
  • Do not treat an in-memory stamp as a durable database version.

title: Java CyclicBarrier timeout: a broken generation needs a recovery rule
summary: A CyclicBarrier generation breaks when a waiting party times out, and later await calls fail until the barrier is reset or replaced.
body:
A CyclicBarrier generation breaks when a waiting party times out, and later await calls fail until the barrier is reset or replaced.

Treat timeout as group failure

A phase cannot be considered complete when one participant abandons the rendezvous. The fixture uses a zero-timeout wait with two required parties, then verifies that the barrier is broken and that a later await reports the broken state. Reset creates a new generation; it does not finish the abandoned work.

CountDownLatch is one-shot and does not have the same generation model. Phaser registration is useful when party membership can change, but it also needs a failure policy.

Do not hide failed work with reset

Reset only after every participant has agreed how to discard or retry the old phase. A caller that simply resets and continues can mix outputs from two generations. Bound waits and retain enough phase identity to reject late results.

Working program

import java.util.concurrent.BrokenBarrierException;
import java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException;

public class BatchPhaseRecovery {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        CyclicBarrier phase = new CyclicBarrier(2);
        try { phase.await(0, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS); }
        catch (TimeoutException expired) { System.out.println("phase timed out"); }
        catch (BrokenBarrierException unexpected) { throw new AssertionError(unexpected); }
        System.out.println("broken=" + phase.isBroken());
        try { phase.await(); }
        catch (BrokenBarrierException rejected) { System.out.println("old phase rejected"); }
        phase.reset();
        System.out.println("broken=" + phase.isBroken());
    }
}

Output

phase timed out
broken=true
old phase rejected
broken=false

Cost and ownership

The demonstration uses constant memory. Real phases incur synchronization and waiting costs for all parties; a timeout does not reclaim unfinished tasks. Recovery must account for those tasks before a new generation begins.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat reset as completion of the failed phase.
  • Do not let an unbounded await hold a worker forever without a failure policy.
  • Do not merge late results from a broken generation into the next one.

title: Java SynchronousQueue: a handoff has no storage capacity
summary: SynchronousQueue transfers an element directly between a producer and a waiting consumer; it does not retain elements in an internal queue.
body:
SynchronousQueue transfers an element directly between a producer and a waiting consumer; it does not retain elements in an internal queue.

Observe the zero-capacity contract

An immediate offer fails when no consumer is ready. A subsequent put waits until a consumer accepts the value. The fixture starts the consumer only after the failed offer, then joins it before printing the received shipment ID.

This handoff can apply backpressure, but a stalled consumer can hold the producer indefinitely. Use a timed offer or cancellation where the caller has a deadline. Buffered blocking queues decouple arrival and consumption up to their configured capacity.

Separate transfer from processing

A successful put means the consumer accepted the element; it does not prove that the consumer completed its business work. If acknowledgment matters, pair the transfer with a separate completion signal or durable result record.

Working program

import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;

public class ShipmentDirectHandoff {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        SynchronousQueue<String> handoff = new SynchronousQueue<>();
        System.out.println("immediate=" + handoff.offer("lot-47"));
        AtomicReference<String> received = new AtomicReference<>();
        Thread receiver = new Thread(() -> {
            try { received.set(handoff.take()); }
            catch (InterruptedException stopped) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        });
        receiver.start();
        handoff.put("lot-82");
        receiver.join();
        System.out.println("received=" + received.get());
    }
}

Output

immediate=false
received=lot-82

Cost and ownership

The queue itself has no element capacity, although producer and consumer tasks still occupy threads or other runtime resources. Transfer can block; its latency is governed by consumer readiness, not a queue traversal cost.

  • Do not assume offer stores work when no consumer exists.
  • Do not treat a completed put as proof that processing completed.
  • Do not use unbounded waits when the request has a deadline.

title: Java volatile counter: visible writes can still lose an update
summary: volatile makes a field's writes visible across threads but does not turn a read-modify-write expression into one atomic operation.
body:
volatile makes a field's writes visible across threads but does not turn a read-modify-write expression into one atomic operation.

Force the stale-read interleaving

Two workers read the same zero before either writes. A barrier holds both until those reads are complete. Each then writes one, so the final counter is one rather than two. This is a deterministic demonstration of the lost-update schedule, not a timing-sensitive stress test.

For a counter, AtomicInteger offers an atomic increment. LongAdder can reduce contention for aggregate statistics, but its sum is not an atomic transaction with other fields.

Choose the invariant

If incrementing the counter must happen with an inventory mutation, use one lock or a transactional boundary for both values. Making both fields volatile does not create a joint invariant. Read-write locks help when a shared state needs coordinated reads and writes.

Working program

import java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier;

public class DispatchCounterRace {
    static class Counter { volatile int accepted; }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Counter counter = new Counter();
        CyclicBarrier bothRead = new CyclicBarrier(2);
        Runnable accept = () -> {
            int observed = counter.accepted;
            try { bothRead.await(); }
            catch (Exception failure) { throw new AssertionError(failure); }
            counter.accepted = observed + 1;
        };
        Thread first = new Thread(accept);
        Thread second = new Thread(accept);
        first.start();
        second.start();
        first.join();
        second.join();
        System.out.println("accepted=" + counter.accepted);
    }
}

Output

accepted=1

Cost and ownership

Each worker uses constant local storage. volatile adds visibility ordering, not a lock or atomic increment; the barrier makes the failed schedule reproducible. A real counter should use an atomic primitive or protect the full invariant under one synchronization rule.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat volatile++ as atomic.
  • Do not infer correctness from a test that happened to produce the expected count.
  • Do not split one invariant across independent volatile fields.

title: Java ConcurrentHashMap.compute: serialize one key's remapping
summary: ConcurrentHashMap.compute applies a remapping for one key atomically, so concurrent callers can update that key without a separate get-then-put race.
body:
ConcurrentHashMap.compute applies a remapping for one key atomically, so concurrent callers can update that key without a separate get-then-put race.

Keep the mapping function bounded

Two workers call compute for the same shipment key. Each sees the current value supplied by the map, and the final count is two regardless of which worker arrived first. A separate get followed by put could lose one increment.

The map may block other updates to the same key while the remapping function runs. Do not perform remote I/O or recursively update the same map from inside it. Concurrent map contracts cover key-level ownership; Map.merge has its own null-removal behavior.

Do not confuse key atomicity with transactions

A compute call protects one key's remapping. Updating a second map, writing a database row, or publishing an event remains outside that atomic boundary. If those effects must succeed together, use a higher-level transaction or explicit recovery protocol.

Working program

import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;

public class ShipmentAttemptTally {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        CountDownLatch begin = new CountDownLatch(1);
        Runnable record = () -> {
            try { begin.await(); }
            catch (InterruptedException stopped) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; }
            counts.compute("lot-47", (key, previous) -> previous == null ? 1 : previous + 1);
        };
        Thread first = new Thread(record);
        Thread second = new Thread(record);
        first.start();
        second.start();
        begin.countDown();
        first.join();
        second.join();
        System.out.println("attempts=" + counts.get("lot-47"));
    }
}

Output

attempts=2

Cost and ownership

The fixture uses one map entry and two threads. A short remapping function performs constant application work per call, while contention on a hot key can serialize callers. The map does not make external effects atomic with its value.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not replace compute with get followed by put for a contended counter.
  • Do not block on remote work inside the remapping function.
  • Do not assume one-key atomicity covers a database write or a second key.

title: Java lockInterruptibly: cancel a worker waiting for ownership
summary: Lock.lockInterruptibly lets a waiting thread stop trying to acquire a lock when it is interrupted.
body:
Lock.lockInterruptibly lets a waiting thread stop trying to acquire a lock when it is interrupted.

Keep cancellation at the wait boundary

The main thread holds a lock while a worker attempts an interruptible acquisition. It interrupts the worker before releasing ownership, so the worker exits without entering the guarded section. A latch makes the ordering visible; the final output does not depend on which core ran first.

Cancellation policy must also cover work after acquisition. A thread that already owns a lock cannot be made safe merely by interrupting it; its critical section needs cleanup and an explicit stop decision.

Track ownership precisely

Only unlock after acquisition succeeded. An InterruptedException from lockInterruptibly means this call did not acquire the lock. Preserve or propagate the cancellation decision at the task boundary instead of quietly retrying forever.

Working program

import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

public class InventoryLockCancellation {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        ReentrantLock guard = new ReentrantLock();
        CountDownLatch attempting = new CountDownLatch(1);
        AtomicBoolean cancelled = new AtomicBoolean();
        guard.lock();
        Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
            attempting.countDown();
            try {
                guard.lockInterruptibly();
                try { throw new AssertionError("unexpected ownership"); }
                finally { guard.unlock(); }
            } catch (InterruptedException stopped) {
                cancelled.set(true);
            }
        });
        try {
            worker.start();
            attempting.await();
            worker.interrupt();
            worker.join();
            System.out.println("cancelled=" + cancelled.get());
        } finally { guard.unlock(); }
    }
}

Output

cancelled=true

Cost and ownership

The coordination uses constant storage and one waiting thread. There is no finite wait bound without an interrupt or a timed tryLock; production callers should decide who owns that timeout or cancellation signal.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not unlock a lock that the interrupted worker never acquired.
  • Do not swallow interruption and silently retry the same wait.
  • Do not assume interruption repairs partially completed work after ownership begins.
