title: Java streams are single-use: create a new pipeline for each pass
summary: A Stream is a traversal plan, not a reusable container; obtain a fresh stream for each terminal operation.
body:
A Stream is a traversal plan, not a reusable container; obtain a fresh stream for each terminal operation.

Keep the source, not the spent pipeline

A report may need both a total and a list of rejected invoices. Retain the collection that owns the data, then request a new stream for each calculation. Calling a second terminal operation on the old stream is invalid, even when its source has not changed.

This matters for database-backed or file-backed sources too: a supplier can build a new pipeline, but it cannot resurrect a consumed cursor. Resource ownership still follows the source lifetime.

Use a supplier when pipeline assembly is repeated

The supplier below creates a fresh pipeline over the same in-memory list. It captures the list, so a later mutation would affect later traversals. Copy or snapshot the source if the two results must describe one fixed state. Stream fundamentals covers lazy execution.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Supplier;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class InvoiceStreamPasses {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> invoiceCents = Arrays.asList(4700, -300, 1250);
        Supplier<Stream<Integer>> amounts = () -> invoiceCents.stream();
        long accepted = amounts.get().filter(cents -> cents >= 0).count();
        int total = amounts.get().filter(cents -> cents >= 0)
                .mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();
        System.out.println("accepted=" + accepted);
        System.out.println("totalCents=" + total);
    }
}

Output

accepted=2
totalCents=5950

Cost and ownership

Each pass is O(n) time over the list; the supplier and pipeline add little state, but a second pass repeats traversal and any mapper work. Materialize an intermediate result only when that extra memory is cheaper than recomputation or when a fixed snapshot is required.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not cache a Stream field for later terminal operations.
  • Do not assume a supplier makes a one-shot I/O cursor reusable.
  • Do not run related calculations over a mutable source without defining snapshot semantics.

title: Java Stream.peek: observation is not a correctness hook
summary: peek can observe elements that a terminal operation traverses, but its action is not a reliable place for required work.
body:
peek can observe elements that a terminal operation traverses, but its action is not a reliable place for required work.

Traversal determines whether the action runs

An intermediate pipeline is lazy. Creating it does not send audit events, update counters or write records. Even after a terminal call, an implementation may skip stages when it can compute the result without visiting elements. For example, count on a sized source may bypass a peek action.

The program uses collect to force traversal for this particular result. Put required audit writes in an explicit loop or an owned service boundary instead of relying on peek. Short-circuit operations have another reason to visit only a prefix.

Separate inspection from mutation

A diagnostic print may help during local inspection, but it changes observable output and can become expensive in a large pipeline. Lambda capture does not turn shared mutable counters into safe parallel reductions; collect a value instead.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class ShipmentPeekBoundary {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Stream<String> pending = Arrays.asList("PK-47", "PK-82").stream()
                .peek(packageId -> System.out.println("visited=" + packageId));
        System.out.println("pipeline-built");
        List<String> packageIds = pending.collect(Collectors.toList());
        System.out.println("collected=" + packageIds.size());
    }
}

Output

pipeline-built
visited=PK-47
visited=PK-82
collected=2

Cost and ownership

This traversal is O(n) time and the collected list is O(n) space. Logging adds I/O cost for each visited element; parallel execution can interleave messages and must not be used to guarantee audit order.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not rely on peek for required writes or validation.
  • Do not assume count will execute every peek action.
  • Do not use a shared mutable counter inside a parallel pipeline.

title: Java Collectors.toMap: choose a duplicate-key rule
summary: Collectors.toMap needs an explicit merge function when distinct input records can produce the same map key.
body:
Collectors.toMap needs an explicit merge function when distinct input records can produce the same map key.

Name the conflict policy

Two shipment updates can share an order ID. The two-argument collector throws when that happens; this is often useful during validation, but it is not a merge strategy. A merge function must state whether the earliest update, latest update or a combined value wins.

This program keeps the larger revision number. That policy is independent of input order for unequal revisions, unlike a last-write-wins lambda that depends on encounter order. If equal revisions carry different payloads, reject the conflict instead of silently picking one. Map key contracts still apply.

Avoid pretending the default map is ordered

This example looks up keys directly and prints explicit fields. The basic toMap overload does not promise the map implementation or iteration order. Use an explicit map supplier when presentation order is part of the result.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class ShipmentRevisionIndex {
    static final class Revision {
        final String orderId;
        final int number;
        Revision(String orderId, int number) {
            this.orderId = orderId;
            this.number = number;
        }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Revision> updates = Arrays.asList(
                new Revision("ORD-47", 2), new Revision("ORD-82", 1),
                new Revision("ORD-47", 4));
        Map<String, Revision> newest = updates.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(
                revision -> revision.orderId,
                revision -> revision,
                (left, right) -> left.number >= right.number ? left : right));
        System.out.println("ORD-47=" + newest.get("ORD-47").number);
        System.out.println("orders=" + newest.size());
    }
}

Output

ORD-47=4
orders=2

Cost and ownership

Collection is O(n) expected time with a hash map and O(k) space for k distinct order IDs; collision-heavy keys can change practical costs. A merge function may run multiple times for the same key, particularly in parallel collection, so it must be associative for parallel use and free of external side effects.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use two-argument toMap when duplicate keys are valid input.
  • Do not use a nonassociative merge policy in parallel collection.
  • Do not infer iteration order from a basic toMap result.

title: Java Collectors.groupingBy: reject or normalize null classifier keys
summary: groupingBy does not accept a null value from its classifier; define an explicit bucket before collecting nullable records.
body:
groupingBy does not accept a null value from its classifier; define an explicit bucket before collecting nullable records.

Make missing classification visible

A warehouse record without a region is not automatically part of a null-key group. The standard groupingBy collector rejects a null classifier result. Treat the missing field as invalid input, or map it to a named bucket with a clear reporting meaning.

The program uses UNASSIGNED for a known reporting bucket. That is a business choice, not a library default. If the bucket could collide with a real region code, use a typed key instead of a string sentinel. Optional can model absence before a boundary chooses its representation.

Keep grouping costs explicit

Grouping stores references to the original records in lists. Mutating those records later changes what a reader sees through the groups; copy immutable values when the report must be a snapshot. The resulting map also has no promised iteration order.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class WarehouseRegionBuckets {
    static final class Dispatch {
        final String id;
        final String region;
        Dispatch(String id, String region) {
            this.id = id;
            this.region = region;
        }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Dispatch> dispatches = Arrays.asList(
                new Dispatch("DSP-47", "WEST"),
                new Dispatch("DSP-82", null),
                new Dispatch("DSP-91", "WEST"));
        Map<String, List<Dispatch>> byRegion = dispatches.stream().collect(
                Collectors.groupingBy(dispatch ->
                        dispatch.region == null ? "UNASSIGNED" : dispatch.region));
        System.out.println("WEST=" + byRegion.get("WEST").size());
        System.out.println("UNASSIGNED=" + byRegion.get("UNASSIGNED").get(0).id);
    }
}

Output

WEST=2
UNASSIGNED=DSP-82

Cost and ownership

Expected grouping time is O(n) and storage is O(n) references plus map and list overhead. The collector keeps group lists in memory; for a very large input, aggregate counts with a downstream collector or process bounded batches.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume groupingBy creates a null-key bucket.
  • Do not use a sentinel that can also be a valid region.
  • Do not expect map iteration order or immutable group snapshots by default.

title: Java Collectors.toMap: preserve encounter order with LinkedHashMap
summary: The basic toMap collector makes no map-order promise; pass a LinkedHashMap supplier when input order belongs in the output.
body:
The basic toMap collector makes no map-order promise; pass a LinkedHashMap supplier when input order belongs in the output.

Choose order at the collector boundary

A receipt summary displayed in arrival order should not depend on whichever map implementation a collector happens to return. The four-argument toMap overload accepts a map supplier, so the result can preserve first insertion order while duplicate keys use a declared merge rule.

Updating an existing key in a default insertion-order LinkedHashMap does not move it to the end. The program retains the first position of RC-47 even though its amount is replaced. LinkedHashMap behavior explains when an access-order map would differ.

Keep parallel assumptions separate

Encounter order and merge behavior should be specified before using a parallel stream. A side-effecting merge function is unsafe; an associative value merge is easier to reason about. Parallel encounter order covers terminal behavior.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class ReceiptArrivalIndex {
    static final class Receipt {
        final String id;
        final int cents;
        Receipt(String id, int cents) {
            this.id = id;
            this.cents = cents;
        }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, Integer> centsByReceipt = Arrays.asList(
                new Receipt("RC-47", 1200), new Receipt("RC-82", 3400),
                new Receipt("RC-47", 1500)).stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(
                receipt -> receipt.id,
                receipt -> receipt.cents,
                (earlier, later) -> later,
                LinkedHashMap::new));
        centsByReceipt.forEach((id, cents) ->
                System.out.println(id + "=" + cents));
    }
}

Output

RC-47=1500
RC-82=3400

Cost and ownership

Expected collection is O(n) time and O(k) map space for k unique receipts, with extra link fields per entry compared with a plain hash map. Explicit ordering costs memory; use it only when a caller relies on stable presentation order.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume HashMap or basic toMap preserves arrival order.
  • Do not expect updating a key to move it in an insertion-order LinkedHashMap.
  • Do not make the merge callback depend on external mutable state.

title: Java parallel streams: forEach and forEachOrdered have different order contracts
summary: A parallel stream may invoke forEach actions in any thread and order; forEachOrdered preserves encounter order when one exists.
body:
A parallel stream may invoke forEach actions in any thread and order; forEachOrdered preserves encounter order when one exists.

Keep computation separate from ordered output

A shipment list has encounter order. Parallel forEach does not promise its actions run in that order, so writing numbered report lines from it can scramble the report. forEachOrdered preserves encounter order for this ordered source, though the ordering constraint can reduce parallel benefit.

The program deliberately prints only the ordered path. An unordered call cannot have one portable expected output. peek actions and parallel terminal callbacks should not be treated as an audit log.

Parallel does not make side effects safe

A non-thread-safe accumulator can lose updates regardless of which terminal method prints in order. Use a collector or reduction for values. Choose parallelism only after measuring enough CPU work to offset splitting, coordination and combining costs.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;

public class OrderedShipmentReport {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> shipmentIds = Arrays.asList("SH-47", "SH-82", "SH-91");
        shipmentIds.parallelStream().forEachOrdered(System.out::println);
    }
}

Output

SH-47
SH-82
SH-91

Cost and ownership

The traversal remains O(n) total work. Parallel execution can use additional worker threads and coordination, while preserving encounter order limits throughput. Three strings are too little work to justify parallelism; the small fixture isolates the contract.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not promise forEach output order on a parallel stream.
  • Do not use forEachOrdered to make a shared mutable accumulator thread-safe.
  • Do not assume parallel traversal is faster for small or blocking workloads.

title: Java Stream.reduce: identity and associative accumulator contracts
summary: A reduction identity must leave any value unchanged under the accumulator, and the accumulator must be associative for parallel reduction.
body:
A reduction identity must leave any value unchanged under the accumulator, and the accumulator must be associative for parallel reduction.

Use the operation's real identity

For integer addition the identity is zero. Starting at one appears to add a single fee in a sequential pass, but a parallel reduction can apply that identity in multiple partitions. Add the fee after the reduction instead. For multiplication the identity is one.

The example sums invoice amounts and adds a fixed handling fee exactly once. It uses long arithmetic to reduce overflow risk, but a long can still overflow; a financial ledger should define bounds or use a decimal representation. Overflow contracts apply before choosing a reduction shape.

Avoid order-sensitive arithmetic

Subtraction and floating-point addition are not generally associative in the way parallel reduce expects. Floating-point rounding can change with grouping. If a stable money total matters, use integer minor units with overflow checks or BigDecimal under a defined scale policy.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;

public class InvoiceAmountReduction {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        long amountCents = Arrays.asList(4700L, 1250L, 800L)
                .parallelStream().reduce(0L, Long::sum);
        long handlingFeeCents = 275L;
        System.out.println("amountCents=" + amountCents);
        System.out.println("withFeeCents=" + Math.addExact(amountCents, handlingFeeCents));
    }
}

Output

amountCents=6750
withFeeCents=7025

Cost and ownership

Summation is O(n) work and O(p) partial results for p parallel tasks, apart from the input list. Parallel scheduling overhead can exceed the useful work for small inputs. Math.addExact checks the final fee addition; check each intermediate addition too when overflow is possible.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use one as the identity for addition.
  • Do not use subtraction as a parallel reduction accumulator.
  • Do not assume long or floating-point totals are safe for every financial input.

title: Java Stream.anyMatch: stop on a decision, not on every element
summary: anyMatch returns true when a matching element is found; callers must not assume the predicate visits every element.
body:
anyMatch returns true when a matching element is found; callers must not assume the predicate visits every element.

Express the question as a predicate

A fraud gate needs to know whether any transaction exceeds a review threshold. A sequential anyMatch can stop once it has enough information. That makes it suitable for a decision, not for sending one notification per transaction. Parallel traversal may evaluate more elements even after the result is known.

An empty stream returns false for anyMatch and true for allMatch. Choose the operation that expresses the business rule for an empty batch, rather than relying on the name alone. A terminal operation consumes its stream.

Keep predicates pure

The predicate should inspect a transaction without mutating shared state. If every record needs validation, use an explicit pass or collect validation results; short-circuiting intentionally skips work once the answer is decided.

Working program

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;

public class TransactionReviewGate {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> transferCents = Arrays.asList(4200, 9800, 750);
        boolean needsReview = transferCents.stream()
                .anyMatch(cents -> cents > 9000);
        boolean emptyBatchNeedsReview = java.util.Collections.<Integer>emptyList()
                .stream().anyMatch(cents -> cents > 9000);
        System.out.println("needsReview=" + needsReview);
        System.out.println("emptyNeedsReview=" + emptyBatchNeedsReview);
    }
}

Output

needsReview=true
emptyNeedsReview=false

Cost and ownership

Worst-case time is O(n) and extra pipeline space is small; the operation may stop earlier when a match is found. A parallel pipeline can spend work beyond the first match, and a predicate with I/O side effects makes both timing and coverage unpredictable.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not rely on a predicate running once for every element.
  • Do not treat empty-input anyMatch as true.
  • Do not use a short-circuit terminal operation as an audit or validation pass.

title: Java walkFileTree: visit failures without hiding incomplete scans
summary: Files.walkFileTree visits a directory tree through callbacks that distinguish entry visits, directory entry, failed visits, and directory completion. A complete inventory must define what happens when any visit fails.
body:
Files.walkFileTree visits a directory tree through callbacks that distinguish entry visits, directory entry, failed visits, and directory completion. A complete inventory must define what happens when any visit fails.

Operational contract

A manifest scanner should not return a green count after permission failure halfway through a tree. SimpleFileVisitor's default failure behavior throws, which is useful when completeness matters. If the application deliberately skips a subtree, it must record the omitted path and mark the inventory partial. The visitor below collects regular files without following symbolic links and lets I/O failures reach the caller. The caller owns the resulting list and the decision to publish it.

Failure case

A fictional dispatch archive has 47 manifest files under several depot folders. If one depot cannot be opened, a count of the other files is not an archive total. Keep that failure beside the scan ID; do not silently treat it as an empty folder. Following directory links would also change the traversal boundary and could create cycles, so the sample retains the default no-follow behavior.

Java code

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class ManifestTreeInventory {
    public static List<Path> scan(Path archiveRoot) throws IOException {
        List<Path> manifests = new ArrayList<>();
        Files.walkFileTree(archiveRoot, new SimpleFileVisitor<Path>() {
            @Override public FileVisitResult visitFile(Path path, BasicFileAttributes attributes) {
                if (attributes.isRegularFile() && path.getFileName().toString().endsWith(".manifest")) {
                    manifests.add(path);
                }
                return FileVisitResult.CONTINUE;
            }
            @Override public FileVisitResult visitFileFailed(Path path, IOException failure) throws IOException {
                throw new IOException("Inventory incomplete at " + path, failure);
            }
        });
        return manifests;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The walk visits N reachable entries in O(N) time. The visitor retains M matching paths in O(M) application memory; traversal bookkeeping grows with depth. A failure is a correctness result, not a performance detail. For huge trees, write bounded inventory records to a controlled sink rather than retaining every path.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not convert visitFileFailed into CONTINUE without recording a partial result.
  • Do not call a symlink target part of the scan unless link traversal is an explicit policy.
  • Do not publish a total before traversal completes.

title: Java WatchService: register, consume, and reset each key
summary: WatchService reports changes to registered watchable objects through signaled keys. The consumer retrieves a key, reads its events, and resets it so later changes can be signaled.
body:
WatchService reports changes to registered watchable objects through signaled keys. The consumer retrieves a key, reads its events, and resets it so later changes can be signaled.

Operational contract

A watched directory is a hint source, not a durable message queue. Register the directory for the event kinds needed by the application, process a key's current batch, then inspect reset's boolean result. A false result means the registration is no longer valid and requires a new ownership decision. The event context for a Path registration is relative to the watched directory. The code keeps resolution local to that directory and returns whether observation remains active; the owner closes the service on shutdown.

Failure case

A depot process watches a staging folder where 47 manifests may arrive over a shift. One create notification prompts an intake check, but a modify notification can arrive while the producer is still writing. The consumer records candidate paths and waits for the publication contract described in the next lesson. It does not parse each event as a complete manifest or promise that every short-lived file will be observed.

Java code

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.FileSystems;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.nio.file.StandardWatchEventKinds;
import java.nio.file.WatchEvent;
import java.nio.file.WatchKey;
import java.nio.file.WatchService;
import java.util.Set;

public class StagingWatchConsumer {
    public record Outcome(boolean rescan, boolean active) {}

    public static WatchService register(Path staging) throws IOException {
        WatchService service = FileSystems.getDefault().newWatchService();
        try {
            staging.register(service, StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_CREATE,
                StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_MODIFY, StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_DELETE);
            return service;
        } catch (IOException | RuntimeException failure) {
            try { service.close(); }
            catch (IOException closeFailure) { failure.addSuppressed(closeFailure); }
            throw failure;
        }
    }

    public static Outcome takeOne(WatchService service, Path staging, Set<Path> candidates)
            throws InterruptedException {
        WatchKey key = service.take();
        boolean rescan = false;
        for (WatchEvent<?> event : key.pollEvents()) {
            if (event.kind() == StandardWatchEventKinds.OVERFLOW) {
                rescan = true;
                continue;
            }
            Object context = event.context();
            if (context instanceof Path) {
                Path relative = (Path) context;
                if (!relative.isAbsolute()) candidates.add(staging.resolve(relative).normalize());
            }
        }
        return new Outcome(rescan, key.reset());
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Processing E delivered events is O(E) plus set insertion. The set retains O(U) distinct candidate paths, where U is the number of unique names. If the producer outruns the consumer, event loss can occur; reset and overflow handling must be paired with a directory reconciliation path.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not forget to reset the key after processing its batch.
  • Do not resolve event context against an unrelated working directory.
  • Do not equate a create event with a finished file.

title: Java WatchService OVERFLOW: reconcile against directory state
summary: WatchService OVERFLOW means changes may have been discarded. A consumer must compare current directory state with its last accepted snapshot rather than trying to reconstruct missing events.
body:
WatchService OVERFLOW means changes may have been discarded. A consumer must compare current directory state with its last accepted snapshot rather than trying to reconstruct missing events.

Operational contract

The event stream does not identify which changes were lost. Treat it as a signal to rescan the registered directory and rebuild the candidate set under the same eligibility rule. A directory listing can itself race with writers or fail; its result is a point-in-time observation, not an atomic filesystem transaction. Keep a scan generation and record failures. The code below demonstrates a bounded reconciliation, refusing a directory with more than 47 visible entries instead of silently truncating it.

Failure case

A depot initially knows 42 names. A burst of writes produces OVERFLOW. The service cannot say whether the remaining five expected manifests were created, renamed, or removed. A fresh listing obtains the current names and replaces the remembered set only if it completes inside the cap. The caller then validates candidate contents using a separate publication rule before counting them as accepted manifests.

Java code

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.DirectoryStream;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

public class DirectoryReconciliation {
    public static Set<Path> snapshot(Path staging) throws IOException {
        Set<Path> visible = new HashSet<>();
        try (DirectoryStream<Path> entries = Files.newDirectoryStream(staging)) {
            for (Path candidate : entries) {
                if (visible.size() >= 47) throw new IOException("Listing cap exceeded");
                visible.add(candidate.getFileName());
            }
        }
        return visible;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Rebuilding a set from N directory entries is O(N) expected time and O(N) memory. Comparing it with the old set is also O(N+K) expected for old-set size K. A cap protects memory but deliberately fails completeness when exceeded; increase capacity or page the intake design, never report the capped set as complete.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat OVERFLOW as one ordinary file event.
  • Do not retain a partial listing as a complete snapshot.
  • Do not assume a rescan is atomic with ongoing writers.

title: Java DirectoryStream: close iteration and reject silent truncation
summary: DirectoryStream iterates directory entries while holding an I/O resource. A bounded listing needs a close scope, an explicit maximum, and a policy for iteration failures.
body:
DirectoryStream iterates directory entries while holding an I/O resource. A bounded listing needs a close scope, an explicit maximum, and a policy for iteration failures.

Operational contract

Unlike a materialized list, iteration can fail after some entries have already been seen. The caller must not confuse the partial result with a complete batch. The program selects manifest names, rejects a forty-eighth match, sorts the accepted names for stable reporting, and unwraps a DirectoryIteratorException as an I/O failure. Directory iteration order is not a business order. If a larger scan is required, design a chunked consumer or use a database-backed inventory instead of quietly dropping entries.

Failure case

A review job expects at most 47 staging manifests. Forty-seven matches fit; a forty-eighth is a capacity error, not the first file of an invisible next page. Sorting makes a report reproducible for the snapshot that was observed, but a producer can still change the directory during iteration. The job records the scan time and verifies each opened file again before processing.

Java code

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;

public class BoundedManifestListing {
    public static List<Path> list(Path staging) throws IOException {
        List<Path> matches = new ArrayList<>();
        try (DirectoryStream<Path> stream = Files.newDirectoryStream(staging, "*.manifest")) {
            for (Path candidate : stream) {
                if (matches.size() == 47) throw new IOException("More than 47 manifests");
                matches.add(candidate);
            }
        } catch (DirectoryIteratorException failure) {
            throw new IOException("Manifest listing failed", failure.getCause());
        }
        matches.sort(Comparator.comparing(path -> path.getFileName().toString()));
        return matches;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The listing visits N entries and sorting M matches takes O(M log M) time with O(M) retained paths. The cap bounds M at 47 for this job. It does not bound the provider's traversal work or prove the directory stayed unchanged between listing and open.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not leave DirectoryStream open after iteration.
  • Do not assume iteration order is sorted.
  • Do not return a partial list after an iteration failure or cap breach.

title: Java symbolic links: inspect attributes without claiming race safety
summary: NOFOLLOW_LINKS makes a metadata read describe a symbolic link itself rather than the target it names. That observation is useful for an intake policy but does not lock the path against replacement.
body:
NOFOLLOW_LINKS makes a metadata read describe a symbolic link itself rather than the target it names. That observation is useful for an intake policy but does not lock the path against replacement.

Operational contract

A manifest intake may reject symbolic links because they can point outside the owned staging tree. readAttributes with NOFOLLOW_LINKS distinguishes a regular file from a link at the moment of inspection. A later open can still follow a path that has been replaced in between. For an adversarial writable directory, move ownership to a trusted staging area or use a supported handle-relative API such as SecureDirectoryStream, with a fallback policy when it is unavailable. The sample is an inspection gate, not a race-free opener.

Failure case

A contractor uploads a candidate named shipment-47.manifest. The metadata gate accepts a regular file and rejects a symbolic link. If another writer can rename entries after the check, the application must not claim that the next path-based read is protected. The job keeps the folder write permissions narrow and validates the opened content before it makes any state change.

Java code

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.LinkOption;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes;

public class ManifestAttributeGate {
    public static void requireRegularEntry(Path candidate) throws IOException {
        BasicFileAttributes observed = Files.readAttributes(
            candidate, BasicFileAttributes.class, LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS);
        if (!observed.isRegularFile()) {
            throw new IOException("Manifest entry is not a regular file");
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

One metadata read is O(1) API work but may involve remote or slow filesystem I/O. Secure open-and-verify designs cost more coordination than a lexical check, yet they are needed when untrusted users can mutate the directory. The observed attributes should never be sold as a permanent property of a path name.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not equate Path.normalize with filesystem containment.
  • Do not assume NOFOLLOW_LINKS prevents a later replacement race.
  • Do not accept a symbolic link because its current target appears regular.

title: Java JDBC batches: inspect update counts and own rollback
summary: PreparedStatement batching queues parameter sets for one executeBatch call. The returned counts and a possible BatchUpdateException describe execution, not automatic transaction success.
body:
PreparedStatement batching queues parameter sets for one executeBatch call. The returned counts and a possible BatchUpdateException describe execution, not automatic transaction success.

Operational contract

Some drivers stop after a failed command, while others continue and mark failed positions. SUCCESS_NO_INFO means success without a row count. A caller must decide whether every position met the business invariant, then commit or roll back the owned transaction. The method stages one receipt ID per parameter set and returns raw counts; it requires auto-commit to be disabled. It does not promise that batch execution alone is atomic, and it leaves commit, rollback, and connection lifetime to its caller.

Failure case

A depot sends 47 receipt IDs. If entry 31 violates a uniqueness rule, the caller records the failing batch result, rolls back the transaction, and resolves whether a retry is safe. It does not report 30 or 46 accepted receipts from a count array while leaving the connection open for another request. The IDs need an idempotency rule before a retry after a network failure.

Java code

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.List;

public class ReceiptBatchWriter {
    public static int[] stage(Connection connection, List<String> receiptIds) throws SQLException {
        if (connection.getAutoCommit()) throw new SQLException("Caller must own a transaction");
        try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                "INSERT INTO receipt_intake (receipt_id) VALUES (?)")) {
            for (String receiptId : receiptIds) {
                statement.setString(1, receiptId);
                statement.addBatch();
            }
            return statement.executeBatch();
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Binding N rows is O(N) client work and O(N) pending parameter state until execution. Batching can reduce round trips, but the actual transport and server plan depend on the driver. Bound batch size and inspect all returned positions; a database transaction remains the durability boundary.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not interpret SUCCESS_NO_INFO as zero affected rows.
  • Do not assume every driver stops at the first failed command.
  • Do not leave rollback ownership ambiguous after any failure.

title: Java ResultSet: cursor position and SQL NULL are separate states
summary: A JDBC ResultSet begins before its first row and advances with next. Primitive getters return a Java primitive even for SQL NULL, so wasNull must be checked immediately after that getter.
body:
A JDBC ResultSet begins before its first row and advances with next. Primitive getters return a Java primitive even for SQL NULL, so wasNull must be checked immediately after that getter.

Operational contract

A zero from getInt can mean a stored zero or SQL NULL. Calling another getter before wasNull changes which read the flag describes. The method below maps an optional reserved quantity to Integer, preserving zero and absence as distinct values. It uses a forward-only read and closes the result and statement together. The SQL orders rows explicitly; ResultSet traversal order without ORDER BY is not a report contract. A missing row remains different from a row with a null quantity.

Failure case

A dispatch report contains one receipt with zero reserved units and another with no quantity reported. Turning both into zero would hide missing source data. The mapping keeps the second value null for an upstream validation decision. The caller can then reject incomplete quantities without distorting the first receipt's legitimate zero.

Java code

import java.sql.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class ReservationRows {
    public static List<Integer> quantities(Connection connection) throws SQLException {
        List<Integer> quantities = new ArrayList<>();
        try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                "SELECT reserved_qty FROM receipt_intake ORDER BY receipt_id");
             ResultSet rows = statement.executeQuery()) {
            while (rows.next()) {
                int quantity = rows.getInt(1);
                quantities.add(rows.wasNull() ? null : quantity);
            }
        }
        return quantities;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Reading N rows is O(N) time and the returned list uses O(N) memory. A streaming consumer can reduce retained memory, but driver fetch behavior and connection lifetime still matter. Never infer a complete business population merely because next eventually returns false; filters and snapshot isolation determine which rows were queried.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call a primitive zero proof that the SQL column was non-null.
  • Do not invoke wasNull after reading another column.
  • Do not read a getter before next positions the cursor on a row.

title: Java JDBC generated keys: validate one insert and one returned identity
summary: A JDBC insert can request generated keys from its PreparedStatement. The caller must check update count, key presence, key type, and transaction outcome before treating the identity as durable.
body:
A JDBC insert can request generated keys from its PreparedStatement. The caller must check update count, key presence, key type, and transaction outcome before treating the identity as durable.

Operational contract

Generated-key support and which columns are returned vary by driver and SQL operation. This example asks for a key for a single inserted manifest, rejects zero or multiple returned key rows, and preserves the connection's transaction boundary for the caller. It does not commit. A key seen before commit can still disappear on rollback. For multi-row inserts, define an explicit mapping between input rows and generated identities rather than assuming a convenient order.

Failure case

A review process inserts manifest-47 and needs the new row ID for a child audit record. It requests the key while using the same transaction, then inserts the child row and commits both together. If the insert reports no row or the driver returns no key, the operation fails and the owner rolls back. The application never invents an ID from the last value seen in another request.

Java code

import java.sql.*;

public class ManifestIdentityWriter {
    public static long insert(Connection connection, String manifestName) throws SQLException {
        try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                "INSERT INTO manifests (name) VALUES (?)", Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS)) {
            statement.setString(1, manifestName);
            if (statement.executeUpdate() != 1) throw new SQLException("Expected one inserted row");
            try (ResultSet keys = statement.getGeneratedKeys()) {
                if (!keys.next()) throw new SQLException("Generated key absent");
                long identity = keys.getLong(1);
                if (keys.wasNull() || keys.next()) throw new SQLException("Invalid generated key result");
                return identity;
            }
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The client performs one insert and one key-result read. Database indexing and transaction work dominate the actual cost. Keeping the child write in the same transaction prevents a published ID from describing a parent row that was later rolled back.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume generated keys are available for every driver and statement.
  • Do not treat a pre-commit key as a committed record.
  • Do not assume multi-row key order without a database-specific contract.

title: Java JDBC fetch size: a hint, not a memory guarantee
summary: Statement.setFetchSize suggests how many rows a JDBC driver should fetch when more rows are needed. Its behavior is driver-dependent and does not by itself cap a query result.
body:
Statement.setFetchSize suggests how many rows a JDBC driver should fetch when more rows are needed. Its behavior is driver-dependent and does not by itself cap a query result.

Operational contract

Use a query predicate and explicit order to define the population. Add a separate maximum-row or pagination contract when a result may be large. The method below reads at most 470 ordered receipt IDs into memory and marks that it is only a page, not a complete report. Some drivers buffer more than the hint or require transaction settings for cursor-based fetching. Measure memory and fetch behavior with the deployed driver before claiming streaming.

Failure case

A depot has 47,000 receipts. The reviewer requests a page of 470 IDs, ordered by stable receipt ID, and carries the last ID into a later keyset query. Asking only for fetch size 47 would still permit a 47,000-row result. The code keeps one page in memory; it does not claim a snapshot across later pages without an isolation policy.

Java code

import java.sql.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class ReceiptPageReader {
    public static List<String> pageAfter(Connection connection, String lastId) throws SQLException {
        List<String> receiptIds = new ArrayList<>();
        try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                "SELECT receipt_id FROM receipt_intake WHERE receipt_id > ? ORDER BY receipt_id")) {
            statement.setString(1, lastId);
            statement.setFetchSize(47);
            statement.setMaxRows(470);
            try (ResultSet rows = statement.executeQuery()) {
                while (rows.next()) receiptIds.add(rows.getString(1));
            }
        }
        return receiptIds;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Each page retains at most 470 IDs in O(P) application memory for page size P, while the database may scan or index-search according to its plan. Fetch size affects transport hints rather than the logical limit. Repeated pages require stable ordering, an index strategy, and a policy for rows inserted between calls.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call fetch size a row limit.
  • Do not promise constant process memory without testing the driver.
  • Do not paginate without a stable order and change policy.

title: Java ProcessBuilder: pass command tokens without a shell
summary: ProcessBuilder receives an executable and individual arguments. It does not need a shell to pass a file path to a known command, and its Process result needs an owner.
body:
ProcessBuilder receives an executable and individual arguments. It does not need a shell to pass a file path to a known command, and its Process result needs an owner.

Operational contract

Never construct a shell command string from a user-supplied manifest name when the job only needs to run a fixed executable. Select the executable from trusted configuration, keep each argument separate, and constrain which inputs the child may read. The sample starts the JDK's own version command and discards output so a full pipe cannot block it. Returning a Process transfers wait, timeout, and cleanup responsibility to the caller; the companion lesson owns that lifecycle.

Failure case

A depot startup check runs the installed Java executable with a fixed '-version' argument solely to confirm that the process starts and exits. This sample discards version text; a caller that needs the numeric version must capture a bounded stream and parse it separately. The command is not a facility for arbitrary user input. If the child fails to launch, the application records the I/O exception and never reports a successful check.

Java code

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class JavaRuntimeProbe {
    public static Process start() throws IOException {
        Path executable = Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java");
        return new ProcessBuilder(executable.toString(), "-version")
            .redirectOutput(ProcessBuilder.Redirect.DISCARD)
            .redirectError(ProcessBuilder.Redirect.DISCARD)
            .start();
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Launching a native process is far more expensive than a Java method call and consumes operating-system resources until reaped. The snippet allocates no output buffer because both streams are discarded. If output is required, drain it under a size limit rather than reading it only after waiting for exit.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not concatenate untrusted arguments into a shell string.
  • Do not ignore the returned Process after starting it.
  • Do not wait for exit while leaving bounded output pipes undrained.

title: Java Process.waitFor timeout: terminate and reap the owned child
summary: Process.waitFor with a timeout reports whether a child has exited; a false return does not stop the child. The owner must terminate it and account for its streams and descendants.
body:
Process.waitFor with a timeout reports whether a child has exited; a false return does not stop the child. The owner must terminate it and account for its streams and descendants.

Operational contract

The method first asks for a normal termination, waits briefly, then requests forceful termination and waits for the child to exit. It restores the interrupt signal if the waiting thread is interrupted. This is a bounded attempt for the direct child only; programs that spawn descendants require a separate process-tree policy, and native termination behavior varies. In the companion command example, output is discarded so a filled pipe cannot keep the child blocked while the parent waits.

Failure case

The depot allows a diagnostic 47 seconds. If it is still alive, timeout is a failure, not a successful zero exit code. The owner terminates the child and records the timeout. If the waiting thread is interrupted, it requests forceful termination before passing the interrupt upward. A production supervisor also checks whether the command launched child processes that outlive this direct handle.

Java code

import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class ChildProcessDeadline {
    public static int await(Process child) throws InterruptedException {
        try {
            if (child.waitFor(47, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) return child.exitValue();
            child.destroy();
            if (!child.waitFor(3, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
                child.destroyForcibly();
                child.waitFor();
            }
            throw new IllegalStateException("Child exceeded its deadline");
        } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
            child.destroyForcibly();
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            throw interrupted;
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Waiting consumes elapsed time rather than CPU in the usual case. One process consumes handles and native memory until exit. A timeout plus cleanup bounds the direct child's lifetime in normal operation, but a forceful kill can still require a reaping wait and cannot guarantee every descendant is gone.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call a false timed wait a terminated child.
  • Do not report timeout as exit code zero.
  • Do not assume killing one Process handle kills its descendants.

title: Java file, JDBC, and subprocess boundaries quiz
summary: Check Java filesystem observations, JDBC result contracts, and subprocess ownership.
body:

questions.prompt: What should walkFileTree do when a required folder cannot be read?
options: Fail or record a partial scan
questions.explanation: A complete inventory cannot hide visit failure.

questions.prompt: When should a WatchKey be reset?
options: After its current events are processed
questions.explanation: Reset permits another signal and reports key validity.

questions.prompt: What does a create event prove about file content?
options: Only that an event was observed
questions.explanation: A writer may still be modifying the file.

questions.prompt: What follows WatchService OVERFLOW?
questions.explanation: Discarded events cannot be reconstructed from the notification.

questions.prompt: What happens after a DirectoryStream cap breach?
options: Return the first 47 as the full directory
questions.explanation: A cap must not turn into silent truncation.

questions.prompt: Does NOFOLLOW_LINKS make a later open race-free?
options: Only when the filename is short
No, the path may be replaced after inspection
questions.explanation: Metadata inspection and later open are separate operations.

questions.prompt: What does SUCCESS_NO_INFO mean in a JDBC batch?
options: Success with no row count available
questions.explanation: The driver cannot report an affected-row count for that position.

questions.prompt: When is ResultSet.wasNull checked for getInt?
questions.explanation: The flag describes the most recent column read.

questions.prompt: Is a generated key durable before commit?
options: Only if it is a long
No, rollback can remove the inserted row
questions.explanation: The transaction owner still decides commit.

questions.prompt: Does setFetchSize cap the result rows?
options: No, it is a driver-dependent fetch hint
questions.explanation: A logical page needs its own limit and order.

questions.prompt: Why pass ProcessBuilder arguments separately?
options: To avoid constructing a shell command from data
questions.explanation: A fixed executable can receive explicit argument tokens.

questions.prompt: What does timed waitFor returning false mean?
options: The child has not exited within the wait
questions.explanation: The owner must terminate and reap under its policy.

title: Java HTTP query values: encode data without changing URI structure
summary: A URI query contains syntax as well as data. Encode each value under the receiving endpoint's query convention before joining it to a trusted base URI; do not encode the complete URI as one value.
body:
A URI query contains syntax as well as data. Encode each value under the receiving endpoint's query convention before joining it to a trusted base URI; do not encode the complete URI as one value.

Operational contract

URLEncoder implements form encoding: a space becomes a plus sign, and other non-safe characters become percent-encoded UTF-8 bytes. That is suitable only when the endpoint decodes its query values as form data. This method requires an HTTPS collection URI with no existing query or fragment, appends exactly one named value, and rejects a null input. A different endpoint may require a different encoding contract, especially for path segments. Keep the base URI in trusted configuration and validate any host supplied by callers before sending a request.

Failure case

A catalog search receives the text 'seal 47 & blue'. The ampersand must remain inside the value; otherwise a server could interpret the tail as another parameter. The method encodes the value, not the separator. It also refuses a base URI that already contains a query because blindly appending a second question mark would change the request target.

Java code

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.URLEncoder;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.Objects;

public class CatalogQueryUri {
    public static URI search(URI collection, String searchText) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(searchText, "searchText");
        if (!"https".equalsIgnoreCase(collection.getScheme())
                || collection.getHost() == null
                || collection.getRawQuery() != null
                || collection.getRawFragment() != null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Expected a bare HTTPS collection URI");
        }
        String value = URLEncoder.encode(searchText, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        return URI.create(collection.toASCIIString() + "?q=" + value);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Encoding B UTF-8 bytes takes O(B) time and O(B) output space. The URI conversion creates another string. These costs are small beside a network call, but the endpoint should still set a length limit on accepted searches.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use URLEncoder on a whole URI or on a path segment.
  • Do not assume every server interprets plus as a space in a query.
  • Do not append a query to a base that already has a query or fragment.

title: Java HttpClient redirects: check the next origin before resending
summary: An HTTP redirect is a new request target. A client carrying credentials or a request body needs an explicit rule for which redirect destinations are acceptable.
body:
An HTTP redirect is a new request target. A client carrying credentials or a request body needs an explicit rule for which redirect destinations are acceptable.

Operational contract

HttpClient can follow redirects automatically, but a controlled client can configure NEVER and inspect the Location header after a 3xx response. The code resolves a relative target and only accepts the same HTTPS scheme, host, and effective port. It returns a URI; the caller must still decide whether the response status permits replaying the original method and body. In particular, 301 and 302 automatic handling may turn POST into GET. Pin a narrower path or allowlist when the application requires it.

Failure case

A shipment API returns a redirect while the caller holds an authorization token. Replaying the request against another host would cross the credential boundary. This gate rejects that move, including a downgrade to plain HTTP. A 307 or 308 response still needs a replayable request body and an idempotency decision before sending again.

Java code

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.util.Locale;

public class ShipmentRedirectGate {
    public static HttpClient client() {
        return HttpClient.newBuilder().followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NEVER).build();
    }

    public static URI sameOrigin(URI current, URI location) {
        URI next = current.resolve(location);
        String oldHost = current.getHost();
        String newHost = next.getHost();
        int oldPort = current.getPort() == -1 ? 443 : current.getPort();
        int newPort = next.getPort() == -1 ? 443 : next.getPort();
        if (!"https".equalsIgnoreCase(current.getScheme())
                || !"https".equalsIgnoreCase(next.getScheme())
                || oldHost == null || newHost == null
                || !oldHost.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT).equals(newHost.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT))
                || oldPort != newPort) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Redirect crosses the configured origin");
        }
        return next;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

URI resolution and comparison take time proportional to URI length and allocate one URI. Redirect chains add network round trips; cap their count in the caller. A same-origin check does not prove that the destination path is authorized for the same token.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not carry credentials to an unapproved origin.
  • Do not assume an automatic 301 or 302 preserves POST.
  • Do not follow an unlimited chain or replay a non-repeatable body.

title: Java HttpClient deadlines: separate connection and request timeouts
summary: HttpClient.connectTimeout bounds connection establishment; HttpRequest.timeout bounds the request's response wait. Neither replaces an overall business deadline that spans retries, parsing, and downstream work.
body:
HttpClient.connectTimeout bounds connection establishment; HttpRequest.timeout bounds the request's response wait. Neither replaces an overall business deadline that spans retries, parsing, and downstream work.

Operational contract

Create a reusable client with a connection timeout and a request with its own timeout. The client default for redirects is NEVER, but this example states that policy explicitly so the owner sees it beside the deadlines. A connection reused from a pool may not establish a new connection, so the connection setting is not the only timer that matters. On a timeout, classify the attempt as uncertain if the server may already have processed a mutation. The outer retry policy must subtract elapsed time from one operation budget.

Failure case

A warehouse lookup allows 47 seconds end to end. Three attempts each allowed 47 seconds could exceed that budget even before the sleeps between attempts. The factory below sets per-attempt limits; its caller still needs a clock-based overall deadline and must avoid retrying a non-idempotent write without a deduplication rule.

Java code

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.time.Duration;

public class WarehouseHttpDeadlines {
    public static HttpClient client() {
        return HttpClient.newBuilder()
            .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
            .followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NEVER)
            .build();
    }

    public static HttpRequest lookup(URI inventoryUri) {
        if (!"https".equalsIgnoreCase(inventoryUri.getScheme())) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("HTTPS inventory URI required");
        }
        return HttpRequest.newBuilder(inventoryUri)
            .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(7))
            .GET()
            .build();
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Builder work is O(1) relative to payload size. Reuse one client rather than rebuilding it for every call so connections can be reused. Timeouts bound waiting in specific phases; they do not cap the total cost of multiple attempts or downstream processing.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not multiply a full business budget across retries.
  • Do not assume connectTimeout applies to a reused connection.
  • Do not interpret a write timeout as proof the server made no change.

title: Java streaming HTTP bodies: close the stream and cap retained bytes
summary: BodyHandlers.ofInputStream exposes the response body as an InputStream. The application owns that stream and must consume or close it; otherwise an HTTP connection may remain occupied.
body:
BodyHandlers.ofInputStream exposes the response body as an InputStream. The application owns that stream and must consume or close it; otherwise an HTTP connection may remain occupied.

Operational contract

A streaming handler avoids immediately materializing the whole body, but it does not impose a size limit by itself. This decoder reads one byte beyond an application cap and rejects overflow. try-with-resources closes the stream on either path. Closing early may prevent connection reuse, which is an acceptable cost for a rejected oversized payload. This is a cap on bytes delivered to the application after any HTTP representation handling, not a claim about wire bytes or compressed expansion. A structured parser should run only after the cap and content-type checks.

Failure case

An inventory response is expected to fit within 47,000 bytes. If the peer sends 47,001 bytes, the parser never receives a truncated record and the request fails. The caller can record response status and content type separately. It must not call the 47,000-byte prefix a complete inventory.

Java code

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.InputStream;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;

public class InventoryBodyReader {
    public static byte[] read(HttpResponse<InputStream> response) throws IOException {
        if (response.statusCode() != 200) {
            try (InputStream discarded = response.body()) {
                throw new IOException("Unexpected inventory status: " + response.statusCode());
            }
        }
        try (InputStream body = response.body()) {
            byte[] bytes = body.readNBytes(47_001);
            if (bytes.length > 47_000) throw new IOException("Inventory body exceeds cap");
            return bytes;
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Reading a response of N bytes below the cap is O(N) time and O(N) retained memory. The one-byte probe makes overflow detection exact at the application boundary. An early close can sacrifice pool reuse; an unbounded read risks process memory instead.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not forget to close the response InputStream.
  • Do not treat a capped prefix as a complete document.
  • Do not rely on Content-Length alone as a verified body-size limit.

title: Java Retry-After: parse a bounded server delay without inventing a retry
summary: Retry-After can suggest when to send another request after a 429 or 503 response. A header value is advice, not permission to exceed the caller's deadline or replay a non-idempotent operation.
body:
Retry-After can suggest when to send another request after a 429 or 503 response. A header value is advice, not permission to exceed the caller's deadline or replay a non-idempotent operation.

Operational contract

Retry-After permits delay seconds or an HTTP date. The deliberately narrow parser below accepts only non-negative decimal seconds of at most 47; longer delays are not shortened into an early retry. It returns empty for unsupported dates and malformed values, leaving the retry policy to decide a safe fallback. A header from an untrusted peer must not create an unbounded sleep. The caller also needs a maximum attempt count and a remaining time budget. If the original request changed state, it needs an idempotency key or reconciliation before retry.

Failure case

A catalog service answers 503 with Retry-After 82. This parser declines that delay rather than suggesting a retry after 47 seconds. The caller with only 12 seconds left stops. If a second response has a date-form header, the parser returns no delay instead of guessing from an invalid numeric conversion.

Java code

import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Optional;

public class CatalogRetryHint {
    public static Optional<Duration> delay(HttpResponse<?> response) {
        int status = response.statusCode();
        if (status != 429 && status != 503) return Optional.empty();
        Optional<String> header = response.headers().firstValue("Retry-After");
        if (header.isEmpty()) return Optional.empty();
        String seconds = header.get().trim();
        if (!seconds.matches("[0-9]{1,12}")) return Optional.empty();
        try {
            long delaySeconds = Long.parseLong(seconds);
            return delaySeconds <= 47 ? Optional.of(Duration.ofSeconds(delaySeconds)) : Optional.empty();
        } catch (NumberFormatException invalid) {
            return Optional.empty();
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Parsing is O(H) in header length and uses O(H) temporary string storage. The regular-expression length cap prevents huge numeric inputs from being parsed. Sleeping consumes elapsed budget even when it consumes little CPU; the outer operation controls whether that cost is affordable.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not sleep longer than the remaining operation budget.
  • Do not treat unsupported date syntax as zero seconds.
  • Do not retry a mutation solely because the server returned 503.

title: Java HttpClient cookies: make session storage an owned policy
summary: A CookieHandler attached to HttpClient controls which cookies are accepted and sent. Sharing a client therefore shares session state as well as connection resources.
body:
A CookieHandler attached to HttpClient controls which cookies are accepted and sent. Sharing a client therefore shares session state as well as connection resources.

Operational contract

A client created without a cookie handler does not provide an application cookie jar. If a workflow genuinely needs cookies, give that workflow its own CookieManager and client, then define its lifetime. The sample accepts cookies only from the original server according to CookiePolicy.ACCEPT_ORIGINAL_SERVER, but that rule is not a substitute for an application allowlist or secure transport. Keep credential-bearing workflows isolated; do not use one mutable cookie jar for unrelated tenants. Session teardown must clear or retire the jar according to the product's logout contract.

Failure case

A back-office tool has two warehouse accounts active in the same process. Giving both accounts one client with one cookie manager could mix their login state. The factory creates one jar per account session. The owner stores the resulting client only within that session and discards it on logout, instead of putting it in a global singleton.

Java code

import java.net.CookieManager;
import java.net.CookiePolicy;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;

public class WarehouseSessionClient {
    public static HttpClient forOneSession() {
        CookieManager sessionCookies = new CookieManager();
        sessionCookies.setCookiePolicy(CookiePolicy.ACCEPT_ORIGINAL_SERVER);
        return HttpClient.newBuilder()
            .cookieHandler(sessionCookies)
            .followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NEVER)
            .build();
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

A cookie jar retains state proportional to accepted cookies; request matching also costs work proportional to the store contents. One client per session uses more connection resources than one global client, so cap session count and retire idle sessions. Isolation is the reason to pay that cost.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not share one cookie jar across unrelated user sessions.
  • Do not assume a client without a handler persists cookies.
  • Do not call an origin cookie policy a complete authorization rule.

title: Java RecursiveTask: split work only above a measured threshold
summary: RecursiveTask returns a value from a fork/join computation. A threshold keeps small ranges local so task scheduling does not cost more than the work being split.
body:
RecursiveTask returns a value from a fork/join computation. A threshold keeps small ranges local so task scheduling does not cost more than the work being split.

Operational contract

This task sums a half-open range of shipment quantities. It splits only when the range exceeds 256 elements, forks one half, computes the other on the current worker, then joins the first. The caller owns the input array for the duration of computation; concurrent writes would break the result contract. Use long for the aggregate because many int quantities can overflow an int sum. The threshold is a workload choice, not a universal constant; measure it with representative array sizes and CPU budgets.

Failure case

An intake batch holds 47,000 unit counts. A task per element would create far more scheduling work than arithmetic. Chunking at 256 keeps each leaf useful while permitting multiple workers to take independent ranges. If the batch has only 82 entries, it stays sequential.

Java code

import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveTask;

public class ShipmentQuantitySum extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    private final int[] quantities;
    private final int start;
    private final int end;

    public ShipmentQuantitySum(int[] quantities, int start, int end) {
        this.quantities = quantities;
        this.start = start;
        this.end = end;
    }

    @Override protected Long compute() {
        if (end - start <= 256) {
            long total = 0;
            for (int index = start; index < end; index++) total += quantities[index];
            return total;
        }
        int middle = start + (end - start) / 2;
        ShipmentQuantitySum left = new ShipmentQuantitySum(quantities, start, middle);
        left.fork();
        long rightTotal = new ShipmentQuantitySum(quantities, middle, end).compute();
        return rightTotal + left.join();
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Total arithmetic work is O(N). Balanced splitting gives O(log N) critical-path depth for enough workers and about O(N/256) leaf tasks, though scheduling and memory traffic can dominate cheap sums. Task and stack storage grow with the split tree and active depth.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not fork a task for every small element.
  • Do not mutate the input while tasks are reading it.
  • Do not sum a large int array into an int without an overflow policy.

title: Java ForkJoinPool: own a custom pool and its shutdown
summary: ForkJoinPool executes fork/join tasks with work stealing. A custom pool gives an application an explicit parallelism setting and a shutdown owner; the common pool is shared by unrelated code.
body:
ForkJoinPool executes fork/join tasks with work stealing. A custom pool gives an application an explicit parallelism setting and a shutdown owner; the common pool is shared by unrelated code.

Operational contract

The method creates a four-worker pool for one CPU-bound calculation, invokes a result-bearing task, then shuts the pool down. Production services normally reuse an owned pool across many batches rather than creating one per call, but its lifecycle remains explicit. Shutdown stops new submissions; awaitTermination waits for existing work and can itself time out. On interruption, preserve the signal and request immediate shutdown. The task shown in the companion lesson stays CPU-bound; blocking I/O needs a different executor or a carefully bounded ManagedBlocker.

Failure case

A nightly shipment audit runs an isolated batch and then exits. It can own a pool for that batch. A long-running server should instead keep a service-owned pool and close it at service shutdown, because rebuilding workers on every HTTP request would waste resources. The four-worker setting is a starting capacity to measure, not a throughput promise.

Java code

import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class ShipmentBatchRunner {
    public static long sum(int[] quantities) throws InterruptedException {
        ForkJoinPool workers = new ForkJoinPool(4);
        try {
            return workers.invoke(new ShipmentQuantitySum(quantities, 0, quantities.length));
        } finally {
            workers.shutdown();
            try {
                if (!workers.awaitTermination(3, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) workers.shutdownNow();
            } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
                workers.shutdownNow();
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                throw interrupted;
            }
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

For an N-element sum, the pool still performs O(N) arithmetic; at most four configured workers can run its tasks concurrently. Starting and tearing down workers adds fixed overhead to each call. Reusing an owned pool amortizes that cost but requires a longer-lived shutdown owner.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not shut down the common pool as if it belonged to one request.
  • Do not create a new pool for each tiny calculation.
  • Do not confuse shutdown with confirmation that every task has finished.

summary: ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker describes a wait that might block a fork/join worker. The pool may compensate with another worker while that wait is in progress.
body:
ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker describes a wait that might block a fork/join worker. The pool may compensate with another worker while that wait is in progress.

Operational contract

A fork/join worker that waits on a queue can starve unrelated tasks if all workers do the same. The blocker checks for a ready item without waiting, then takes an item only when necessary. The pool may activate a spare worker; this is not an unlimited capacity guarantee and does not turn arbitrary I/O into CPU work. For sustained network or disk waits, a separate bounded executor is usually easier to account for. The queue producer must also have a termination or cancellation policy so the consumer cannot wait forever.

Failure case

A parallel audit occasionally waits for one receipt to arrive in a handoff queue. The wait is rare, so a ManagedBlocker can tell the pool that one worker is parked. If all 47,000 receipts require remote fetches, that workload needs an I/O concurrency limit instead of 47,000 blockers.

Java code

import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool;

public class ReceiptQueueBlocker implements ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker {
    private final BlockingQueue<String> receipts;
    private String receipt;

    public ReceiptQueueBlocker(BlockingQueue<String> receipts) {
        this.receipts = receipts;
    }

    @Override public boolean isReleasable() {
        return receipt != null || (receipt = receipts.poll()) != null;
    }

    @Override public boolean block() throws InterruptedException {
        if (!isReleasable()) receipt = receipts.take();
        return true;
    }

    public String await() throws InterruptedException {
        ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(this);
        return receipt;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

A successful poll is O(1) queue work in typical implementations; a miss can wait indefinitely unless an outer cancellation policy interrupts it. Compensation can create extra workers and memory pressure. Bound both queue size and the number of waits.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expect managedBlock to create unlimited workers.
  • Do not use it to hide sustained blocking I/O inside a CPU pool.
  • Do not leave an unbounded take without a producer or cancellation contract.

title: Java fork/join failures: one failed task does not roll back sibling work
summary: A runtime failure from RecursiveTask.compute propagates through join or invoke. A sibling task may already have run, so failure of the result is not an atomic rollback of side effects.
body:
A runtime failure from RecursiveTask.compute propagates through join or invoke. A sibling task may already have run, so failure of the result is not an atomic rollback of side effects.

Operational contract

Keep fork/join computations pure or confine mutations to disjoint owned ranges. The sample validates each shipment quantity before contributing to an aggregate. If one leaf fails, the caller receives a computation failure, but other leaves may have completed. No database or external mutation occurs, so discarding the final sum is safe. If a task writes outside its range, the caller needs separate reconciliation and cancellation; a thrown exception alone will not undo that work. Use an owned pool with a finite batch and record the original cause.

Failure case

A batch contains 47,000 counts and one negative quantity. The validation task throws instead of returning a misleading sum. Other subranges may already have been summed. That wasted computation is acceptable; writing partial totals to a ledger from each leaf would not be, because the exception cannot retract those ledger entries.

Java code

import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveTask;

public class ValidatedShipmentSum extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    private final int[] quantities;
    private final int start;
    private final int end;

    public ValidatedShipmentSum(int[] quantities, int start, int end) {
        this.quantities = quantities;
        this.start = start;
        this.end = end;
    }

    @Override protected Long compute() {
        if (end - start <= 256) {
            long total = 0;
            for (int index = start; index < end; index++) {
                if (quantities[index] < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative quantity at " + index);
                total += quantities[index];
            }
            return total;
        }
        int middle = start + (end - start) / 2;
        ValidatedShipmentSum left = new ValidatedShipmentSum(quantities, start, middle);
        left.fork();
        long rightTotal = new ValidatedShipmentSum(quantities, middle, end).compute();
        return rightTotal + left.join();
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

A valid batch does O(N) validation and summation. An invalid item can reduce useful work, but parallel siblings may still complete, so the failure path has no fixed early-stop cost. The split threshold limits task count to roughly O(N/256) leaves.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume an exception cancels sibling work immediately.
  • Do not write irreversible side effects from each leaf and expect rollback.
  • Do not swallow a validation exception and publish a partial total.
