title: Java Exchanger: swap buffers at a two-party rendezvous
summary: Exchanger pairs two threads so each hands over one object and receives the other's object. A missing partner means waiting, timeout, or interruption rather than queued delivery.
body:
Exchanger pairs two threads so each hands over one object and receives the other's object. A missing partner means waiting, timeout, or interruption rather than queued delivery.

Operational contract

A producer and consumer can exchange ownership of same-size byte buffers after each processing stage. The timed call bounds how long this method waits for a partner. Neither side may keep mutating the buffer it hands away after a successful exchange; the recipient now owns it. The exchanger passes object references, not copies. A timeout means this method did not complete an exchange, so the caller retains its original buffer and must decide whether to retry or stop. This sample has exactly two participants by contract.

Failure case

One worker fills a 47-byte parcel label buffer while another has an empty 47-byte buffer ready. They meet and swap. If the second worker fails before reaching the rendezvous, the first returns through a timeout rather than blocking forever.

Java code

import java.util.concurrent.Exchanger;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException;

public class ParcelBufferSwap {
    private final Exchanger<byte[]> buffers = new Exchanger<>();

    public byte[] swap(byte[] ownedBuffer) throws InterruptedException, TimeoutException {
        if (ownedBuffer.length != 47) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Expected 47 bytes");
        byte[] received = buffers.exchange(ownedBuffer, 3, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        if (received.length != 47) throw new IllegalStateException("Partner used wrong buffer size");
        return received;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The exchange transfers references in O(1) application work and requires two live participants; scheduling and contention control actual latency. Both 47-byte arrays already exist. It is not a queue or a capacity policy for arbitrary producer volume.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not retain write ownership of a buffer after handing it over.
  • Do not assume the partner always arrives; handle timeout and interruption.
  • Do not use a two-party exchanger as a many-message backlog.

title: Java LinkedTransferQueue: wait until a consumer receives work
summary: LinkedTransferQueue can hand an item directly to a waiting consumer. Its transfer operation waits until receipt, which is different from merely enqueuing an item.
body:
LinkedTransferQueue can hand an item directly to a waiting consumer. Its transfer operation waits until receipt, which is different from merely enqueuing an item.

Operational contract

tryTransfer with a timeout waits up to three seconds for a consumer to receive the receipt ID, then reports success or failure. The consumer uses take. Successful transfer proves handoff to a consumer, not completion of that consumer's business work. The underlying linked queue can grow without an application cap if regular offer is used; this sample exposes only the timed handoff operation. On a timeout, the producer must decide whether to retry, persist the work, or reject it. Interruption propagates to the caller.

Failure case

A depot publisher has an urgent receipt-47 notification. A worker already waiting on take can receive it immediately. If no worker receives within three seconds, the publisher sees false and can persist the notification for later delivery instead of silently treating it as processed.

Java code

import java.util.concurrent.LinkedTransferQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class ReceiptTransferLane {
    private final LinkedTransferQueue<String> handoffs = new LinkedTransferQueue<>();

    public boolean handoff(String receiptId) throws InterruptedException {
        return handoffs.tryTransfer(receiptId, 3, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    }

    public String awaitReceipt() throws InterruptedException {
        return handoffs.take();
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The handoff uses constant application storage per pending producer, but waiting producers still consume thread or virtual-thread resources. The timed operation has up to three seconds of wait and scheduling overhead. This class is not a durable broker; a received item can be lost if the consumer fails before committing its work.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not equate consumer receipt with successful business processing.
  • Do not assume this unbounded queue enforces capacity.
  • Do not discard work silently when the timed transfer returns false.

title: Java LongAccumulator: track a concurrent high-water mark
summary: LongAccumulator combines submitted long values with a supplied associative function. A max accumulator records an observed high-water mark under concurrent updates.
body:
LongAccumulator combines submitted long values with a supplied associative function. A max accumulator records an observed high-water mark under concurrent updates.

Operational contract

The function Long::max has Long.MIN_VALUE as its identity, so an untouched accumulator is distinguishable from a recorded zero. The sample rejects negative queue depths and returns zero before any sample. get is a metric read, not a coordination signal or a transaction with the queue whose depth was measured. Use an atomic variable when one exact compare-and-set result controls a state transition. Resetting an accumulator while writers run is a separate interval policy and can lose a clean boundary between reporting periods.

Failure case

Forty-seven workers sample backlog depth while shipments arrive. The maximum sample is useful for capacity monitoring. It does not prove the queue never briefly exceeded that value between samples, nor does it freeze the current queue length.

Java code

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAccumulator;

public class BacklogHighWaterMark {
    private final LongAccumulator maximum =
        new LongAccumulator(Long::max, Long.MIN_VALUE);

    public void observe(long pendingShipments) {
        if (pendingShipments < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative backlog");
        maximum.accumulate(pendingShipments);
    }

    public long highestObserved() {
        long observed = maximum.get();
        return observed == Long.MIN_VALUE ? 0 : observed;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

A single update has expected low overhead, but contention can cause internal cells and extra O(T) metric-read work for T cells. Space can grow with contention. The max reduction is associative; a side-effecting or order-dependent function would not fit this design.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use a metric read as an exact queue-state invariant.
  • Do not reset while writers run without a period boundary.
  • Do not choose a nonassociative or side-effecting accumulation function.

title: Java ThreadLocal: restore request context when a pooled thread is reused
summary: ThreadLocal stores a value for each thread, not for each logical request. A worker reused for another request can retain stale context unless a scoped operation restores or removes it.
body:
ThreadLocal stores a value for each thread, not for each logical request. A worker reused for another request can retain stale context unless a scoped operation restores or removes it.

Operational contract

The helper saves the current tenant, sets the new tenant for one synchronous Runnable, then restores the old value in finally. If there was no previous value it removes the entry, which prevents a pooled worker from carrying a tenant into the next task. Restoring rather than blindly removing also supports nested scopes on the same thread. This mechanism does not propagate to an asynchronous task automatically; pass identity explicitly or use a context mechanism whose lifetime matches the task. The tenant string here is diagnostic context, not authorization by itself.

Failure case

A worker processes depot-47 and then depot-82 on the same pool thread. A failure during the first task still executes finally. The second task cannot inherit depot-47 from this helper, and a nested call returns to its outer tenant after the inner call completes.

Java code

public class TenantTraceScope {
    private static final ThreadLocal<String> CURRENT_TENANT = new ThreadLocal<>();

    public static void run(String tenantId, Runnable operation) {
        String previous = CURRENT_TENANT.get();
        CURRENT_TENANT.set(tenantId);
        try {
            operation.run();
        } finally {
            if (previous == null) CURRENT_TENANT.remove();
            else CURRENT_TENANT.set(previous);
        }
    }

    public static String current() {
        return CURRENT_TENANT.get();
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

get, set, and remove are expected O(1) per thread-local operation with per-thread storage. Each live worker can retain its current value until cleared or the worker ends. The finally block runs on ordinary exceptions; a process termination is outside that guarantee.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat a thread-local tenant as a security check.
  • Do not assume a child or executor task inherits the caller's context.
  • Do not remove unconditionally when nested scopes must restore a previous value.

title: Java LockSupport: park only inside a checked condition loop
summary: LockSupport gives each thread at most one park permit. unpark can arrive before park, and park can return for timeout, interruption, or no reported reason.
body:
LockSupport gives each thread at most one park permit. unpark can arrive before park, and park can return for timeout, interruption, or no reported reason.

Operational contract

This one-waiter gate publishes its waiting thread in a volatile field before checking the volatile ready flag. signal publishes ready first, then unparks the registered waiter. The waiting loop always rechecks ready after park; a wakeup alone does not prove the state changed. The deadline limits waiting to three seconds. A pre-existing interrupt returns false without consuming the interrupt status. This low-level primitive is best reserved for synchronization implementations; a CountDownLatch is simpler for ordinary one-shot application gates.

Failure case

A release signal arrives just before the worker parks. The ready flag lets the worker proceed without sleeping. A spurious wakeup while ready remains false sends it around the loop. A missing signal eventually reaches its timeout rather than blocking forever.

Java code

import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport;

public class OneWaiterDispatchGate {
    private final AtomicReference<Thread> waiter = new AtomicReference<>();
    private volatile boolean ready;

    public boolean await() {
        Thread current = Thread.currentThread();
        if (!waiter.compareAndSet(null, current))
            throw new IllegalStateException("Only one waiter is supported");
        long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(3);
        try {
            while (!ready) {
                if (current.isInterrupted()) return false;
                long remaining = deadline - System.nanoTime();
                if (remaining <= 0) return false;
                LockSupport.parkNanos(this, remaining);
            }
            return true;
        } finally {
            waiter.compareAndSet(current, null);
        }
    }

    public void signal() {
        ready = true;
        LockSupport.unpark(waiter.get());
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The condition check and permit transfer use O(1) application state. Waiting consumes scheduling time until signal, interrupt, or the three-second deadline. This is a one-shot, single-waiter gate; resetting it or supporting many waiters requires more state and an explicit race policy.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat a return from park as proof that the condition holds.
  • Do not assume permits accumulate beyond one.
  • Do not use a one-waiter field to coordinate multiple waiting threads.

title: Java generic wildcards: copy from a producer into a consumer
summary: An extends wildcard permits reading values as a bound; a super wildcard permits writing values of that bound. A copy method can combine both without claiming two lists have the same element type.
body:
An extends wildcard permits reading values as a bound; a super wildcard permits writing values of that bound. A copy method can combine both without claiming two lists have the same element type.

Operational contract

The source produces ParcelEvent values or a subtype. The destination consumes ParcelEvent values and may be a list of ParcelEvent or Object. The method rejects a source over 47 entries before changing the destination, then appends each element. It does not promise all-or-nothing delivery: a destination that throws during add may already contain a prefix. When atomic publication matters, build a separate immutable result and replace one owner reference instead. The wildcard bounds express allowed operations at compile time; they do not check runtime business rules on each event.

Failure case

A depot has a List of ScannedParcel values and needs to add them to a List of ParcelEvent values. List<ScannedParcel> cannot be assigned to List<ParcelEvent>, because that would permit adding a different event subtype to the scanned list. The bounded-copy method accepts the two lists safely while keeping ownership of mutation at the destination.

Java code

import java.util.List;

public class ParcelEventCopy {
    public interface ParcelEvent { String parcelId(); }
    public record ScannedParcel(String parcelId) implements ParcelEvent { }

    public static <T extends ParcelEvent> void append(
            List<? extends T> source, List<? super T> destination) {
        if (source.size() > 47) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Batch exceeds 47 events");
        for (T event : source) destination.add(event);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Reading and appending N elements costs O(N) time and O(1) extra application space. A destination array list may occasionally resize, while a linked destination allocates per entry. The size check is a policy cap, not a rollback mechanism.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat List<Subtype> as a subtype of List<Supertype>.
  • Do not assume a wildcard copy is transactional if a destination add fails.
  • Do not use a lower-bounded source when the code needs subtype-specific reads.

title: Java type erasure: validate elements with an explicit Class token
summary: Java erases most generic type arguments from runtime class identity. A Class token can validate each element when an unchecked external list crosses into a typed API.
body:
Java erases most generic type arguments from runtime class identity. A Class token can validate each element when an unchecked external list crosses into a typed API.

Operational contract

The method accepts a List<?> from an untyped integration boundary and a requested element class. Class.cast checks each value and creates a fresh List<T>. It rejects null input and null elements before List.copyOf, which itself does not allow null members. The token checks the runtime class of each element; it cannot validate a nested type such as List<String> inside a List<List<String>>. A wire-format parser must still validate field meaning, range, and schema. Two overloads that differ only by List<String> versus List<Long> are illegal because their erased signatures collide.

Failure case

A plug-in returns 23 raw receipt values, and the application expects String IDs. The first Long value fails at the boundary with ClassCastException rather than much later inside a billing routine. Calling getClass on the list itself would reveal its implementation class, not its erased element argument.

Java code

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;

public class TypedReceiptBoundary {
    public static <T> List<T> checkedCopy(List<?> incoming, Class<T> elementType) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(incoming);
        Objects.requireNonNull(elementType);
        if (incoming.size() > 47) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Too many values");
        List<T> checked = new ArrayList<>(incoming.size());
        for (Object value : incoming) checked.add(elementType.cast(value));
        return List.copyOf(checked);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Validation and copying take O(N) time and O(N) new list storage for N values, capped at 47. Class.cast checks each runtime element; the one-time copy also prevents later mutations of the incoming list from changing the returned membership.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expect a List instance to retain its String or Long type argument at runtime.
  • Do not use Class<T> to claim validation of nested generic arguments.
  • Do not defer unchecked casts until after data enters domain logic.

title: Java bridge methods: preserve overrides after generic erasure
summary: A compiler may generate a synthetic bridge method when erasure would otherwise break an overriding method's dispatch signature.
body:
A compiler may generate a synthetic bridge method when erasure would otherwise break an overriding method's dispatch signature.

Operational contract

The base source declares a generic fee method and the concrete source returns Long. At the source level, calling through FeeSource<Long> invokes the concrete override. The compiler can emit an Object-returning bridge alongside the Long-returning method so erased callers still reach that override. Reflection may show both; method scanners should inspect isBridge and isSynthetic before treating every declared method as a separate business API. Do not call the synthetic method directly. An unchecked raw-type call can still move a type error to runtime.

Failure case

An audit tool lists methods on a fee provider and reports two rate methods. Only one was written by the developer. The second is a compiler bridge that preserves polymorphism; registering both as separate handlers would double-count one operation.

Java code

import java.lang.reflect.Method;

public class FeeBridgeInspection {
    static abstract class FeeSource<T> { abstract T rate(); }
    static final class FixedFee extends FeeSource<Long> {
        @Override Long rate() { return 4700L; }
    }

    public static long rateThroughBase() {
        FeeSource<Long> source = new FixedFee();
        return source.rate();
    }

    public static int bridgeCount() {
        int bridges = 0;
        for (Method method : FixedFee.class.getDeclaredMethods()) {
            if (method.isBridge()) bridges++;
        }
        return bridges;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The virtual call is ordinary dispatch after compilation. Reflecting over M declared methods costs O(M) time and O(1) application space here, aside from reflection's method objects. Bridge generation is a compatibility detail, not a reason to add runtime casts to correctly typed code.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expose compiler bridge methods as separate service endpoints.
  • Do not assume generic parameters survive as distinct runtime classes.
  • Do not remove an override because reflection shows an extra method.

title: Java interface defaults: resolve a two-parent method conflict
summary: When two unrelated interfaces provide default methods with the same signature, an implementing class must resolve the conflict explicitly.
body:
When two unrelated interfaces provide default methods with the same signature, an implementing class must resolve the conflict explicitly.

Operational contract

The concrete formatter chooses the audit label and receipt label in a fixed order. It calls the two parent defaults with qualified InterfaceName.super syntax, then returns a new label. This decision belongs in the class that combines both contracts. A superclass concrete method can take precedence over interface defaults, so changing a class hierarchy may change dispatch even when interface source remains the same. Default methods add API behavior; they do not replace a review of semantic compatibility between the interfaces.

Failure case

A reporting type implements both a receipt naming interface and an audit naming interface. Each supplies label(). Without an override, compilation fails. The explicit result 'AUDIT-82 / RECEIPT-47' makes the combined naming rule visible to callers and reviewers.

Java code

public class CombinedReceiptLabel {
    interface ReceiptLabel { default String label() { return "RECEIPT-47"; } }
    interface AuditLabel { default String label() { return "AUDIT-82"; } }

    static final class ReportLabel implements ReceiptLabel, AuditLabel {
        @Override public String label() {
            return AuditLabel.super.label() + " / " + ReceiptLabel.super.label();
        }
    }

    public static String render() {
        return new ReportLabel().label();
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Dispatch and concatenation are constant work for these fixed strings; the returned string allocates storage proportional to its length. The main cost is API governance: every conflict resolution should encode a deliberate business rule rather than blindly pick the first parent.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expect Java to select one of two unrelated defaults automatically.
  • Do not resolve a conflict with an arbitrary parent when both semantics matter.
  • Do not overlook superclass methods when reasoning about inherited behavior.

title: Java compact record constructors: normalize before field assignment
summary: A compact record constructor receives component parameters and implicitly assigns them to fields after its body completes. It can reject or normalize values before that assignment.
body:
A compact record constructor receives component parameters and implicitly assigns them to fields after its body completes. It can reject or normalize values before that assignment.

Operational contract

The sample strips surrounding whitespace from a shipment identifier, rejects a blank value, and limits mass to 47,000 grams. Assigning a new value to the constructor parameter changes what the implicit field assignment stores. The record is only shallowly immutable; if a component holds a mutable collection or array, copy it on entry and control what its accessor returns. Validation in the canonical constructor gives every ordinary construction path the same invariant. Deserialization and reflection still require separate trust considerations.

Failure case

A carrier sends ' parcel-82 ' with a mass of 23,000 grams. The stored record ID is 'parcel-82'. A blank ID or 47,001-gram mass fails before a record exists, preventing downstream code from quietly accepting an invalid shipment.

Java code

public class ShipmentMassPolicy {
    public record ShipmentMass(String shipmentId, int grams) {
        public ShipmentMass {
            if (shipmentId == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Missing shipment ID");
            shipmentId = shipmentId.strip();
            if (shipmentId.isBlank() || grams < 0 || grams > 47_000)
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid shipment mass");
        }
    }

    public static ShipmentMass accept(String id, int grams) {
        return new ShipmentMass(id, grams);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

strip scans the identifier in O(L) time and may allocate a new string; the numeric checks are O(1). The record stores one reference and one integer. The constructor does not copy a mutable object because these components are a String and a primitive.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assign directly to a record component field in a compact constructor.
  • Do not call a record deeply immutable when it contains mutable components.
  • Do not scatter validation only across selected factory methods.

title: Java instanceof patterns: keep a narrowed value inside its valid scope
summary: An instanceof type pattern tests a reference and binds a narrowed variable only on control-flow paths where the test succeeded.
body:
An instanceof type pattern tests a reference and binds a narrowed variable only on control-flow paths where the test succeeded.

Operational contract

The method rejects every value that is not a RefundEvent, including null. After the throwing guard, the compiler knows refund is a RefundEvent for the remaining method body. No explicit cast is needed. Pattern matching does not validate the record's business fields; this code checks the amount separately. This narrow branch is appropriate when an API receives a mixed event type. For a closed set of event kinds, a sealed hierarchy can give stronger compile-time coverage.

Failure case

An event router receives an Object representing a refund of 2,300 cents. It returns 2,300. A String or null fails at the routing boundary instead of becoming a zero-value refund, which would hide a bad integration payload.

Java code

public class RefundPatternGate {
    public record RefundEvent(String receiptId, long cents) { }

    public static long acceptedCents(Object event) {
        if (!(event instanceof RefundEvent refund))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Expected refund event");
        if (refund.cents() < 0 || refund.cents() > 47_000)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Refund outside policy");
        return refund.cents();
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The runtime type test and field checks take O(1) time and no collection storage. The pattern variable is a reference to the same object; it is not a copy or a separate validated instance.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume the pattern variable exists on the branch where the test is false.
  • Do not treat type matching as validation of record fields.
  • Do not map unsupported input to a plausible business value without an explicit rule.

title: Java switch expressions: return one value from every state
summary: A switch expression computes a value. Arrow cases avoid statement fall-through, and a block case uses yield to supply its result.
body:
A switch expression computes a value. Arrow cases avoid statement fall-through, and a block case uses yield to supply its result.

Operational contract

The enum has three states, and the switch handles each one without a default. Adding a new enum constant makes the source require another case when recompiled, rather than quietly classifying the new state as an old one. The HELD branch uses Math.addExact so an overflow does not produce a negative fee. Passing null still raises a NullPointerException before a case is selected; validate it at the call boundary when null is expected. A switch expression selects a branch; it does not make the arithmetic or state transition atomic with external storage.

Failure case

An order has a 2,300-cent base charge. READY keeps it; HELD adds a 47-cent hold fee and returns 2,347; CLOSED returns zero. A fourth state cannot be silently priced by a generic default branch in this source.

Java code

public class OrderChargeSwitch {
    public enum State { READY, HELD, CLOSED }

    public static long charge(State state, long baseCents) {
        if (baseCents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative charge");
        return switch (state) {
            case READY -> baseCents;
            case HELD -> {
                long holdCharge = Math.addExact(baseCents, 47);
                yield holdCharge;
            }
            case CLOSED -> 0;
        };
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Branch selection and arithmetic take O(1) time and O(1) extra space. Exhaustive handling is a source-level maintenance property; it does not guarantee that an old compiled binary will understand a newer enum class without recompilation.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use break where a block case must yield a value.
  • Do not hide a newly introduced enum state behind a permissive default.
  • Do not forget overflow or null policy just because the switch is exhaustive.

title: Java sealed hierarchies: switch over permitted request kinds
summary: A sealed interface limits its direct implementations. A pattern switch can then handle the permitted types as an exhaustive set at compile time.
body:
A sealed interface limits its direct implementations. A pattern switch can then handle the permitted types as an exhaustive set at compile time.

Operational contract

The sample permits two nested record request kinds and uses a switch expression without a default. If a third permitted kind is added, recompiling this method requires an explicit branch. Both records validate their own values, so each case can work with a constructed domain request. Passing null is not covered by the two type cases and throws at runtime; callers should reject null at intake. Sealing controls direct Java implementations in the same module or package rules; it is not a security boundary for untrusted serialized data.

Failure case

An invoicing service handles a ChargeRequest of 2,300 cents or a RefundRequest of 47 cents. If the model later adds a CreditRequest, the switch must be revisited. A fallback that returns zero for every unknown request would conceal a missing billing rule.

Java code

public class BillingRequestRouter {
    public sealed interface Request permits ChargeRequest, RefundRequest { }
    public record ChargeRequest(long cents) implements Request {
        public ChargeRequest { if (cents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative charge"); }
    }
    public record RefundRequest(long cents) implements Request {
        public RefundRequest { if (cents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative refund"); }
    }

    public static long signedCents(Request request) {
        return switch (request) {
            case ChargeRequest charge -> charge.cents();
            case RefundRequest refund -> Math.negateExact(refund.cents());
        };
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Type dispatch and checked negation are O(1) work with O(1) extra space. Exhaustiveness reduces omitted-source-branch risk; it does not replace input limits, authorization, or a durable transaction.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not add a broad default merely to suppress a missing case.
  • Do not treat sealed types as validation of wire-format input.
  • Do not forget the null boundary when callers can pass null.

title: Java annotation retention: expose metadata without pretending it enforces policy
summary: A runtime-retained annotation can be read through reflection. Its presence is metadata; application code must still decide and enforce the associated behavior.
body:
A runtime-retained annotation can be read through reflection. Its presence is metadata; application code must still decide and enforce the associated behavior.

Operational contract

The marker targets methods and remains available at runtime. The lookup selects a method by name and parameter types, avoiding accidental selection of an overload. A true result means the annotation was declared on that method, not that access checks have run. The method handles an absent declaration by throwing NoSuchMethodException to its caller. A policy engine should bind permissions and authentication separately; an annotation alone is not an authorization boundary. Annotation inspection can be cached for stable classes if it sits on a hot request path.

Failure case

An invoice handler marks its approve(long) operation for auditing. Reflection finds the marker. The caller must still emit a durable audit record and deny unauthorized callers; an unannotated method should not quietly be treated as approved merely because no marker is present.

Java code

import java.lang.annotation.ElementType;
import java.lang.annotation.Retention;
import java.lang.annotation.RetentionPolicy;
import java.lang.annotation.Target;

public class AuditMarkerInspection {
    @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
    @Target(ElementType.METHOD)
    public @interface AuditRequired { }

    public static final class InvoiceActions {
        @AuditRequired public void approve(long invoiceId) { }
    }

    public static boolean marked(Class<?> owner, String methodName,
            Class<?>... parameters) throws NoSuchMethodException {
        return owner.getDeclaredMethod(methodName, parameters)
            .isAnnotationPresent(AuditRequired.class);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

A reflective lookup scans or indexes class metadata according to the JVM implementation and can allocate Method objects. Treat it as setup work and cache a resolved policy if every request repeats it. Marker presence itself consumes little per-class metadata; the audit action has separate I/O cost.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume an annotation performs its own enforcement.
  • Do not inspect by name alone when overloads exist.
  • Do not use SOURCE or CLASS retention when runtime reflection must read the marker.

title: Java repeatable annotations: read every declared routing label
summary: A repeatable annotation lets one declaration carry several values of the same annotation type. getAnnotationsByType returns the contained values to runtime code.
body:
A repeatable annotation lets one declaration carry several values of the same annotation type. getAnnotationsByType returns the contained values to runtime code.

Operational contract

The Label annotation names a container through @Repeatable; both definitions use runtime retention and the same METHOD target. The sample copies the reflected labels into an immutable list of route names. It rejects a method without labels rather than silently treating it as public. The order of labels is the declared container order, but callers should not use annotation order as a priority rule unless that rule is explicit and tested. Route labels are configuration metadata, not proof that the request is allowed to access a route.

Failure case

A dispatch method carries labels 'depot-47' and 'depot-82'. A router reads both, then applies its own authorization and conflict rules. Reading only getAnnotation(Label.class) may miss the intended repeated values when a container is present.

Java code

import java.lang.annotation.ElementType;
import java.lang.annotation.Repeatable;
import java.lang.annotation.Retention;
import java.lang.annotation.RetentionPolicy;
import java.lang.annotation.Target;
import java.lang.reflect.Method;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class DispatchLabelReader {
    @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
    @Target(ElementType.METHOD)
    @Repeatable(Labels.class)
    public @interface Label { String value(); }

    @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
    @Target(ElementType.METHOD)
    public @interface Labels { Label[] value(); }

    @Label("depot-47") @Label("depot-82")
    public void dispatch() { }

    public static List<String> labels(Method method) {
        Label[] declared = method.getAnnotationsByType(Label.class);
        if (declared.length == 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("No route labels");
        List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(declared.length);
        for (Label label : declared) names.add(label.value());
        return List.copyOf(names);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Reflection returns R annotation values, and copying their strings costs O(R) time and O(R) list storage. Annotation lookups in a hot route should be resolved once at startup, while per-request authorization still uses current security state.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not query a repeated annotation as if only one instance can exist.
  • Do not give the container a different target or retention contract.
  • Do not treat labels as access-control decisions.

summary: An enum constant can provide its own implementation of an abstract method. This binds a finite set of named choices to distinct behavior without string-based branching elsewhere.
body:
An enum constant can provide its own implementation of an abstract method. This binds a finite set of named choices to distinct behavior without string-based branching elsewhere.

Operational contract

The tier validates parcel grams at the method entry, then each constant computes its own fee with checked arithmetic. The formulas are policy examples: STANDARD charges 47 cents per kilogram rounded up, and EXPRESS charges 82 cents per kilogram rounded up. The result of 1,001 grams is two kilograms by policy. Enum constants are singletons, so do not place mutable per-request state inside a constant body. Adding a tier still requires a business review of callers and persisted names.

Failure case

A 1,001-gram parcel costs 94 cents at STANDARD or 164 cents at EXPRESS. If fees change, the code review can see the two named policies separately. The method rejects negative or over-47,000-gram inputs before pricing.

Java code

public class ParcelTierFees {
    public enum Tier {
        STANDARD { @Override long centsPerKilogram() { return 47; } },
        EXPRESS { @Override long centsPerKilogram() { return 82; } };

        abstract long centsPerKilogram();

        public long fee(int grams) {
            if (grams < 0 || grams > 47_000)
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Mass outside policy");
            long kilograms = (grams + 999L) / 1_000L;
            return Math.multiplyExact(kilograms, centsPerKilogram());
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Selection, integer rounding, and multiplication are O(1) time with O(1) extra space. The enum instances are initialized once. The 47,000-gram cap bounds the result here, while multiplyExact keeps later policy changes from silently overflowing.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not store mutable request data on a shared enum constant.
  • Do not divide before adding the rounding offset when the policy requires ceiling.
  • Do not persist enum names as an unreviewed long-term compatibility contract.

title: Java JDBC savepoints: roll back one optional step inside a transaction
summary: A JDBC savepoint marks a position inside a caller-owned transaction. Rolling back to it undoes later database changes while retaining earlier uncommitted changes.
body:
A JDBC savepoint marks a position inside a caller-owned transaction. Rolling back to it undoes later database changes while retaining earlier uncommitted changes.

Operational contract

This method requires auto-commit to be off and assumes the caller owns the transaction. It creates a savepoint immediately before an optional audit insert. If the insert fails, it rolls back to the savepoint and rethrows the original SQLException. The caller then decides whether the earlier shipment work may be committed or whether the entire transaction must be rolled back. Some drivers or transaction managers do not support savepoints; detect support before making this policy mandatory. This helper never commits, changes isolation, or closes the connection.

Failure case

A shipment update succeeds, then an optional audit row conflicts with an existing key. The helper rolls back only its attempted audit insert. The outer service can decide whether a missing audit record is acceptable; it must not blindly commit after every SQL failure, especially if the connection itself is unusable.

Java code

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Savepoint;

public class OptionalShipmentAudit {
    public static void insert(Connection connection, long shipmentId) throws SQLException {
        if (connection.getAutoCommit()) throw new IllegalStateException("Transaction required");
        Savepoint beforeAudit = connection.setSavepoint();
        try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                "INSERT INTO shipment_audit (shipment_id, event_code) VALUES (?, ?)")) {
            statement.setLong(1, shipmentId);
            statement.setString(2, "REVIEW-47");
            if (statement.executeUpdate() != 1) throw new SQLException("Audit row not inserted");
        } catch (SQLException failure) {
            try { connection.rollback(beforeAudit); }
            catch (SQLException rollbackFailure) { failure.addSuppressed(rollbackFailure); }
            throw failure;
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Creating and rolling back a savepoint involve driver and database round trips or local transaction bookkeeping. The Java method retains O(1) application state. Database undo work depends on changes after the savepoint; it is not free merely because the Java code is short.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not create a savepoint while auto-commit is enabled.
  • Do not treat a rollback-to-savepoint failure as permission to commit.
  • Do not assume every driver or managed transaction supports savepoints.

title: Java JDBC setNull: bind a nullable column with its SQL type
summary: PreparedStatement.setNull binds SQL NULL with a specified SQL type. A nullable parameter should follow the column's type contract instead of relying on a driver to infer one from a Java null.
body:
PreparedStatement.setNull binds SQL NULL with a specified SQL type. A nullable parameter should follow the column's type contract instead of relying on a driver to infer one from a Java null.

Operational contract

The method updates a nullable VARCHAR courier note by shipment ID. It uses setNull with Types.VARCHAR when the note is absent and setString otherwise. It rejects a note longer than 47 characters before contacting the database, then requires exactly one updated row. The database schema may impose a different length or character rule, so this application cap must be aligned with migration policy. SQL NULL is not the same as an empty string. The connection and transaction remain owned by the caller.

Failure case

A carrier clears the note for shipment 82. Passing null to setString may be handled by a driver, but this code states the SQL type explicitly. A zero-row update signals an unknown shipment rather than reporting success, and a two-row update signals a broken uniqueness assumption.

Java code

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Types;

public class CourierNoteUpdate {
    public static void apply(Connection connection, long shipmentId, String note)
            throws SQLException {
        if (note != null && note.length() > 47)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Courier note exceeds 47 characters");
        try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                "UPDATE shipments SET courier_note = ? WHERE shipment_id = ?")) {
            if (note == null) statement.setNull(1, Types.VARCHAR);
            else statement.setString(1, note);
            statement.setLong(2, shipmentId);
            if (statement.executeUpdate() != 1)
                throw new SQLException("Expected one shipment update");
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Parameter binding is O(L) or driver-dependent for a note of length L; this code holds at most 47 Java UTF-16 code units. Database update cost depends on indexing, locks, and transaction work. The method allocates no result collection.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not equate SQL NULL with an empty string.
  • Do not ignore a zero-row or multi-row update when one row is required.
  • Do not assume a Java string-length cap exactly matches database byte or character semantics.

title: Java JDBC query timeout: bound a statement without claiming a whole-request deadline
summary: Statement.setQueryTimeout asks the driver to limit execution time for that statement in seconds. It is not a complete deadline for connection acquisition, network stalls, or all work in a request.
body:
Statement.setQueryTimeout asks the driver to limit execution time for that statement in seconds. It is not a complete deadline for connection acquisition, network stalls, or all work in a request.

Operational contract

This method sets a three-second query timeout before executing a parameterized lookup. It closes the ResultSet and PreparedStatement in one scope, returns at most one status value, and rejects a second matching row. A driver may attempt to cancel a timed-out statement and report SQLTimeoutException; cancellation and server behavior are driver-dependent. A connection-pool acquisition timeout and Connection.setNetworkTimeout govern different waiting phases. Never assume this setter interrupts every JDBC call at exactly three seconds.

Failure case

A shipment-status query waits on a database lock. The statement timeout may terminate the query and surface an exception; the outer request must still decide whether to retry. A request that spent five seconds waiting for a pool connection before creating the statement was never protected by this three-second setting.

Java code

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;

public class TimedShipmentLookup {
    public static String status(Connection connection, long shipmentId) throws SQLException {
        try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                "SELECT status FROM shipments WHERE shipment_id = ?")) {
            statement.setQueryTimeout(3);
            statement.setLong(1, shipmentId);
            try (ResultSet rows = statement.executeQuery()) {
                if (!rows.next()) return null;
                String status = rows.getString(1);
                if (rows.next()) throw new SQLException("Duplicate shipment ID");
                return status;
            }
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The Java cursor retains O(1) application data, while indexed lookup and lock wait determine database cost. The timeout limits one driver operation according to its implementation; it does not cap total request wall time or establish idempotent retry semantics.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not count pool wait or connection setup inside a statement timeout.
  • Do not assume timed-out SQL had no side effect without checking transaction state.
  • Do not leave result sets open after timeout or error.

title: Java JDBC ResultSet binary streams: read before advancing the cursor
summary: ResultSet.getBinaryStream exposes a column stream tied to the current row and statement lifetime. Its bytes must be consumed before another column getter or cursor advance can close or invalidate that stream.
body:
ResultSet.getBinaryStream exposes a column stream tied to the current row and statement lifetime. Its bytes must be consumed before another column getter or cursor advance can close or invalidate that stream.

Operational contract

The sample selects one document column, reads at most 47,000 bytes in 8,192-byte chunks, and closes the stream before advancing the cursor. It distinguishes no row by throwing and SQL NULL by returning null. A length cap protects application memory, but a driver can still have its own buffering and database transfer behavior. The caller owns the Connection; the method owns its PreparedStatement, ResultSet, and returned InputStream. A second row is treated as a uniqueness violation after the first stream is closed.

Failure case

A receipt document is 47,001 bytes. The read fails at the cap instead of returning a truncated document. If the method called rows.next() before consuming the stream, a driver could close it and produce an incomplete result or an exception.

Java code

import java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.InputStream;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;

public class BoundedReceiptDocumentRead {
    public static byte[] read(Connection connection, long receiptId)
            throws SQLException, IOException {
        try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                "SELECT document_bytes FROM receipts WHERE receipt_id = ?")) {
            statement.setLong(1, receiptId);
            try (ResultSet rows = statement.executeQuery()) {
                if (!rows.next()) throw new SQLException("Receipt not found");
                InputStream column = rows.getBinaryStream(1);
                if (column == null) {
                    if (rows.next()) throw new SQLException("Duplicate receipt ID");
                    return null;
                }
                ByteArrayOutputStream output = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
                try (InputStream input = column) {
                    byte[] chunk = new byte[8_192];
                    int count;
                    while ((count = input.read(chunk)) != -1) {
                        if (count > 47_000 - output.size())
                            throw new IOException("Receipt document exceeds cap");
                        output.write(chunk, 0, count);
                    }
                }
                if (rows.next()) throw new SQLException("Duplicate receipt ID");
                return output.toByteArray();
            }
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Reading B returned bytes takes O(B) time and O(B) output memory, capped at 47,000 plus the chunk buffer. The byte-array return may allocate one more O(B) copy. Database and driver buffering are additional costs not controlled by this application cap.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not advance the ResultSet before finishing a column stream.
  • Do not treat SQL NULL as an empty binary value.
  • Do not return a truncated prefix after the size cap is crossed.

title: Java JDBC read-only mode: use the hint without treating it as authorization
summary: Connection.setReadOnly is a hint to the driver and database for read-oriented work. It is not an access-control mechanism and must be set outside an active transaction.
body:
Connection.setReadOnly is a hint to the driver and database for read-oriented work. It is not an access-control mechanism and must be set outside an active transaction.

Operational contract

The method requires an auto-commit connection at entry, saves its previous read-only flag, enables the hint, performs a bounded one-row lookup, then restores the flag when its scope closes. The caller still owns the connection. A pooled connection must not leak a read-only setting into the next borrower. If both lookup and reset fail, try-with-resources preserves the lookup error and suppresses the reset error; production pool code should discard a connection it cannot reset. Database credentials, SQL privileges, and service authorization determine whether writes are allowed.

Failure case

A reporting service reads depot 47 through a pooled connection. The hint may help a driver choose a route or plan. When the method returns, the next borrower must not unexpectedly inherit the hint. A malicious caller does not gain or lose write permission merely because this flag changed.

Java code

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;

public class ReadOnlyDepotLookup {
    private static final class ReadOnlyScope implements AutoCloseable {
        private final Connection connection;
        private final boolean previous;

        private ReadOnlyScope(Connection connection) throws SQLException {
            if (!connection.getAutoCommit())
                throw new IllegalStateException("Active transaction policy");
            this.connection = connection;
            this.previous = connection.isReadOnly();
            connection.setReadOnly(true);
        }

        @Override public void close() throws SQLException {
            connection.setReadOnly(previous);
        }
    }

    public static String name(Connection connection, long depotId) throws SQLException {
        try (ReadOnlyScope scope = new ReadOnlyScope(connection);
             PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                "SELECT depot_name FROM depots WHERE depot_id = ?")) {
            statement.setLong(1, depotId);
            try (ResultSet rows = statement.executeQuery()) {
                if (!rows.next()) return null;
                String depotName = rows.getString(1);
                if (rows.next()) throw new SQLException("Duplicate depot ID");
                return depotName;
            }
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The flag changes may involve driver or database calls; the lookup's indexed and lock behavior dominates work. The Java method holds O(1) data. Scope closure restores ordinary paths, but a broken connection after a network failure must be handled by the connection owner or pool.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat setReadOnly as a security permission.
  • Do not toggle it inside a transaction.
  • Do not return a connection with uncertain reset state to a pool.

title: Java SQLWarning: inspect nonfatal database diagnostics before reuse
summary: SQLWarning objects can be chained to a Connection, Statement, or ResultSet after an operation that did not throw. A successful call may still carry a diagnostic the application should record or reject.
body:
SQLWarning objects can be chained to a Connection, Statement, or ResultSet after an operation that did not throw. A successful call may still carry a diagnostic the application should record or reject.

Operational contract

This helper reads a Statement's warning chain while the statement remains open, collects at most 47 SQLState values, and returns an immutable list. It uses getNextWarning rather than a generic next-exception traversal. Warnings vary by driver and database; a missing warning does not prove that no truncation or conversion occurred. The caller decides whether a given SQLState is tolerable and clears or closes the statement before reuse according to its lifecycle. The method does not log message text, which can contain data the application should not expose.

Failure case

A bulk import executes without SQLException but a driver reports a data-conversion warning. The import inspects the SQLState before considering the operation accepted. Reusing the same Statement and reading warnings later could mix or clear diagnostics from different operations.

Java code

import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.SQLWarning;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class StatementWarningStates {
    public static List<String> inspect(Statement statement) throws SQLException {
        List<String> states = new ArrayList<>();
        for (SQLWarning warning = statement.getWarnings(); warning != null;
                warning = warning.getNextWarning()) {
            if (states.size() == 47) throw new SQLException("Too many SQL warnings");
            states.add(warning.getSQLState() == null ? "UNKNOWN" : warning.getSQLState());
        }
        return List.copyOf(states);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Traversing W warnings costs O(W) time and O(W) list memory, capped at 47. Fetching warning metadata may invoke a driver call. This is diagnostic work, not an alternative to checking update counts or result values.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume no SQLException means no warning.
  • Do not inspect a closed Statement or wait until after unrelated reuse.
  • Do not treat every warning as the same failure class without a policy.

title: Java DatabaseMetaData: check features before depending on them
summary: DatabaseMetaData reports capabilities of a particular JDBC connection. A feature needed by an algorithm should be checked against the deployed driver and database, then verified in integration tests.
body:
DatabaseMetaData reports capabilities of a particular JDBC connection. A feature needed by an algorithm should be checked against the deployed driver and database, then verified in integration tests.

Operational contract

The helper checks savepoint support and whether cursors can be closed at commit. It raises SQLFeatureNotSupportedException when either required feature is unavailable. The result describes this connection's reported capabilities; it is not proof that every edge case works on every server version. Run capability checks when a pool or data source is configured rather than on every request. Changes of driver, connection settings, or database version can alter behavior, so keep a real integration test for each required feature.

Failure case

A shipment workflow requires partial rollback. It fails at startup if the target driver reports no savepoints, rather than reaching the first production conflict and discovering the feature is absent. A separate test still verifies rollback semantics against that database.

Java code

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DatabaseMetaData;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.SQLFeatureNotSupportedException;

public class JdbcFeatureGate {
    public static void requireWorkflowFeatures(Connection connection) throws SQLException {
        DatabaseMetaData metadata = connection.getMetaData();
        if (!metadata.supportsSavepoints())
            throw new SQLFeatureNotSupportedException("Savepoints required");
        if (!metadata.supportsResultSetHoldability(ResultSet.CLOSE_CURSORS_AT_COMMIT))
            throw new SQLFeatureNotSupportedException("Close-at-commit cursors required");
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Metadata calls can perform driver or database work and should usually be paid once per configured data source, not once per row. The method retains O(1) Java state. Its result is a compatibility gate, not a substitute for database-backed tests.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume every JDBC driver implements optional features.
  • Do not use a metadata flag as proof of correct deployment semantics without tests.
  • Do not query metadata in a tight per-row loop.

title: Java JDBC cursor holdability: choose what commit does to a ResultSet
summary: ResultSet holdability specifies whether a cursor remains open or closes when its transaction commits. Code that reads rows should make its commit boundary explicit.
body:
ResultSet holdability specifies whether a cursor remains open or closes when its transaction commits. Code that reads rows should make its commit boundary explicit.

Operational contract

The sample requests CLOSE_CURSORS_AT_COMMIT, then consumes up to 47 rows before the caller can commit. It does not commit inside the method. Driver support should be checked through DatabaseMetaData and exercised in a database integration test; some drivers may reject the requested combination of type, concurrency, and holdability. A close-at-commit cursor is not a memory limit, so the method also caps returned IDs. The caller owns the Connection and transaction, while this method closes the statement and cursor.

Failure case

An export starts reading receipt IDs and another layer commits the same connection halfway through iteration. With close-at-commit policy, the cursor can close, making the remaining read invalid. This method returns a bounded list before the caller reaches its commit point.

Java code

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class ReceiptCursorBeforeCommit {
    public static List<Long> ids(Connection connection, long depotId) throws SQLException {
        try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                "SELECT receipt_id FROM receipts WHERE depot_id = ? ORDER BY receipt_id",
                ResultSet.TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY, ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY,
                ResultSet.CLOSE_CURSORS_AT_COMMIT)) {
            statement.setLong(1, depotId);
            List<Long> result = new ArrayList<>();
            try (ResultSet rows = statement.executeQuery()) {
                while (rows.next()) {
                    if (result.size() == 47) throw new SQLException("Too many receipts");
                    result.add(rows.getLong(1));
                }
            }
            return List.copyOf(result);
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Reading R rows is O(R) application time and O(R) result storage, capped at 47. Query execution, sorting, cursor buffering, and database I/O have additional costs. Holdability controls cursor lifetime at commit, not the number of rows a query can produce.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not commit a transaction while still depending on a close-at-commit cursor.
  • Do not assume requested holdability is supported on every driver.
  • Do not treat cursor holdability as a row or memory cap.

Connected lessons

  • Java DatabaseMetaData: check features before depending on them

title: Java SQLException chains: preserve SQLState and linked failures
summary: SQLException can carry an SQLState, vendor error code, cause, and linked next exceptions. A diagnostic boundary should retain machine-readable fields without depending on message text.
body:
SQLException can carry an SQLState, vendor error code, cause, and linked next exceptions. A diagnostic boundary should retain machine-readable fields without depending on message text.

Operational contract

The method walks at most 47 linked SQLException objects and returns their SQLState and vendor code as immutable entries. It uses getNextException, which is distinct from the normal cause chain. SQLState can be null, so this sample emits UNKNOWN. A service should classify known states under its database policy and preserve the original exception for logging or propagation; collapsing everything to a message string loses useful detail. Do not expose vendor messages directly to clients because they can reveal SQL or data values.

Failure case

A batched write fails and the driver links a primary transaction error to a detailed constraint failure. Recording only the first message loses the later SQLState. This helper retains both codes for an internal decision, while the caller still handles rollback and request response.

Java code

import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class SqlFailureCodes {
    public record Code(String state, int vendorCode) { }

    public static List<Code> inspect(SQLException failure) {
        List<Code> codes = new ArrayList<>();
        for (SQLException current = failure; current != null;
                current = current.getNextException()) {
            if (codes.size() == 47) throw new IllegalStateException("Exception chain exceeds cap");
            String state = current.getSQLState();
            codes.add(new Code(state == null ? "UNKNOWN" : state, current.getErrorCode()));
        }
        return List.copyOf(codes);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Walking E linked exceptions costs O(E) time and O(E) result storage, capped at 47. It does not query the database. A chain cap prevents pathological diagnostic traversal from monopolizing error handling.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not discard next exceptions when diagnosing a batch failure.
  • Do not assume SQLState is always non-null or portable across vendors.
  • Do not send raw database exception messages to external clients.

title: Java JDBC binary parameters: cap bytes before binding a BLOB
summary: PreparedStatement.setBytes binds one byte array as a binary parameter. The application should bound that array before database I/O and keep the connection's transaction owner clear.
body:
PreparedStatement.setBytes binds one byte array as a binary parameter. The application should bound that array before database I/O and keep the connection's transaction owner clear.

Operational contract

The method accepts a complete byte array no larger than 47,000 bytes, binds it to an INSERT, and requires one inserted row. The caller owns the array and Connection; this method does not mutate the array or commit. A driver may copy or buffer bytes internally, so the application cap does not describe total database-side memory. Do not share and mutate the array concurrently while executeUpdate is using it. For larger data, a stream API with explicit length, lifetime, and expanded-size policy is needed. A BLOB column and database limit must agree with this service cap.

Failure case

An intake receives 47,001 receipt bytes. The Java method rejects the payload before preparing a statement. A 47,000-byte payload can be bound, but database constraints may still reject it; the caller handles that SQLException and transaction rollback.

Java code

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.Objects;

public class BoundedReceiptBlobInsert {
    public static void insert(Connection connection, long receiptId, byte[] document)
            throws SQLException {
        Objects.requireNonNull(document);
        if (document.length > 47_000)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Receipt document exceeds cap");
        try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                "INSERT INTO receipt_documents (receipt_id, document_bytes) VALUES (?, ?)")) {
            statement.setLong(1, receiptId);
            statement.setBytes(2, document);
            if (statement.executeUpdate() != 1)
                throw new SQLException("Expected one receipt document insert");
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The Java input already occupies O(B) bytes for B <= 47,000; driver buffering can add another O(B) or more. Database insert cost depends on transaction log, storage, and indexes. This bound protects intake memory but is not a total resource budget.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not accept unbounded byte arrays before binding.
  • Do not mutate a bound array from another thread during execution.
  • Do not assume the application byte cap replaces database column limits.

title: Java thenCompose: flatten a dependent asynchronous request
summary: CompletableFuture.thenCompose starts a stage that depends on a prior result and flattens its CompletionStage into one resulting future.
body:
CompletableFuture.thenCompose starts a stage that depends on a prior result and flattens its CompletionStage into one resulting future.

Operational contract

A receipt lookup cannot start until a shipment lookup supplies its identifier. The method accepts both operations as functions so its caller owns transport, timeout, and executor policy. thenApply would return a nested future and make completion ownership harder to reason about. If the first stage fails, the lookup function is not called; if the second fails, the composed stage fails. Neither failure automatically cancels other work.

Failure case

The shipment lookup fails before it has an ID. No receipt lookup runs. If the receipt lookup never completes, the composed future also never completes unless the caller applies a deadline or completes it by another policy.

Java code

import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.function.Function;

public class ShipmentReceiptChain {
    public static CompletableFuture<String> receipt(
            CompletableFuture<Long> shipmentLookup,
            Function<Long, CompletableFuture<String>> receiptLookup) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(shipmentLookup);
        Objects.requireNonNull(receiptLookup);
        return shipmentLookup.thenCompose(receiptLookup);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Registering one dependent stage uses O(1) bookkeeping. End-to-end latency is the first operation followed by the second, so these dependent calls cannot run concurrently. The transport and executor determine the actual work and memory cost.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use thenApply when the callback returns another future and a flat result is required.
  • Do not assume a failed first stage invokes the second request.
  • Do not confuse composition with a deadline or cancellation policy.

title: Java thenCombine: join two independent results without serializing them
summary: CompletableFuture.thenCombine combines the normal results of two stages after both finish; it does not impose an order on independent work.
body:
CompletableFuture.thenCombine combines the normal results of two stages after both finish; it does not impose an order on independent work.

Operational contract

The two futures are supplied by the caller, which can start them concurrently on a controlled executor. This method only combines their results. A failed input makes the dependent result fail, while the other input can still keep running. A null value is rejected explicitly because a missing rate cannot produce a valid quote. If one input never finishes, the combined stage needs a separate deadline policy.

Failure case

The insurance service fails while the base-rate service remains busy. The combined quote cannot succeed, but combining the futures does not cancel the base-rate request or release its resource.

Java code

import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;

public class InsuredShipmentQuote {
    public static CompletableFuture<Long> totalCents(
            CompletableFuture<Long> baseRate,
            CompletableFuture<Long> insuranceRate) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(baseRate);
        Objects.requireNonNull(insuranceRate);
        return baseRate.thenCombine(insuranceRate, (base, insurance) -> {
            if (base == null || insurance == null || base < 0 || insurance < 0)
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Rates must be nonnegative");
            return Math.addExact(base, insurance);
        });
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The combination adds O(1) local time and space. If operations truly start concurrently, latency is near the slower input rather than their sum, plus callback overhead. Each upstream call still consumes its own resources.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not start the second independent request inside a thenCompose callback.
  • Do not assume thenCombine cancels the surviving input after failure.
  • Do not ignore overflow when amounts are stored in integer cents.

title: Java applyToEither: use the first normal result of two stages
summary: CompletableFuture.applyToEither applies a function when either input completes normally. It is a result race, not automatic hedging, timeout, or loser cancellation.
body:
CompletableFuture.applyToEither applies a function when either input completes normally. It is a result race, not automatic hedging, timeout, or loser cancellation.

Operational contract

Two already-started replica lookups can feed this method. It rejects null results in the winning callback, then returns the first normal value that reaches that callback. Exceptional completion rules should be tested for the application's failure combinations; do not assume the other request always rescues an early failure. A service that needs guaranteed first-success behavior across failures should coordinate those results explicitly. Both replica requests can still consume bandwidth after one result is chosen.

Failure case

The east replica responds normally while the west request is still blocked. The returned future can complete from east, but west remains active unless its caller cancels or times it out. An early failure must be handled under an explicit fallback policy rather than presumed harmless.

Java code

import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;

public class ReplicaReceiptRace {
    public static CompletableFuture<String> firstReceipt(
            CompletableFuture<String> eastReplica,
            CompletableFuture<String> westReplica) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(eastReplica);
        Objects.requireNonNull(westReplica);
        return eastReplica.applyToEither(westReplica, receipt ->
                Objects.requireNonNull(receipt, "Replica returned no receipt"));
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The continuation adds O(1) bookkeeping. Starting two requests can nearly double upstream resource use, even when one wins quickly; latency follows completion timing and failure handling, not a fixed bound.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume the losing request is cancelled.
  • Do not describe this stage as a guaranteed first-success fallback for every failure order.
  • Do not launch duplicate writes through a result race without idempotency rules.

title: Java exceptionallyCompose: recover with another asynchronous stage
summary: CompletableFuture.exceptionallyCompose replaces an exceptional outcome with a new CompletionStage, allowing recovery that itself finishes asynchronously.
body:
CompletableFuture.exceptionallyCompose replaces an exceptional outcome with a new CompletionStage, allowing recovery that itself finishes asynchronously.

Operational contract

A primary receipt lookup can fail into a secondary lookup supplied by the caller. The callback may receive a CompletionException wrapper, so classification should inspect causes under a deliberate policy. This sample only retries an unavailable primary; validation failures and cancellation remain failures. The secondary future is created only after failure. Java 17 is the declared baseline for this lesson, and the method is available there. A fallback also needs its own deadline and resource budget.

Failure case

A primary read fails with a transient depot-unavailable exception. The backup read begins. If the primary fails because the receipt ID is malformed, the original failure is preserved instead of issuing a pointless backup request.

Java code

import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

public class ReceiptReplicaFallback {
    public static class DepotUnavailable extends RuntimeException {
        public DepotUnavailable(String message) { super(message); }
    }

    public static CompletableFuture<String> recover(
            CompletableFuture<String> primary,
            Supplier<CompletableFuture<String>> backup) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(primary);
        Objects.requireNonNull(backup);
        return primary.exceptionallyCompose(failure -> {
            Throwable cause = failure instanceof CompletionException && failure.getCause() != null
                    ? failure.getCause() : failure;
            if (!(cause instanceof DepotUnavailable))
                return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(cause);
            return Objects.requireNonNull(backup.get(), "Backup stage missing");
        });
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Successful primary requests pay O(1) stage bookkeeping and no backup work. A qualifying failure incurs the secondary request's full latency and resource cost. A fallback that fans out repeatedly can amplify load during an outage.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not route cancellation or invalid input to a backup automatically.
  • Do not forget that a backup stage can fail or never complete.
  • Do not implement unbounded recursive recovery during an outage.

title: Java CompletableFuture join versus get: preserve failure and interruption contracts
summary: CompletableFuture.join waits and reports failure through unchecked CompletionException; get waits and reports failure through checked ExecutionException, and its wait is interruptible.
body:
CompletableFuture.join waits and reports failure through unchecked CompletionException; get waits and reports failure through checked ExecutionException, and its wait is interruptible.

Operational contract

A blocking boundary must choose which exception and interruption contract it promises. The helper using get restores the thread's interrupt flag and rethrows InterruptedException, leaving higher layers able to stop the request. It unwraps ExecutionException once for diagnostics but preserves that checked exception. The join helper unwraps CompletionException for its caller; direct cancellation may throw CancellationException. Neither method imposes a deadline unless a timed get or another deadline is used.

Failure case

A server thread is interrupted during a receipt wait. The get-based path exits and preserves the interrupt signal. Calling join at the same boundary would not give the same checked interruption path.

Java code

import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException;

public class ReceiptWaitBoundary {
    public static String interruptible(CompletableFuture<String> receipt)
            throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
        Objects.requireNonNull(receipt);
        try { return receipt.get(); }
        catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            throw interrupted;
        }
    }

    public static String unchecked(CompletableFuture<String> receipt) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(receipt);
        return receipt.join();
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Both methods take O(1) application memory while waiting, but each blocks one caller thread until completion. Waiting time is unbounded without a separate deadline; the distinction is failure and interruption behavior, not computational complexity.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not swallow InterruptedException or clear its signal without a policy.
  • Do not treat join as a nonblocking observation method.
  • Do not log only a wrapper type and lose the underlying cause.

title: Java CompletableFuture cancellation: distinguish result status from worker interruption
summary: CompletableFuture.cancel completes an unfinished future with CancellationException; it does not control the computation that might have produced that future.
body:
CompletableFuture.cancel completes an unfinished future with CancellationException; it does not control the computation that might have produced that future.

Operational contract

The method cancels a future handed to it and reports whether this call changed its state. The mayInterruptIfRunning argument has no effect for CompletableFuture itself. A producer that owns an HTTP request, thread, or database statement needs a separate cancellation hook. Unfinished dependent stages become exceptional. Calling cancel on an already completed future does not retract its result, and canceling one stage is not a general cascade to every upstream operation.

Failure case

A caller times out a receipt request and cancels its result future. A network operation started elsewhere can still complete and consume a connection. Its owner must close or cancel that operation under a separate resource policy.

Java code

import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;

public class ReceiptCancellationBoundary {
    public static boolean abandonResult(CompletableFuture<String> receipt) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(receipt);
        return receipt.cancel(true);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Cancellation changes O(1) future state, plus completion work for dependent stages. It saves no predictable CPU or I/O by itself because producer interruption and resource cleanup are outside this future's control.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume cancel(true) interrupts the producer of a CompletableFuture.
  • Do not equate an abandoned result with released sockets or database resources.
  • Do not rely on cancellation to undo side effects.
