title: Java ExecutorService invokeAll: wait for a bounded batch with a deadline
summary: ExecutorService.invokeAll submits a collection of Callables and returns one Future per input after completion or a specified timeout, canceling unfinished tasks on return.
body:
ExecutorService.invokeAll submits a collection of Callables and returns one Future per input after completion or a specified timeout, canceling unfinished tasks on return.

Operational contract

This method limits the batch to 47 receipt tasks and waits up to three seconds. It keeps result positions aligned with task positions; cancelled tasks are reported as missing, while a task that failed raises ExecutionException to its caller. Timeout cancellation is an interrupt request, not proof that a blocked I/O operation stopped. The executor remains caller-owned and must be shut down by its owner. The deadline is for invokeAll, not for work done before constructing the task list.

Failure case

Forty-seven receipt checks are submitted. Three remain unfinished at the deadline and their futures are cancelled. Completed results retain input order even if task finish order differed.

Java code

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.Callable;
import java.util.concurrent.CancellationException;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class ReceiptBatchDeadline {
    public static List<String> collect(ExecutorService executor,
            List<Callable<String>> lookups) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
        Objects.requireNonNull(executor);
        Objects.requireNonNull(lookups);
        if (lookups.size() > 47) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Batch exceeds 47");
        List<Future<String>> results = executor.invokeAll(lookups, 3, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        List<String> receipts = new ArrayList<>(results.size());
        for (Future<String> result : results) {
            try { receipts.add(result.get()); }
            catch (CancellationException timedOut) { receipts.add(null); }
        }
        return receipts;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

For N tasks, collecting futures and results costs O(N) application time and memory, with N capped at 47. Pool size and task duration determine execution time. The waiting phase is bounded by the invokeAll timeout, but cancellation cleanup may continue afterward.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume returned futures are in completion order.
  • Do not interpret cancel as guaranteed I/O termination.
  • Do not submit an unbounded collection or forget who shuts down the executor.

title: Java ExecutorService invokeAny: return one successful result from competing tasks
summary: ExecutorService.invokeAny returns one successfully completed Callable result and cancels unfinished tasks when it returns.
body:
ExecutorService.invokeAny returns one successfully completed Callable result and cancels unfinished tasks when it returns.

Operational contract

A bounded set of replica lookups can race under a three-second deadline. Failure of one Callable does not prevent another from succeeding. If all fail, invokeAny raises ExecutionException; if no success arrives before the deadline, it raises TimeoutException. The caller owns the executor and its queue limits. Cancellation of losers requests interruption but does not guarantee their network or database work stopped. Use only for safe duplicate reads or operations with explicit idempotency.

Failure case

The east receipt replica throws, and the west replica returns a record. invokeAny returns west's value. If both throw, it raises an error instead of returning null, and unfinished tasks receive cancellation requests.

Java code

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.Callable;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException;

public class ReceiptReplicaSelection {
    public static String read(ExecutorService executor,
            List<Callable<String>> replicaReads)
            throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException, TimeoutException {
        Objects.requireNonNull(executor);
        Objects.requireNonNull(replicaReads);
        if (replicaReads.isEmpty() || replicaReads.size() > 3)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Expected one to three replicas");
        return executor.invokeAny(replicaReads, 3, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Submitting R calls uses O(R) queue and task bookkeeping, with R capped at three. Concurrent reads may reduce latency but multiply backend load. The timeout bounds waiting for a successful result, not guaranteed completion of cancelled loser cleanup.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not confuse the first finished task with the first successful task.
  • Do not use competing non-idempotent writes as replicas.
  • Do not assume a timeout means every backend task has stopped.

title: Java reflection: separate an invoked method failure from lookup failure
summary: Method.invoke wraps an exception thrown by the invoked method in InvocationTargetException. Lookup and access failures remain separate reflective failures.
body:
Method.invoke wraps an exception thrown by the invoked method in InvocationTargetException. Lookup and access failures remain separate reflective failures.

Operational contract

The method looks up one fixed public operation and propagates the policy's RuntimeException as the policy failure. It leaves checked target failures wrapped, so the caller can inspect the cause without silently changing its checked-exception contract. The target class and method must be accessible under Java language and module rules. A string supplied by an untrusted caller should not select arbitrary methods. Cache a Method when the same fixed operation runs repeatedly, while still checking target compatibility.

Failure case

A shipment policy throws IllegalStateException while evaluating shipment 47. That is a policy failure, not NoSuchMethodException. Reporting only InvocationTargetException hides the meaningful cause; treating every reflective exception as retryable can repeat a rejected shipment.

Java code

import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException;
import java.lang.reflect.Method;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ShipmentPolicyInvocation {
    public static String evaluate(Object policy, long shipmentId)
            throws ReflectiveOperationException {
        Objects.requireNonNull(policy);
        Method method = policy.getClass().getMethod("evaluate", long.class);
        try {
            return (String) method.invoke(policy, shipmentId);
        } catch (InvocationTargetException failure) {
            Throwable target = failure.getCause();
            if (target instanceof RuntimeException runtime) throw runtime;
            throw failure;
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Looking up and invoking a method takes O(1) application space and adds reflective dispatch and boxing overhead to the policy's own work. Repeated lookup can be cached, but the cache must be scoped to class identity and class-loader lifetime.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not classify a target exception as a missing method or access failure.
  • Do not let arbitrary user input name a method to invoke.
  • Do not ignore that Method.invoke returns Object and may require a checked cast.

title: Java getMethod: resolve an overload by its exact parameter types
summary: Class.getMethod selects a public method by name and exact parameter-type array. It does not search for the overload that would be chosen by a normal source-code call.
body:
Class.getMethod selects a public method by name and exact parameter-type array. It does not search for the overload that would be chosen by a normal source-code call.

Operational contract

The lookup specifies long and int primitives, then invokes a single rate method. A Long.class parameter is not long.class. Method.invoke may box arguments during invocation, but that conversion does not change the method selected during lookup. If the requested signature is absent, NoSuchMethodException signals a contract mismatch; selecting the first method with the right name can silently call a different overload. The sample checks the result type before unboxing it.

Failure case

A pricing plugin adds rate(Long, int) beside rate(long, int). Looking up Long.class when the integration contract calls for long.class fails instead of silently choosing a different policy.

Java code

import java.lang.reflect.Method;
import java.util.Objects;

public class DepotRateLookup {
    public static long cents(Object rateTable, long depotId, int parcelCount)
            throws ReflectiveOperationException {
        Objects.requireNonNull(rateTable);
        Method rate = rateTable.getClass().getMethod("rate", long.class, int.class);
        Object result = rate.invoke(rateTable, depotId, parcelCount);
        if (!(result instanceof Long cents) || cents < 0)
            throw new IllegalStateException("Rate must be nonnegative long cents");
        return cents;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Signature lookup and invocation add reflective overhead and O(1) application storage. For a fixed plugin API, validate and cache the selected Method at registration instead of scanning overloads on each request.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not substitute Long.class for long.class in an exact lookup.
  • Do not pick an overload by name alone.
  • Do not assume a reflected result has the required type or valid business range.

title: Java trySetAccessible: handle a denied deep-reflection request
summary: AccessibleObject.trySetAccessible attempts to suppress language access checks and returns false when access cannot be enabled under module boundaries.
body:
AccessibleObject.trySetAccessible attempts to suppress language access checks and returns false when access cannot be enabled under module boundaries.

Operational contract

The sample reflects a fixed private auditCode method on an application-owned object. It refuses to invoke when the declaring module does not allow deep reflection to the caller. This operation is appropriate only for a deliberate integration contract; public APIs are preferable. An exported package does not necessarily permit access to private members. If the target belongs to another named module, its package normally needs an opens directive to the caller's module. A failed request must not be worked around by silently depending on runtime flags.

Failure case

A plugin updates to a named module and stops opening its internal package. The check rejects the integration clearly rather than assuming setAccessible can override the module boundary.

Java code

import java.lang.reflect.Method;
import java.util.Objects;

public class AuditCodeAccess {
    public static String read(Object auditRecord) throws ReflectiveOperationException {
        Objects.requireNonNull(auditRecord);
        Method method = auditRecord.getClass().getDeclaredMethod("auditCode");
        if (!method.canAccess(auditRecord) && !method.trySetAccessible())
            throw new IllegalStateException("Audit package is not open to this module");
        return (String) method.invoke(auditRecord);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Method lookup, access check, and invocation add O(1) application space with reflective overhead. Reflection does not make module encapsulation free; configuration and compatibility testing are part of this integration cost.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume exports also opens private members.
  • Do not ignore a false trySetAccessible result.
  • Do not call deep reflection on arbitrary classes supplied by untrusted input.

title: Java dynamic proxies: define Object-method behavior explicitly
summary: A java.lang.reflect.Proxy routes interface calls through an InvocationHandler, including equals, hashCode, and toString declared by Object.
body:
A java.lang.reflect.Proxy routes interface calls through an InvocationHandler, including equals, hashCode, and toString declared by Object.

Operational contract

The adapter counts receipt reads and delegates the business call. It implements identity-based equals and hashCode for the proxy itself, and a fixed diagnostic toString. That avoids accidentally forwarding Object calls to an unrelated delegate, recursing through the proxy, or returning a value with the wrong type. A dynamic proxy only implements interfaces; a concrete class cannot be proxied this way. The method handler runs on the caller's thread, so a blocking delegate still blocks that caller.

Failure case

A metrics registry inserts a receipt-reader proxy into a hash map. If hashCode returns null or changes with a read count, lookup breaks even though the read method works. This adapter preserves stable identity semantics.

Java code

import java.lang.reflect.Proxy;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

public class ReceiptReaderProxy {
    public interface Reader { String read(long receiptId); }

    public static Reader counting(Reader delegate, AtomicLong reads) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(delegate);
        Objects.requireNonNull(reads);
        return (Reader) Proxy.newProxyInstance(
                Reader.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[] { Reader.class },
                (proxy, method, arguments) -> {
                    if (method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) {
                        return switch (method.getName()) {
                            case "equals" -> proxy == arguments[0];
                            case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy);
                            case "toString" -> "ReceiptReaderProxy";
                            default -> throw new UnsupportedOperationException(method.getName());
                        };
                    }
                    if (!method.getName().equals("read"))
                        throw new UnsupportedOperationException(method.getName());
                    reads.incrementAndGet();
                    return delegate.read((long) arguments[0]);
                });
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Each call adds proxy dispatch and an atomic increment before the delegate's work. Storage is O(1) per proxy. A hot call path can make the shared counter contended, so measure it before placing a single counter on every high-volume invocation.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not forget equals, hashCode, and toString can reach the handler.
  • Do not return null for primitive-returning methods such as hashCode.
  • Do not expect Proxy to subclass a concrete class or make a blocking delegate asynchronous.

title: Java ServiceLoader: treat provider discovery as fallible startup work
summary: ServiceLoader locates implementations registered for a service interface. Iteration can fail when provider metadata, construction, or linkage is broken.
body:
ServiceLoader locates implementations registered for a service interface. Iteration can fail when provider metadata, construction, or linkage is broken.

Operational contract

The loader selects one provider during startup and converts ServiceConfigurationError into a clear configuration failure. It does not silently skip a broken provider, because doing so could change the selected receipt codec. The classpath registration file or named-module provides directive belongs in the deployment artifact; a service interface alone does not register implementations. ServiceLoader lazily discovers and instantiates providers, so moving iteration into a request path can turn a packaging problem into a customer-visible failure. If multiple providers are legal, selection needs an explicit stable policy.

Failure case

A deployment lists a provider whose constructor throws. The service fails initialization instead of pretending no codec exists and processing receipts with an unintended fallback.

Java code

import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.ServiceConfigurationError;
import java.util.ServiceLoader;

public class ReceiptCodecDiscovery {
    public interface ReceiptCodec { byte[] encode(String receipt); }

    public static ReceiptCodec requiredProvider() {
        try {
            Iterator<ReceiptCodec> providers = ServiceLoader.load(ReceiptCodec.class).iterator();
            if (!providers.hasNext())
                throw new IllegalStateException("No receipt codec registered");
            ReceiptCodec selected = providers.next();
            if (providers.hasNext())
                throw new IllegalStateException("Multiple receipt codecs registered");
            return selected;
        } catch (ServiceConfigurationError broken) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Receipt codec registration is invalid", broken);
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Discovery scans P registered providers and instantiates at least those visited, costing O(P) startup time and provider-dependent memory; this sample visits enough to reject a second provider. Holding the selected provider afterward makes per-request discovery cost O(0).

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expect an interface declaration to register a provider.
  • Do not swallow ServiceConfigurationError and select a different provider without policy.
  • Do not repeat lazy discovery on every request when providers are deployment configuration.

title: Java Class.forName: inspect an allowlisted class without initializing it
summary: Class.forName(name, false, loader) loads and links a class without requesting its initialization. The three-argument form makes loader and initialization policy explicit.
body:
Class.forName(name, false, loader) loads and links a class without requesting its initialization. The three-argument form makes loader and initialization policy explicit.

Operational contract

The method maps a short trusted key to a fixed receipt implementation name, then verifies that the loaded type implements the expected interface. Using arbitrary user text as a class name could load unrelated types or increase attack surface. The false flag avoids initialization during discovery; constructing an instance or using a static member later can still initialize the class. Linkage errors can occur while loading, and loader identity determines whether a class is assignable to this service interface.

Failure case

A configuration key names the built-in warehouse codec. The service checks its type at startup without constructing it. A key that is not on the allowlist fails before any class lookup.

Java code

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ReceiptCodecTypeGate {
    public interface ReceiptCodec { byte[] encode(String receipt); }
    public static class WarehouseCodec implements ReceiptCodec {
        public byte[] encode(String receipt) {
            return receipt.getBytes(java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        }
    }

    private static final Map<String, String> ALLOWED = Map.of(
            "warehouse", WarehouseCodec.class.getName());

    public static Class<? extends ReceiptCodec> resolve(String configurationKey)
            throws ClassNotFoundException {
        String className = ALLOWED.get(Objects.requireNonNull(configurationKey));
        if (className == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown receipt codec key");
        ClassLoader loader = ReceiptCodecTypeGate.class.getClassLoader();
        return Class.forName(className, false, loader).asSubclass(ReceiptCodec.class);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The allowlist lookup is O(1) average for a fixed small map. Class loading and linking may perform I/O and verification once per loader; class initialization is deferred, not removed. Retaining references to classes can retain their defining loader.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not pass an untrusted class name directly to Class.forName.
  • Do not claim false prevents later static initialization.
  • Do not assume two classes with the same name but different defining loaders are interchangeable.

title: Java modules: distinguish exported APIs from open packages
summary: A named module's exported package supports access to public API types; an open package permits deeper reflection to another module. Module inspection exposes these separate conditions.
body:
A named module's exported package supports access to public API types; an open package permits deeper reflection to another module. Module inspection exposes these separate conditions.

Operational contract

The helper reports whether the provider module exports or opens its class package to a consumer module, and whether the consumer reads the provider. These checks describe module relationships, not whether a particular private member may be invoked; member accessibility, caller context, and lookup mode still matter. Unnamed modules report broad export/open behavior. For a named plugin, declaring exports is not a substitute for opens when a framework needs deep reflection. Code should prefer a public interface if possible and validate module setup at startup.

Failure case

A public receipt interface remains callable after a plugin removes opens. A serializer that reads private fields can fail. The report shows that exported and opened are separate deployment decisions.

Java code

import java.util.Objects;

public class PluginModuleVisibility {
    public record Access(boolean consumerReadsProvider,
                         boolean packageExported, boolean packageOpen) { }

    public static Access inspect(Class<?> providerType, Module consumer) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(providerType);
        Objects.requireNonNull(consumer);
        Module provider = providerType.getModule();
        String packageName = providerType.getPackageName();
        return new Access(consumer.canRead(provider),
                provider.isExported(packageName, consumer),
                provider.isOpen(packageName, consumer));
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The inspection uses O(1) application data and small module-graph lookups. It is a configuration check, not a performance path; run it when a plugin is registered rather than for each receipt.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat exports as permission for private-member reflection.
  • Do not ignore the consumer's readability relationship.
  • Do not interpret a package-level report as proof a particular Method or Field is accessible.

title: Java MethodHandle.invokeExact: make the call-site type part of the contract
summary: MethodHandle.invokeExact requires the call site's argument and return types to match the handle's MethodType exactly; a mismatch raises WrongMethodTypeException.
body:
MethodHandle.invokeExact requires the call site's argument and return types to match the handle's MethodType exactly; a mismatch raises WrongMethodTypeException.

Operational contract

The sample caches a public String.substring handle with receiver String and two int arguments. Its cast to String establishes the return type of the invokeExact call site. A Long argument in place of int, or discarding the return value, changes the call-site type and fails; invoke is the adapting form when conversions are deliberate. The handle is resolved once and its lookup obeys access rules. Index validation belongs to the business boundary, not to MethodHandle, so this method checks the requested slice first.

Failure case

A receipt code is sliced from index 8 to 10. The result is 47. A refactor that changes one index to long without changing the handle type fails at the exact invocation boundary rather than silently choosing a different overload.

Java code

import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle;
import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles;
import java.lang.invoke.MethodType;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ReceiptCodeSlice {
    private static final MethodHandle SLICE = findSlice();

    private static MethodHandle findSlice() {
        try {
            return MethodHandles.publicLookup().findVirtual(String.class,
                    "substring", MethodType.methodType(String.class, int.class, int.class));
        } catch (ReflectiveOperationException failure) {
            throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(failure);
        }
    }

    public static String read(String receiptCode, int start, int end) throws Throwable {
        Objects.requireNonNull(receiptCode);
        if (start < 0 || end < start || end > receiptCode.length())
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid receipt-code slice");
        return (String) SLICE.invokeExact(receiptCode, start, end);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The cached lookup is paid once per class initialization. Each invocation adds method-handle dispatch and substring's O(L) copy for L selected characters, with O(L) new string storage. Wrong call-site types are contract failures, not a fallback lookup mechanism.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not confuse invokeExact with the adapting invoke call.
  • Do not omit the return cast when it defines the expected call-site type.
  • Do not assume a handle bypasses public-lookup access rules or input range validation.

title: Java BitSet: distinguish logical length, capacity, and set-bit count
summary: BitSet.length returns one beyond the highest set index, cardinality counts true bits, and size reports implementation storage capacity. These values answer different questions.
body:
BitSet.length returns one beyond the highest set index, cardinality counts true bits, and size reports implementation storage capacity. These values answer different questions.

Operational contract

The method reports the highest active receipt slot and total active slots without mistaking allocated capacity for a business identifier. An empty BitSet has length zero, so the highest index is represented as -1. A sparse set with only slot 82 active has cardinality one and length 83. BitSet grows to hold high indexes, which can make a single erroneous ID expensive. Validate identifiers before calling set; BitSet is not synchronized for concurrent mutation.

Failure case

The importer marks slot 82 and then clears it. Its logical length returns to zero even though its backing storage may remain allocated. Using size as the number of processed receipts would report capacity instead of work done.

Java code

import java.util.BitSet;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ActiveReceiptSlots {
    public record Summary(int highestSlot, int activeCount) { }

    public static Summary summarize(BitSet activeSlots) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(activeSlots);
        int logicalLength = activeSlots.length();
        return new Summary(logicalLength == 0 ? -1 : logicalLength - 1,
                activeSlots.cardinality());
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Computing cardinality scans the words used by the bit set, taking O(W) time for W stored machine words; highest-set-bit lookup is tied to that representation. The method adds O(1) result storage. A very high index can enlarge the underlying bit vector far beyond the number of true bits.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use size as the count of true bits.
  • Do not return length as the highest index without subtracting one for a nonempty set.
  • Do not set unvalidated huge indexes in a sparse business ID space.

title: Java BitSet nextSetBit: scan a bounded index range without walking gaps
summary: BitSet.nextSetBit finds the next true bit at or after a starting index, returning -1 when none exists. A bounded scan must still enforce its end index and result cap.
body:
BitSet.nextSetBit finds the next true bit at or after a starting index, returning -1 when none exists. A bounded scan must still enforce its end index and result cap.

Operational contract

The method returns at most 47 receipt slots in a half-open interval. It validates nonnegative ordered bounds, then jumps between set bits rather than testing every possible index. The loop stops before the exclusive upper bound. Because every visited bit is strictly less than an int upper bound, incrementing that bit cannot overflow here. A cap protects output memory and prevents one request from enumerating an enormous set. The input is caller-owned and must not be mutated concurrently without synchronization.

Failure case

Active slots are 3, 47, and 82. A scan of [40, 82) returns only 47. Slot 82 is outside the half-open range even though its bit is set.

Java code

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.BitSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ReceiptSlotWindow {
    public static List<Integer> active(BitSet slots, int fromInclusive, int toExclusive) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(slots);
        if (fromInclusive < 0 || toExclusive < fromInclusive)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid slot range");
        List<Integer> found = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int slot = slots.nextSetBit(fromInclusive);
                slot >= 0 && slot < toExclusive;
                slot = slots.nextSetBit(slot + 1)) {
            if (found.size() == 47) throw new IllegalStateException("Too many active slots");
            found.add(slot);
        }
        return List.copyOf(found);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The scan visits K set bits and searches the underlying words across the requested span, rather than performing one test per missing index. Result memory is O(K) with K capped at 47. The returned immutable list copies its elements once.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not include the exclusive end slot.
  • Do not forget that nextSetBit returns -1 when no later bit exists.
  • Do not scan an unbounded range into an unbounded output list.

title: Java EnumSet complementOf: derive a default-deny capability set
summary: EnumSet.complementOf returns a new set containing enum constants absent from the supplied EnumSet. Its universe is the entire enum type, not just constants known to one caller.
body:
EnumSet.complementOf returns a new set containing enum constants absent from the supplied EnumSet. Its universe is the entire enum type, not just constants known to one caller.

Operational contract

The helper constructs a fresh denied set from an allowed capability set. Adding a new enum constant automatically puts it in denied until the policy explicitly allows it, which is appropriate for this default-deny design. The result is a separate mutable EnumSet; changing allowed later does not update the previous result. If a product instead interprets the complement as granted permissions, a newly introduced constant could become granted accidentally. The allowed set itself still requires an authorization source and review.

Failure case

A release adds ARCHIVE. Existing callers allow only READ and EXPORT. The computed denied set includes ARCHIVE without changing the callers' allowlists.

Java code

import java.util.EnumSet;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ReceiptCapabilityPolicy {
    public enum Capability { READ, EXPORT, DELETE, ARCHIVE }

    public static EnumSet<Capability> denied(EnumSet<Capability> allowed) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(allowed);
        return EnumSet.complementOf(allowed);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Complement construction visits the enum universe and copies a compact bit representation, taking O(E) work in the number of enum constants under a portable cost model and O(E) result bits. The policy computation is small but should not replace explicit authorization checks at the action boundary.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use a complement as granted permissions without reviewing new enum constants.
  • Do not assume the returned set is a live view of allowed.
  • Do not treat enum membership alone as proof that a caller is authorized.

title: Java EnumSet: retain element type when a source collection is empty
summary: EnumSet.copyOf a non-EnumSet collection needs at least one element to infer its enum type; noneOf states the element class explicitly and works for an empty source.
body:
EnumSet.copyOf a non-EnumSet collection needs at least one element to infer its enum type; noneOf states the element class explicitly and works for an empty source.

Operational contract

The helper starts with a typed empty EnumSet, then adds supplied review states. It returns an independent mutable set even when the source is empty. Duplicate states collapse by set semantics, and null elements are rejected. If the API promises an immutable result, wrap or copy it separately; returning EnumSet transfers mutation ownership to the caller. This lesson concerns type inference and collection ownership, not permission policy.

Failure case

An intake has no review flags. Building EnumSet.copyOf from an ordinary empty List throws because the enum type cannot be inferred. The typed empty set returns normally.

Java code

import java.util.Collection;
import java.util.EnumSet;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ReceiptReviewStates {
    public enum State { NEW, CHECKED, HELD, RELEASED }

    public static EnumSet<State> copy(Collection<State> states) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(states);
        EnumSet<State> result = EnumSet.noneOf(State.class);
        result.addAll(states);
        return result;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Copying N source elements costs O(N) time and compact O(E) bit storage for E enum constants. It is a new set, so later mutation of the source does not change the result.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call EnumSet.copyOf on an ordinary empty collection and expect type inference.
  • Do not assume the returned EnumSet is immutable.
  • Do not silently accept null states; EnumSet rejects them.

title: Java NavigableSet subSet: account for a live backed range
summary: NavigableSet.subSet returns a backed view of keys in a specified range. Mutations through either view or source are visible through the other.
body:
NavigableSet.subSet returns a backed view of keys in a specified range. Mutations through either view or source are visible through the other.

Operational contract

The method returns a half-open receipt-ID range. Its caller owns the underlying set and must keep it alive and coordinate any concurrent access; TreeSet itself is not thread-safe. Inserting an out-of-range value through the view throws IllegalArgumentException. If a stable snapshot is needed, copy the view into a new TreeSet under appropriate synchronization. Comparator order defines the meaning of from and to; this sample assumes natural long ordering. The range validates reversed endpoints before construction.

Failure case

A report asks for IDs [40, 80). After the view is created, the owner adds ID 47 to the source set. The view now contains 47. Attempting to add 82 through the view fails as out of range.

Java code

import java.util.NavigableSet;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ReceiptIdRangeView {
    public static NavigableSet<Long> between(NavigableSet<Long> receiptIds,
            long fromInclusive, long toExclusive) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(receiptIds);
        if (toExclusive < fromInclusive)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Reversed receipt range");
        return receiptIds.subSet(fromInclusive, true, toExclusive, false);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Creating the view uses O(1) wrapper state. Tree-based lookup or insertion through it is O(log N) for N stored IDs; iterating K matching IDs is O(K) after locating the start. A stable copy costs O(K) storage and additional insertion work.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat the returned range as a snapshot.
  • Do not insert outside its bounds.
  • Do not mutate an unsynchronized TreeSet concurrently through source and view.

title: Java PriorityBlockingQueue: add an admission limit to an unbounded priority queue
summary: PriorityBlockingQueue orders retrieval by priority but is logically unbounded; its constructor argument is an initial capacity, not a maximum backlog.
body:
PriorityBlockingQueue orders retrieval by priority but is logically unbounded; its constructor argument is an initial capacity, not a maximum backlog.

Operational contract

The wrapper acquires one of 47 permits before offering a job and releases it when a worker takes that job. This bounds jobs waiting in the queue, not jobs already being processed by workers. The queue comparator orders priority descending and receipt ID ascending for a defined tie break. A failed offer releases the permit. The queue remains private so callers cannot bypass the gate with direct insertion or removal. A production service must also cap producer concurrency and define shutdown and task-failure handling.

Failure case

All 47 waiting slots are filled. A new receipt job is rejected immediately even though PriorityBlockingQueue itself would otherwise accept it and grow. A worker take releases one waiting slot.

Java code

import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.PriorityBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;

public class BoundedPriorityReceiptInbox {
    public record Job(int priority, long receiptId) { }
    private final Semaphore waitingSlots = new Semaphore(47);
    private final PriorityBlockingQueue<Job> jobs = new PriorityBlockingQueue<>(47,
            Comparator.comparingInt(Job::priority).reversed()
                    .thenComparingLong(Job::receiptId));

    public boolean submit(Job job) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(job);
        if (!waitingSlots.tryAcquire()) return false;
        boolean added = false;
        try {
            added = jobs.offer(job);
            return added;
        } finally {
            if (!added) waitingSlots.release();
        }
    }

    public Job take() throws InterruptedException {
        Job job = jobs.take();
        waitingSlots.release();
        return job;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Insertion and removal are O(log N) heap operations for N queued jobs, capped here at 47 by the permit gate. The gate uses O(1) extra state. Worker execution and producer tasks are outside this queue bound.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat initial capacity or remainingCapacity as a backlog cap.
  • Do not expose the underlying queue for bypass insertion or removal.
  • Do not forget that priority service can starve low-priority jobs even with bounded storage.

title: Java CopyOnWriteArraySet: publish against a stable listener snapshot
summary: CopyOnWriteArraySet provides snapshot iterators and copies its backing array on writes. It fits small listener registries with frequent reads and infrequent changes.
body:
CopyOnWriteArraySet provides snapshot iterators and copies its backing array on writes. It fits small listener registries with frequent reads and infrequent changes.

Operational contract

A receipt listener added during one publication is absent from that publication's iterator and can participate in the next one. Removing a listener likewise does not retroactively remove it from an iterator already obtained. Duplicate listeners are judged by equals, not object identity. Callbacks run on the publisher's thread; one slow or failing listener can delay or abort later callbacks. The sample leaves callback failure visible so the service can set an explicit isolation policy.

Failure case

A listener registers an audit listener while handling receipt 47. The audit listener does not receive 47 from that in-progress publication, but it can receive receipt 82 afterward.

Java code

import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArraySet;

public class ReceiptListenerRegistry {
    public interface Listener { void received(long receiptId); }
    private final CopyOnWriteArraySet<Listener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArraySet<>();

    public boolean add(Listener listener) {
        return listeners.add(Objects.requireNonNull(listener));
    }

    public boolean remove(Listener listener) {
        return listeners.remove(listener);
    }

    public void publish(long receiptId) {
        for (Listener listener : listeners) listener.received(receiptId);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Publishing to L listeners is O(L) callback dispatch without copying for each read. Adding or removing is O(L) search plus an O(L) array copy on change, with a temporary second array. This is expensive for high-churn large sets.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expect a newly added listener to join an iteration already in progress.
  • Do not treat callbacks as asynchronous or isolated from each other's failures.
  • Do not choose copy-on-write for frequent writes and large registries without measuring allocation.

title: Java LinkedBlockingDeque: bound urgent and normal work in one queue
summary: LinkedBlockingDeque can enforce a fixed capacity while admitting work at either end. offerFirst and offerLast report a full queue without blocking.
body:
LinkedBlockingDeque can enforce a fixed capacity while admitting work at either end. offerFirst and offerLast report a full queue without blocking.

Operational contract

The inbox uses 47 slots. Urgent receipts enter at the front, normal receipts at the back, and workers take from the front. Both admission paths share the same capacity. Repeated urgent arrivals can starve older normal items, so a production scheduler may need fairness or separate reserved capacity. The dequeue operation is interruptible. The wrapper owns the queue and does not expose mutating methods that could circumvent admission policy.

Failure case

There are 47 waiting receipts. Both urgent and normal submission return false rather than growing memory. When a worker takes one, exactly one slot opens for either class.

Java code

import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingDeque;

public class ReceiptWorkDeque {
    private final LinkedBlockingDeque<String> waiting = new LinkedBlockingDeque<>(47);

    public boolean submitUrgent(String receiptId) {
        return waiting.offerFirst(Objects.requireNonNull(receiptId));
    }

    public boolean submitNormal(String receiptId) {
        return waiting.offerLast(Objects.requireNonNull(receiptId));
    }

    public String take() throws InterruptedException {
        return waiting.takeFirst();
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

End insertion and removal are O(1) queue work aside from lock contention or blocking, with O(N) node storage capped at 47. The cap covers waiting items; worker execution and upstream request retention need separate limits.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use the no-argument constructor when a real queue cap is required.
  • Do not ignore false from offerFirst or offerLast.
  • Do not assume urgent-first ordering guarantees fair service for normal work.
